pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: No. NICE does not recommend fibrates for mixed dyslipidaemia or as an add-on to a statin for CVD prevention (no outcome benefit and myopathy risk). Their role is limited to severe hypertriglyceridaemia.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: What are the key contraindications to fibrates?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Severe renal or hepatic impairment, gallbladder disease, and pregnancy/breast-feeding.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: Which fibrate + statin combination is contraindicated, and why? What is done if a statin combination is needed?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Gemfibrozil + any statin is contraindicated due to a high risk of rhabdomyolysis. If a statin combination is needed, use fenofibrate instead, with vigilance for muscle symptoms.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: What are the important side effects of fibrates?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: GI upset, myopathy (risk compounds when combined with a statin), gallstones, a reversible rise in creatinine, and deranged LFTs.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: How do fibrates interact with warfarin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Fibrates enhance the effect of warfarin -> increased bleeding risk -> monitor INR.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: How do high-dose omega-3 fatty acids (e.g. icosapent ethyl, purified EPA) affect lipids?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: High-dose omega-3 lowers triglycerides.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: What is the place of omega-3 fatty acids in lipid management according to NICE?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: NICE does not recommend omega-3 for cardiovascular prevention. Use is confined to severe hypertriglyceridaemia when other measures fail - a niche adjunct, not for routine LDL lowering.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: What are the side effects of high-dose omega-3 fatty acids, and their key interaction?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: GI upset/fishy aftertaste, a slight increase in bleeding time, and a small AF signal at high dose. They add to the bleeding risk of anticoagulants and antiplatelets.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: How do bile acid sequestrants (colestyramine, colesevelam) lower LDL?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: They bind bile acids in the gut and block their reabsorption. The liver then diverts cholesterol to make new bile acids, upregulating LDL receptors and lowering LDL. They are not absorbed systemically.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: What are the uses of bile acid sequestrants?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: LDL lowering in statin-intolerant patients or as an add-on (largely superseded). Their niche is familial hypercholesterolaemia and pregnancy (as they are not systemically absorbed). Also used for cholestatic pruritus and bile-acid diarrhoea.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: What are the side effects of bile acid sequestrants, and why are they poorly tolerated?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: GI effects - bloating, constipation and flatulence - make them poorly tolerated. They can also raise triglycerides.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: Why must other medicines be timed carefully around bile acid sequestrants?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: They impair absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and other drugs, so take other medicines 1 hour before or 4-6 hours after the sequestrant.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does warfarin work at a molecular level, and which clotting factors does it affect?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist -> it blocks the recycling of vitamin K, preventing activation (carboxylation) of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X, plus anticoagulant proteins C and S. This reduces the liver's ability to make functional clotting factors.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why does warfarin take several days to become fully effective rather than working immediately?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It has a slow onset (days). Warfarin does not remove existing circulating clotting factors -> the anticoagulant effect only appears as already-made factors are naturally used up and cannot be replaced. Full effect takes several days.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why can warfarin actually make a patient temporarily MORE prone to clotting when first started?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Warfarin also lowers the natural anticoagulants protein C and S, and protein C falls FIRST (before the clotting factors drop). This creates an early prothrombotic state, which is why bridging cover is needed at initiation.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: A patient is started on warfarin for an acute DVT. Why must you also give heparin/LMWH at the same time?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Because warfarin is initially prothrombotic (protein C falls first) and takes days to work. You bridge with heparin or LMWH to provide immediate anticoagulation, continuing until the INR is therapeutic, then stop the heparin/LMWH.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Name two conditions where warfarin is still preferred over a DOAC.
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Mechanical (prosthetic) heart valves and antiphospholipid syndrome -> DOACs are inferior or contraindicated in these. Warfarin remains the anticoagulant of choice.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: A patient with AF needs anticoagulation but a DOAC is felt unsuitable. Give two reasons warfarin might be chosen instead.
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Severe renal impairment and extremes of body weight -> in these situations DOAC dosing/reliability is uncertain, so warfarin (which is monitored by INR) may be chosen for AF or VTE.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the target INR for a patient anticoagulated with warfarin for AF or VTE?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Target INR 2.5 (range roughly 2-3). This applies to atrial fibrillation and venous thromboembolism.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What INR target is required for a patient with a mechanical mitral valve, and how does it differ from AF?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: A mechanical mitral valve needs a higher target INR of 3.5 (mechanical valves need more intense anticoagulation), compared with 2.5 for AF/VTE.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: A woman on warfarin becomes pregnant. What is the problem and what should she be switched to?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Warfarin is teratogenic -> it can cause warfarin embryopathy. It is contraindicated in pregnancy and she should be switched to LMWH, which does not cross the placenta.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: List the main contraindications/cautions to starting warfarin.
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Pregnancy (teratogenic -> use LMWH), active bleeding or a bleeding disorder, recent haemorrhagic stroke, high falls risk, and severe hepatic impairment.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the most important and common serious adverse effect of warfarin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Bleeding -> this is the major risk, ranging from minor bruising to life-threatening major haemorrhage. It is the main reason for careful INR monitoring.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: A patient develops painful skin necrosis a few days after starting warfarin. Why does this happen and who is at highest risk?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Early warfarin-induced skin necrosis is caused by the initial rapid fall in protein C (a natural anticoagulant) creating transient hypercoagulability. It is worse in patients with underlying protein C or protein S deficiency.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Besides bleeding and skin necrosis, name two other recognised adverse effects of warfarin.
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Warfarin embryopathy (teratogenicity in pregnancy) and purple-toe syndrome.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: A patient stable on warfarin is started on clarithromycin. What happens to the INR and why does it matter?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: The INR rises -> macrolides (like clarithromycin) are among many drugs that increase warfarin's effect, raising bleeding risk. The INR should be rechecked and the warfarin dose may need reducing.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Give several common drugs/substances that RAISE the INR in a patient on warfarin.
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Macrolides, metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, fluconazole, amiodarone, cranberry juice and acute alcohol binges all raise the INR -> increased bleeding risk. In general, many drugs potentiate warfarin, so recheck the INR whenever new drugs are added.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why can ANY broad-spectrum antibiotic raise a patient's INR, even one not classically listed as an interaction?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Broad-spectrum antibiotics kill vitamin-K-producing gut flora -> less vitamin K available -> warfarin's effect is enhanced and the INR rises. Always recheck the INR when a patient on warfarin is given antibiotics.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which drugs LOWER the INR (reduce warfarin's effect), risking clot?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's Wort and chronic (regular) alcohol use all reduce warfarin's effect -> the INR falls, risking under-anticoagulation and thrombosis. Note this contrasts with an acute alcohol binge, which raises INR.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does eating lots of green leafy vegetables affect warfarin control?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Green leafy vegetables are rich in vitamin K -> they oppose warfarin and lower its effect (reducing the INR). Patients should keep their dietary vitamin K intake consistent rather than suddenly changing it.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why should NSAIDs, antiplatelets and SSRIs be used cautiously in a patient on warfarin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They do not necessarily change the INR but cause additive bleeding risk -> NSAIDs and antiplatelets impair platelets/gastric mucosa and SSRIs impair platelet function, all increasing the chance of haemorrhage on top of warfarin.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: A patient on warfarin presents with major life-threatening bleeding. How do you reverse the warfarin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Stop warfarin, give IV vitamin K (e.g. 5 mg) AND prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC, e.g. Beriplex) -> PCC replaces the clotting factors immediately because IV vitamin K alone is too slow.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: An asymptomatic patient on warfarin has an INR >8 with no or minor bleeding. What is the management?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Stop (withhold) warfarin and give oral vitamin K (1-5 mg). Restart warfarin at a lower dose once the INR falls into range.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: A patient on warfarin has an INR of 5-8 with no bleeding. What do you do?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Withhold 1-2 doses of warfarin, then restart at a lower maintenance dose. No vitamin K is needed as there is no bleeding and the INR is only modestly raised.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the essential monitoring for a patient on warfarin, and when should it be done more frequently?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Monitor the INR regularly (target 2.5 for AF/VTE; ~3.5 for mechanical mitral valves). Check it more often after any change in drugs or diet, as these commonly alter warfarin's effect.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How do apixaban and rivaroxaban work as anticoagulants?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They directly inhibit factor Xa (the '-xabans' are direct factor Xa inhibitors). Being oral, fixed-dose and predictable, they need no routine coagulation monitoring.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does dabigatran work, and how does its target differ from apixaban/rivaroxaban?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Dabigatran is a direct thrombin (factor IIa) inhibitor, whereas apixaban and rivaroxaban directly inhibit factor Xa. All are oral DOACs given at fixed dose without routine monitoring.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: For stroke prevention in AF, does NICE recommend a DOAC or warfarin first-line?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: A DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran or edoxaban) is first-line, preferred over warfarin. DOACs are also first-line for VTE treatment.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which score assesses stroke risk in AF, and at what threshold is anticoagulation offered?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: CHA2DS2-VASc. Offer anticoagulation at a score >=2; consider it in men with a score of 1. It guides whether the stroke risk justifies anticoagulation.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which bleeding-risk score does NICE now prefer in AF, and how should the result be used?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: ORBIT (preferred over HAS-BLED). Use it to identify and modify reversible bleeding risk factors — do NOT withhold anticoagulation on the basis of the score alone.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: A patient with a mechanical heart valve needs anticoagulation for AF — can you use a DOAC?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: No. Mechanical heart valves require warfarin; DOACs are contraindicated. The same applies to moderate–severe (rheumatic) mitral stenosis and antiphospholipid syndrome.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Name the situations where a DOAC is contraindicated and warfarin must be used instead.
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Mechanical heart valves, moderate–severe (rheumatic) mitral stenosis, and antiphospholipid syndrome. Other DOAC contraindications include severe renal impairment, active bleeding and pregnancy.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Are DOACs safe in pregnancy?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: No — DOACs are contraindicated in pregnancy. LMWH is the anticoagulant of choice in pregnancy.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the standard apixaban dose for AF, and when is it reduced?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 5 mg BD, reduced to 2.5 mg BD if the patient has >=2 of: age >=80, weight <=60 kg, or creatinine >=133 micromol/L (also reduced if CrCl 15–29).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How is apixaban dosed for treatment of VTE (e.g. DVT/PE)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 10 mg BD for 7 days, then 5 mg BD. No separate LMWH lead-in is needed because there is a built-in higher-dose loading phase.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is important about how rivaroxaban is taken for AF, and the standard dose?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 20 mg once daily taken WITH FOOD (food is needed for adequate absorption at treatment doses), reduced to 15 mg OD if CrCl 15–49.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the standard dabigatran dose for AF, and when is the lower 110 mg BD dose used?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 150 mg BD, reduced to 110 mg BD if age >=80, high bleeding risk, or taking verapamil. Avoid dabigatran if CrCl <30.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Below what creatinine clearance should all DOACs be avoided?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: CrCl <15 — avoid all DOACs. Dabigatran, being ~80% renally cleared, should already be avoided if CrCl <30 (eGFR <30) as it accumulates and causes bleeding.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does DOAC bleeding risk compare to warfarin, particularly for the brain?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: DOACs still cause bleeding but produce LESS intracranial haemorrhage than warfarin — a key safety advantage. Rivaroxaban carries a slightly higher risk of GI bleeding.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which DOAC commonly causes dyspepsia/GI upset, and why does it matter?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Dabigatran — dyspepsia/GI upset is its main tolerability issue and a common reason patients stop it or are switched to another DOAC.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: A patient on apixaban or rivaroxaban has life-threatening bleeding — what is the reversal agent?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Andexanet alfa (the specific factor Xa antidote), or prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) if andexanet is unavailable.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: A patient on dabigatran has major bleeding or needs emergency surgery — what reverses it?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Idarucizumab, a specific monoclonal antibody antidote that rapidly reverses dabigatran's anticoagulant effect.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What monitoring do DOACs require if not routine coagulation tests?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: No routine coagulation monitoring, but check renal function at least annually (and before procedures), because dosing and safety depend on renal function — especially for the renally-cleared dabigatran.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Comparing apixaban and rivaroxaban for a patient, what practical points guide the choice?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Apixaban is BD, has the lowest bleeding risk and is better tolerated in mild renal impairment. Rivaroxaban is once daily (more convenient) but MUST be taken with food for absorption.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does starting dabigatran for VTE treatment differ from starting apixaban or rivaroxaban?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Dabigatran (and edoxaban) need at least 5 days of initial LMWH lead-in before switching, as they have no oral loading phase. Apixaban and rivaroxaban are started orally with a built-in higher-dose loading period instead.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does unfractionated heparin (UFH) work at a molecular level, and which clotting factors does it inhibit?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It potentiates antithrombin, which then inactivates BOTH thrombin (factor IIa) AND factor Xa roughly equally. This dual action distinguishes it from LMWH and fondaparinux.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why is IV unfractionated heparin the preferred parenteral anticoagulant when you need tight, minute-to-minute control (e.g. peri-procedure or a high bleeding risk)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It has an immediate onset and a short half-life, so the infusion can be rapidly titrated up or down and, if bleeding occurs, stopped and fully reversed. This makes it highly controllable and reversible.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: A patient with severe chronic kidney disease needs therapeutic anticoagulation. Why is unfractionated heparin often chosen over LMWH here?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: UFH is NOT renally cleared, so it is safe in severe renal failure/CKD. LMWH accumulates when eGFR <30 -> bleeding, so UFH is preferred in that setting.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which laboratory test is used to monitor and titrate an unfractionated heparin infusion?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: The APTT (activated partial thromboplastin time); the infusion is adjusted to keep it in the target range. Anti-Xa levels can be used as an alternative.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: A patient on a heparin infusion has significant bleeding. What agent fully reverses unfractionated heparin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Protamine sulfate, which fully reverses UFH. (In contrast, it only partly reverses LMWH and does not reverse fondaparinux.)

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the key contraindications to unfractionated heparin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Active bleeding, previous heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), severe thrombocytopenia, and recent neurosurgery or haemorrhagic stroke.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why must you be cautious giving heparin around spinal or epidural (neuraxial) anaesthesia?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Anticoagulation during neuraxial procedures risks a spinal/epidural haematoma, which can cause cord compression. Careful timing intervals between the drug and the procedure must be observed.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How do low-molecular-weight heparins (e.g. enoxaparin) differ from UFH in mechanism?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They also potentiate antithrombin, but being smaller they MAINLY inhibit factor Xa with little anti-thrombin (anti-IIa) activity. They are given subcutaneously with a predictable dose-response, so no routine monitoring is needed.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which parenteral anticoagulant is the agent of choice in pregnancy, and why?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: LMWH, because it does not cross the placenta so it is safe for the fetus. It is used for both VTE prophylaxis and treatment in pregnancy.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the prophylactic and the treatment dose of enoxaparin you should recognise?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Prophylaxis: 40 mg once daily SC. Treatment: 1.5 mg/kg once daily SC (or 1 mg/kg twice daily).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why is LMWH avoided in severe renal impairment (eGFR <30), and what is used instead?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: LMWH is renally cleared, so it accumulates -> increased bleeding risk. Use unfractionated heparin instead (or reduce dose and monitor anti-Xa).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: When would you check anti-Xa levels in a patient on LMWH, given it needs no routine monitoring?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: In severe renal impairment, pregnancy, and extremes of body weight, where the predictable dose-response can no longer be assumed.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: If a patient on LMWH bleeds, how effective is protamine sulfate?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Protamine only PARTLY reverses LMWH (around 60%), unlike its full reversal of UFH. This partial reversal is another reason to avoid LMWH when tight reversibility is needed.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: A patient's platelet count falls on day 5-10 of heparin therapy and they develop a new clot. What is the diagnosis and immediate management?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) — an immune reaction that is paradoxically PROTHROMBOTIC despite the low platelets. STOP all heparin immediately and switch to a non-heparin anticoagulant (e.g. argatroban).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Does UFH or LMWH carry the higher risk of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: UFH carries the higher risk; LMWH has a lower (but not zero) risk of HIT. Fondaparinux has negligible HIT risk.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does fondaparinux work, and how does its target differ from UFH?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It is a synthetic pentasaccharide that binds antithrombin to give selective, indirect factor Xa inhibition — pure anti-Xa with no anti-IIa (anti-thrombin) activity. It is given once daily SC and is renally excreted.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the first-line anticoagulant for a patient with medically managed NSTEMI/ACS?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Fondaparinux (2.5 mg OD SC). It is also used for VTE prophylaxis and treatment, and when heparin is contraindicated.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the main safety advantage of fondaparinux over heparins, and its key limitation?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Advantage: negligible HIT risk (it doesn't cross-react). Limitations: it is renally cleared so avoid in eGFR <30, and it is NOT reversed by protamine.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Contrast UFH, LMWH and fondaparinux on target, monitoring and renal handling.
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: UFH: inhibits IIa + Xa, monitored by APTT, protamine-reversible, safe in renal failure. LMWH: mainly Xa, no routine monitoring, accumulates in renal failure. Fondaparinux: pure Xa, no monitoring, negligible HIT risk, renally cleared and not protamine-reversible.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does low-dose aspirin work as an antiplatelet?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It irreversibly inhibits COX-1 in platelets -> blocks thromboxane A2 synthesis -> platelets can no longer aggregate for the rest of their lifespan.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why does a single dose of aspirin affect platelets for about 7-10 days?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Platelets cannot make new COX enzyme, so once aspirin irreversibly inactivates their COX-1 they are disabled for their whole lifespan (~7-10 days). Effect only recovers as new platelets are produced.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the role of aspirin in secondary prevention of coronary/cardiovascular disease?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Lifelong low-dose aspirin 75 mg once daily after MI or in established coronary disease.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Is aspirin first-line for secondary prevention after ischaemic stroke/TIA or in PAD?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: No. Clopidogrel monotherapy is first-line for ischaemic stroke/TIA and PAD; aspirin is used only if clopidogrel is unsuitable.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What aspirin dose is given as a loading dose in ACS or acute ischaemic stroke?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 300 mg (chewed/dispersible) as a loading dose. In ACS it is then continued as part of dual antiplatelet therapy; in acute ischaemic stroke 300 mg is given for 2 weeks then switched to long-term antithrombotic therapy.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: After a minor ischaemic stroke or high-risk TIA, what short-course antiplatelet regimen is used?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Aspirin plus clopidogrel (dual antiplatelet) for 21 days, then clopidogrel alone long-term.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why is aspirin NOT routinely recommended for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: In people without established cardiovascular disease the bleeding risk outweighs the modest reduction in cardiovascular events.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why must aspirin be avoided in children under 16 with a febrile/viral illness?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Risk of Reye's syndrome (encephalopathy and liver failure). The main exception where aspirin is used in children is Kawasaki disease.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: List the key contraindications to low-dose aspirin.
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Active peptic ulcer or GI bleed, children <16 (Reye's, except Kawasaki), aspirin-sensitive asthma, haemophilia/bleeding disorder, and severe hepatic or renal impairment.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the main adverse effect of aspirin, and how can the risk be reduced?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: GI irritation, peptic ulceration and GI bleeding. In patients at risk, add PPI cover (gastroprotection).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which respiratory adverse effect can aspirin cause in susceptible patients?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive asthmatics.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the features of aspirin (salicylate) overdose?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Tinnitus/deafness and a mixed acid-base disturbance (early respiratory alkalosis with a metabolic acidosis). Check salicylate levels and an ABG.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why should ibuprofen not be taken at the same time as low-dose aspirin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Ibuprofen taken close together can competitively block aspirin's access to COX-1 -> reduces aspirin's antiplatelet (cardioprotective) effect.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which drugs increase bleeding risk when combined with aspirin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Anticoagulants, other antiplatelets, NSAIDs and SSRIs all add to the bleeding risk.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Does aspirin need routine blood monitoring?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: No routine bloods are needed; monitor clinically for bleeding and GI symptoms.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the shared mechanism of clopidogrel, ticagrelor and prasugrel?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They all block the platelet P2Y12 (ADP) receptor -> prevent ADP-driven platelet activation and aggregation. They are combined with aspirin as dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) in ACS.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does clopidogrel work, and why does its effect vary between patients?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It irreversibly blocks the P2Y12 receptor. It is a prodrug that must be activated by the liver, and the degree of activation varies between individuals -> variable response.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: For which conditions is clopidogrel the first-line SINGLE antiplatelet agent?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Long-term secondary prevention after ischaemic stroke/TIA, and in peripheral arterial disease (PAD).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the standard maintenance dose of clopidogrel, and the loading dose in ACS/PCI?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 75 mg once daily maintenance; a 300-600 mg loading dose in ACS or at PCI.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: A patient on clopidogrel needs gastroprotection. Which PPI should be avoided and why?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Avoid omeprazole and esomeprazole -> they reduce clopidogrel's activation and blunt its antiplatelet effect. Use pantoprazole or lansoprazole instead.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: When should clopidogrel be stopped before major surgery?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: About 7 days beforehand (it irreversibly inhibits platelets, so recovery requires new platelet production).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the main adverse effects of clopidogrel?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Bleeding, GI upset and rash; rarely thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does ticagrelor differ mechanistically from clopidogrel?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Ticagrelor is a REVERSIBLE P2Y12 antagonist and is directly active (not a prodrug) -> faster, more predictable and more potent platelet inhibition than clopidogrel.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the place of ticagrelor in ACS?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: With aspirin as dual antiplatelet therapy, usually preferred over clopidogrel for 12 months after ACS.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the ticagrelor dose after ACS, and the reduced dose for extended use beyond 12 months?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 90 mg twice daily (with a 180 mg loading dose); reduced to 60 mg twice daily for extended long-term use beyond 12 months post-MI.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What characteristic side effect of ticagrelor should you warn patients about?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Dyspnoea (breathlessness) in about 15% of patients -> usually mild and transient. It can also cause ventricular pauses/bradyarrhythmia and a rise in uric acid and creatinine.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why does adherence matter so much with ticagrelor?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It is reversible and taken twice daily, so a missed dose causes platelet function to recover quickly and antiplatelet cover is lost -> strict adherence is essential.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What aspirin dose limit applies when a patient is on ticagrelor?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Keep aspirin at <=100 mg daily -> higher aspirin doses reduce ticagrelor's benefit.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: When should ticagrelor be stopped before elective surgery?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 5 days beforehand.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does prasugrel compare with clopidogrel?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Prasugrel is also an irreversible P2Y12 blocker but is activated more reliably and potently -> stronger, more consistent inhibition, at the cost of a higher bleeding risk.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: In which ACS setting is prasugrel typically used?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: ACS managed with PCI (with aspirin) -> often the first choice at the time of PCI.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the prasugrel dosing, including the dose reduction?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 60 mg loading dose then 10 mg once daily; reduce to 5 mg once daily if weight <60 kg or age >=75 years.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why is prasugrel contraindicated in a patient with a previous stroke or TIA?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It markedly increases the risk of intracranial haemorrhage in these patients -> contraindicated after previous stroke/TIA.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which P2Y12 inhibitors are irreversible and which is reversible, and why does it matter for surgery?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Clopidogrel and prasugrel are irreversible (stop ~7 days before surgery for platelets to regenerate); ticagrelor is reversible (stop 5 days before, but effect is lost quickly if doses are missed).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is a pharmacokinetic advantage of prasugrel over clopidogrel and ticagrelor?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Prasugrel has no clinically significant interactions of the clopidogrel/ticagrelor type; the main added risk is bleeding (including intracranial).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does dipyridamole reduce platelet aggregation?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It inhibits phosphodiesterase (and blocks adenosine reuptake) -> raises platelet cAMP -> less aggregation. It is also a vasodilator.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the role of dipyridamole in secondary stroke prevention?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Modified-release dipyridamole PLUS aspirin is a second-line option for secondary prevention of ischaemic stroke/TIA when clopidogrel monotherapy (first-line) is unsuitable.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Besides antiplatelet use, what other clinical role does dipyridamole have?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It is used as a pharmacological stressor in myocardial perfusion (stress) imaging.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the typical dose of dipyridamole for stroke prevention?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Modified-release dipyridamole 200 mg twice daily (often combined with low-dose aspirin 25 mg).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the commonest side effect of dipyridamole that limits its use?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Headache (common, often dose-limiting); also dizziness, flushing and GI upset.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: In which cardiac conditions should dipyridamole be used with caution?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Unstable angina/recent MI (risk of coronary steal), aortic stenosis, and haemodynamic instability/decompensated heart failure. It may also aggravate myasthenia gravis.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What key drug interaction must you remember with dipyridamole and adenosine?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Dipyridamole potentiates adenosine -> the adenosine dose must be reduced.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How do GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors (eptifibatide, tirofiban, abciximab) work?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They block the platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor -> the final common pathway of aggregation where fibrinogen cross-links platelets -> very potent inhibition. They are given IV only.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: When are IV GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors used?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: As a specialist in-hospital IV adjunct (to aspirin and heparin) in high-risk ACS or during PCI.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the two major adverse effects of GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Bleeding (major risk) and thrombocytopenia, which can be profound -> the platelet count must be checked.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the platelet monitoring schedule when starting a GPIIb/IIIa inhibitor?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Check the platelet count at 2-4 hours after starting, then daily, watching for profound thrombocytopenia; also monitor for bleeding and clotting when co-given with heparin.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the contraindications to GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Active bleeding, recent stroke or surgery, severe uncontrolled hypertension, and thrombocytopenia.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors need dose adjustment in renal impairment?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Eptifibatide and tirofiban are renally cleared -> dose-reduce in renal impairment (avoid eptifibatide if eGFR <30 or on dialysis).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What distinguishes GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors from the oral antiplatelets in how and where they are used?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They are potent IV-only agents acting at the final common pathway of aggregation, used peri-PCI/in high-risk ACS in hospital, whereas aspirin and P2Y12 inhibitors are oral drugs for ongoing prevention.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: How do thrombolytic (fibrinolytic) drugs work?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: They are plasminogen activators -> convert plasminogen to plasmin, which breaks down fibrin in an established thrombus -> clot lysis and reperfusion.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: What is the key difference between thrombolytics and anticoagulants/antiplatelets?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: Thrombolytics actively DISSOLVE an existing clot (clot lysis), whereas anticoagulants and antiplatelets only prevent new clot forming or extending.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: Which thrombolytic is the standard tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), and how is it given?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: Alteplase -> used in stroke, STEMI and massive PE. It has a very short duration of action, so it is given as a bolus followed by an infusion.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: What is the practical advantage of tenecteplase over alteplase?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: Tenecteplase is more fibrin-specific and longer-acting, so it can be given as a single weight-based IV bolus -> convenient for STEMI and pre-hospital use.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: How does streptokinase differ from the tPA-type thrombolytics?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: Streptokinase is a bacterial (streptococcal) protein that works non-specifically -> more systemic fibrinogen breakdown and hypotension. It is antigenic (allergy/anaphylaxis) and can only be used ONCE.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: Why can streptokinase only be given once?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: It is antigenic -> neutralising antibodies form after exposure, so a repeat dose is ineffective (and risks allergy). Use a tPA (e.g. alteplase) if thrombolysis is needed again.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: What is the time window for alteplase in acute ischaemic stroke, and what must be excluded first?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: Within 4.5 hours of symptom onset, after intracranial haemorrhage has been excluded on CT.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: For an acute ischaemic stroke due to large-vessel occlusion, what treatment is preferred over/alongside thrombolysis?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: Mechanical thrombectomy (generally within 6 hours, or later if perfusion imaging is favourable), with or without thrombolysis.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: In STEMI, when is thrombolysis (fibrinolysis) used instead of primary PCI?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: Primary PCI is first-line reperfusion. Give fibrinolysis (e.g. a tenecteplase bolus) only if PCI cannot be delivered within 120 minutes of diagnosis (ideally within 12 hours of symptom onset), then transfer for rescue/routine PCI.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: When is thrombolysis indicated in pulmonary embolism?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: In massive PE with haemodynamic instability (e.g. systemic IV alteplase).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: What are the ABSOLUTE contraindications to thrombolysis?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: Active bleeding, previous intracranial haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke within 6 months, CNS neoplasm/AVM/aneurysm, recent major trauma/surgery/head injury (<3 weeks), GI bleed within 1 month, a known bleeding disorder, and aortic dissection.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: Give some RELATIVE contraindications to thrombolysis.
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: Severe uncontrolled hypertension (>180/110), TIA within 6 months, current oral anticoagulation, pregnancy or <1 week postpartum, advanced liver disease, traumatic/prolonged CPR, recent non-compressible puncture, active peptic ulcer, and infective endocarditis.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: What is the alteplase dose for acute ischaemic stroke?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: 0.9 mg/kg (maximum 90 mg): 10% given as a bolus and the remainder infused over 1 hour.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: How is tenecteplase dosed, and what adjustment is made in older patients?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: A single weight-banded IV bolus. Give HALF the dose if the patient is >=75 years, to reduce the risk of intracranial haemorrhage.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: What is the most feared complication of thrombolysis?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: Major bleeding, especially intracranial haemorrhage. This is why contraindications must be screened for carefully before giving a thrombolytic.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: Besides bleeding, what other side effects can occur with thrombolytics?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: Reperfusion arrhythmias and hypotension. Streptokinase specifically causes allergic reactions/anaphylaxis and hypotension.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: Which co-prescribed drugs increase the bleeding risk of thrombolytics?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: Anticoagulants (heparin, DOACs, warfarin) and antiplatelets -> additive major bleeding risk. These are routinely co-prescribed in STEMI, so bleeding risk must be weighed carefully.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: What interaction is specific to streptokinase and ACE inhibitors?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: ACE inhibitors increase the risk of anaphylactoid (hypotensive/allergic) reactions with streptokinase.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: What monitoring and precautions are needed during and after thrombolysis for stroke?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: Neuro observations/GCS (urgent CT if deterioration -> suspect intracranial bleed), strict blood pressure control (keep <185/110 in stroke), cardiac monitoring for reperfusion arrhythmias, and FBC/clotting.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: What should be available at the bedside in case of major bleeding after thrombolysis?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: Reversal/haemostatic support: tranexamic acid, cryoprecipitate and fresh frozen plasma (FFP).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: A patient who received streptokinase years ago now needs thrombolysis again. What should you use and why?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: Use a tPA such as alteplase, not streptokinase -> neutralising antibodies from the previous exposure make repeat streptokinase ineffective and more allergenic.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.front: Which thrombolytic is most convenient for pre-hospital STEMI treatment, and why?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Thro.back: Tenecteplase -> it is given as a single weight-based bolus (longer-acting, fibrin-specific), unlike alteplase which needs a bolus plus infusion.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: In asthma and COPD management, what is the difference between a 'reliever' and a 'preventer'?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: A reliever is a bronchodilator taken to relieve acute symptoms fast (e.g. salbutamol, or low-dose ICS/formoterol). A preventer is a regular maintenance drug (typically an inhaled corticosteroid) that controls underlying airway inflammation to reduce future symptoms and exacerbations.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: By what mechanism does salbutamol relieve bronchoconstriction?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: It is a short-acting beta-2 agonist: stimulating beta-2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle raises intracellular cAMP, causing rapid bronchodilation (onset within minutes, lasting about 4-6 hours).

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: How quickly does inhaled salbutamol work and how long does it last?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: Onset within minutes and duration of roughly 4-6 hours, which is why it is used as a short-acting reliever rather than for maintenance.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: Name two short-acting beta-2 agonists (SABAs) used as relievers.
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: Salbutamol and terbutaline.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: What are the common side effects of salbutamol that a student should recognise?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: Fine tremor, tachycardia and palpitations, headache and anxiety. At high or nebulised doses it can cause hypokalaemia.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: Why should potassium be monitored in a patient receiving repeated high-dose nebulised salbutamol for acute severe asthma?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: High-dose beta-2 agonists drive potassium into cells and cause hypokalaemia; this is additive with steroids and theophylline and increases arrhythmia risk, so serum K+ (along with heart rate and response) should be checked.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: A patient with asthma is using their salbutamol inhaler increasingly often. What does this tell you and what should you do?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: Escalating reliever use signals poorly controlled asthma. It should prompt review and stepping up ICS-based therapy (e.g. AIR or MART), not simply more reliever.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: Besides asthma and COPD, in what emergency is nebulised or IV salbutamol used?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: Hyperkalaemia - beta-2 stimulation drives potassium intracellularly, lowering serum K+.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: What are salmeterol and formoterol, and how do they differ from salbutamol?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: They are long-acting beta-2 agonists (LABAs) giving sustained bronchodilation for about 12 hours, used as add-on maintenance rather than as short-acting relievers.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: What is the critical safety rule about prescribing a LABA in asthma?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: A LABA must NEVER be used alone in asthma - LABA monotherapy increases the risk of asthma death. It must always be given together with an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS).

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: Which LABA has a fast enough onset to double as a reliever, and how is this used?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: Formoterol has a fast onset, so an ICS/formoterol combination inhaler can serve as both maintenance and reliever - the basis of MART (maintenance and reliever therapy). Salmeterol has a slow onset and is maintenance-only.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: Where do LABAs fit in COPD management?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: They are used as add-on maintenance bronchodilators to improve symptoms; unlike in asthma, LABA use in COPD does not carry the same monotherapy-mortality restriction.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: What side effects do LABAs share with SABAs?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: Tremor, tachycardia, palpitations and hypokalaemia (longer-lasting than with SABAs), plus muscle cramps.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: What class of drug is ipratropium and how does it produce bronchodilation?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: A short-acting muscarinic antagonist (SAMA). It blocks muscarinic (M3) receptors on airway smooth muscle and glands, reducing vagally-mediated bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion (onset around 30-60 minutes).

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: When is nebulised ipratropium used in acute asthma or COPD?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: It is added to nebulised salbutamol in acute exacerbations of COPD and in severe or life-threatening asthma as an add-on bronchodilator.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: What antimuscarinic side effects and cautions apply to ipratropium?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: Dry mouth is common. Use caution in glaucoma (nebulised mist reaching the eyes can trigger acute angle-closure - protect the eyes) and in bladder outflow obstruction/prostatism (urinary retention). It can also cause constipation.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: Name the long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMAs) and how often they are typically taken.
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: Tiotropium, umeclidinium, glycopyrronium and aclidinium. They are long-acting maintenance bronchodilators, usually taken once daily (e.g. tiotropium).

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: What is the role of LAMAs in COPD and asthma?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: LAMAs are a cornerstone maintenance bronchodilator in COPD, reducing exacerbations. Tiotropium is also used as an add-on in poorly controlled asthma already on ICS/LABA.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: Why should a LAMA (e.g. tiotropium) not be co-prescribed with a SAMA (ipratropium)?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: Both are antimuscarinics, so combining them adds antimuscarinic burden (dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, glaucoma risk) without added benefit.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: What cautions apply when starting a patient on a LAMA?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: Caution in glaucoma, bladder outflow obstruction/prostatism, recent MI or arrhythmia, and in significant renal impairment (tiotropium is renally excreted and can accumulate). Antimuscarinic effects include dry mouth, constipation and urinary retention.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: What class of drug is theophylline, and what is the IV form called?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: Theophylline is a methylxanthine bronchodilator. The IV form is aminophylline (theophylline combined with ethylenediamine to make it more soluble).

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: Where do theophylline and aminophylline sit in asthma/COPD management?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: They are add-on agents in severe or poorly controlled asthma and COPD. IV aminophylline may be used, under specialist/monitored care, in acute severe asthma not responding to standard treatment.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: Why does theophylline require monitoring of serum drug levels?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: It has a narrow therapeutic index, so the gap between an effective and a toxic level is small. Levels are monitored (target around 10-20 mg/L) to keep the patient in the therapeutic range and avoid toxicity.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: What are the features of theophylline toxicity?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: Nausea and vomiting, tachyarrhythmias and seizures, plus tremor, palpitations, insomnia and hypokalaemia. These are level-related, reflecting its narrow therapeutic index.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: Why is theophylline considered a high-interaction drug, and what practical rule follows?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: Because its therapeutic range is narrow, the many drugs that raise its level (e.g. macrolides, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine) can push it into toxicity, while enzyme inducers and smoking lower it. The practical rule is to check levels and be alert whenever an interacting drug is started or stopped.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.front: Why must the IV aminophylline loading dose be omitted in a patient already taking oral theophylline?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Broncho.back: They already have a therapeutic (or higher) blood level, so giving a loading dose on top would push them into toxicity. Only theophylline-naive patients receive the loading dose; others go straight to the maintenance infusion with level monitoring.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.front: How do inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) such as beclometasone work in asthma, and what class of drug are they?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.back: They are anti-inflammatory corticosteroids. They act on the airway to suppress the underlying inflammation (reducing eosinophils, cytokines, mucosal oedema and bronchial hyper-responsiveness), which lowers airway hyper-responsiveness and the frequency of exacerbations.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.front: Is an inhaled corticosteroid a preventer or a reliever, and why?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.back: It is a PREVENTER, taken regularly to control the underlying airway inflammation. It has no immediate bronchodilator effect, so it does not relieve an acute attack (that is the job of a bronchodilator like a SABA/formoterol).

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.front: Why is an inhaled corticosteroid described as the cornerstone of asthma maintenance treatment?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.back: Asthma is fundamentally an inflammatory disease. ICS treats the underlying inflammation rather than just the symptoms, improving day-to-day control and, crucially, reducing the risk of exacerbations and asthma deaths. Bronchodilators alone do not treat the inflammation.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.front: Under modern UK asthma guidance, is SABA-only (reliever-only) treatment appropriate for mild asthma?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.back: No. Every asthma patient should be on ICS-containing treatment, even mild disease. SABA-only therapy is no longer recommended because it leaves the inflammation untreated and is associated with increased exacerbations and death. Treatment is now built around ICS/formoterol.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.front: What do the terms AIR and MART mean in asthma management?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.back: Both use a single ICS/formoterol inhaler that provides both anti-inflammatory prevention and symptom relief. AIR (Anti-Inflammatory Reliever) is used as-needed only; MART (Maintenance And Reliever Therapy) is a regular daily dose plus the same inhaler used as needed for relief.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.front: How does the role of an inhaled corticosteroid differ in COPD compared with asthma?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.back: In COPD, ICS is NOT first-line for everyone. It is added (as LABA+LAMA+ICS triple therapy) for patients with frequent/continuing exacerbations or an eosinophilic/asthmatic phenotype. ICS also carries a pneumonia risk in COPD, so it is used more selectively than in asthma.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.front: What are the two classic LOCAL side effects of inhaled corticosteroids?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.back: Oral candidiasis (oral thrush) and dysphonia (a hoarse or croaky voice). Both result from steroid deposited in the mouth and throat rather than reaching the lungs.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.front: How can the local side effects of inhaled corticosteroids be prevented?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.back: Use a spacer device (improves lung delivery and reduces oropharyngeal deposition) and rinse the mouth (and gargle/spit) with water after each dose. These simple measures greatly reduce thrush and hoarse voice.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.front: Why should a patient rinse their mouth out after using an inhaled corticosteroid?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.back: A large fraction of an inhaled dose lands in the mouth and throat rather than the lungs. Rinsing and spitting removes this residual steroid, preventing oral thrush and a hoarse voice, and reduces the amount swallowed and absorbed systemically.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.front: What are the potential SYSTEMIC side effects of high-dose, long-term inhaled corticosteroids?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.back: Adrenal suppression, reduced bone density/osteoporosis, easy bruising, cataracts and glaucoma, and in children a reduction in growth velocity. These are dose-related, so the lowest dose that maintains control is used.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.front: What is the benefit of using a spacer with a metered-dose inhaler corticosteroid?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.back: A spacer improves drug delivery to the lungs (less coordination needed, more even distribution) and reduces oropharyngeal deposition, which means better disease control and fewer local side effects such as thrush and hoarse voice.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.front: A child is on medium-to-high dose inhaled corticosteroid. What specific monitoring is needed and why?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.back: Monitor the child's height/growth, because high-dose ICS can reduce growth velocity. At each review also check inhaler technique and adherence, and step down to the lowest effective dose.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.front: Why might a patient on high-dose long-term inhaled corticosteroids need a steroid emergency card?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.back: Chronic high-dose steroid can suppress the adrenal axis, so the patient cannot mount a normal stress response. During illness, surgery or if steroid is stopped abruptly they risk adrenal crisis (hypotension, hypoglycaemia). The card alerts clinicians to give stress/sick-day steroid cover.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.front: Why can certain strong enzyme-inhibiting drugs (e.g. ritonavir, cobicistat, azole antifungals) be a problem with inhaled fluticasone/budesonide?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.back: They markedly increase systemic exposure to the inhaled steroid -> Cushingoid effects and adrenal suppression. Inhaled fluticasone with ritonavir is specifically avoided.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.front: Beclometasone brands are described as 'not interchangeable' - what is the practical prescribing implication?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Inhaled.back: Different beclometasone inhalers have different potencies, so it must be prescribed by brand. For example, extrafine Qvar is roughly twice as potent as Clenil (Qvar 100 mcg approximately equals Clenil 200 mcg), so switching brands without adjusting dose can under- or over-dose the patient.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.front: What are the three main types of combination inhaler, and what does each contain?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.back: 1) ICS/LABA (steroid + long-acting beta-agonist), e.g. Symbicort, Seretide, Fostair, Relvar. 2) LABA/LAMA (two long-acting bronchodilators, no steroid), e.g. Anoro, Spiolto. 3) ICS/LABA/LAMA 'triple therapy', e.g. Trelegy.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.front: Why are combination inhalers used instead of separate devices — what are the two main advantages?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.back: They improve adherence by putting two or three drugs in one device. Crucially in asthma, an ICS/LABA combination guarantees the LABA is never taken without an ICS, which is a key safety principle (LABA alone increases asthma death risk).

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.front: What does a Symbicort inhaler contain, and what does Seretide contain?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.back: Symbicort = budesonide (ICS) + formoterol (LABA). Seretide = fluticasone (ICS) + salmeterol (LABA). Both are ICS/LABA combinations, but only the formoterol-containing one can be used as MART.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.front: What is MART (Maintenance And Reliever Therapy) in asthma?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.back: A single ICS/formoterol inhaler used as BOTH the regular daily preventer AND the reliever taken for symptoms. Because it delivers ICS with every reliever puff, a separate SABA is not routinely needed.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.front: Which combination inhalers can be used for MART, and why can salmeterol-containing ones not?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.back: Only ICS/FORMOTEROL inhalers (e.g. Symbicort, Fostair). Formoterol is a LABA with a fast onset, so it works as a reliever. Salmeterol has a slow onset, so ICS/salmeterol inhalers (Seretide, Relvar) cannot be used as a reliever and are maintenance-only.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.front: An asthmatic on ICS/formoterol MART asks whether they still need their blue salbutamol inhaler for symptoms. What do you advise?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.back: On MART the ICS/formoterol inhaler is itself the reliever, so a separate SABA is not routinely required. Each reliever puff also delivers anti-inflammatory ICS, unlike a SABA which only relieves symptoms.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.front: What is the main clinical use of an ICS/LABA combination inhaler?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.back: Asthma maintenance (as MART if it contains formoterol, or as fixed maintenance dosing). Also used in COPD when there are asthmatic/eosinophilic features or ongoing exacerbations, where the ICS component reduces exacerbation frequency.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.front: A LABA/LAMA inhaler (e.g. Anoro, Spiolto) contains no steroid. In which condition is it used and why is the absence of ICS an advantage?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.back: COPD maintenance in patients with breathlessness/exacerbations but WITHOUT asthmatic or eosinophilic features. With no ICS there is no risk of pneumonia, oral thrush or hoarse voice from an inhaled steroid.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.front: What does 'triple therapy' mean, and when is it used in COPD?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.back: Triple therapy = ICS + LABA + LAMA in one inhaler (e.g. Trelegy). Used in COPD with continued exacerbations despite dual LABA/LAMA therapy, or upfront where asthmatic/eosinophilic features are present. In asthma it is a later specialist add-on step.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.front: A COPD patient still has frequent exacerbations despite a LABA/LAMA inhaler. What is the logical next step-up?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.back: Add an inhaled corticosteroid to make it triple therapy (ICS/LABA/LAMA, e.g. Trelegy). The general logic is: dual bronchodilator first, then step up to triple if exacerbations continue, particularly if blood eosinophils are raised.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.front: What is the key safety concern with using an ICS-containing inhaler in COPD?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.back: Inhaled corticosteroids increase the risk of pneumonia in COPD. This is why LABA/LAMA (no steroid) is preferred in COPD patients without asthmatic/eosinophilic features, and why ICS is reserved for those with exacerbations or eosinophilia.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.front: Why must combination inhalers be prescribed by brand name?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.back: Different brands use different devices, drug strengths and dosing, and are not interchangeable. Prescribing by brand (e.g. Symbicort 200/6) ensures the patient gets the correct device and dose they are trained to use.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.front: What are the class-based side effects to expect from a triple-therapy inhaler (ICS/LABA/LAMA)?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.back: ICS -> oral thrush, hoarse voice, pneumonia risk in COPD. LABA -> tremor, tachycardia, hypokalaemia. LAMA -> dry mouth, urinary retention, and acute angle-closure glaucoma.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.front: A patient on a LAMA-containing combination inhaler develops a painful red eye with blurred vision. What must you consider?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.back: Acute angle-closure glaucoma from the antimuscarinic (LAMA) component. This is an ophthalmic emergency — the patient needs urgent assessment. Use LAMA-containing inhalers with caution in those at risk of glaucoma.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.front: A patient takes budesonide/formoterol as MART. What practical safety point should you counsel about the total daily puffs?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.back: There is a maximum total number of inhalations per day (e.g. Symbicort 200/6 max 12/day; Fostair 100/6 max 8/day). If they are regularly reaching the cap, their asthma is poorly controlled and they need urgent review, not simply more reliever puffs.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.front: Which combination inhaler type carries essentially no risk of oral thrush or pneumonia, and why?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Combina.back: LABA/LAMA inhalers (e.g. Anoro, Spiolto), because they contain no inhaled corticosteroid. Thrush, hoarse voice and pneumonia risk all come from the ICS component.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Leukotr.front: How do leukotriene receptor antagonists (montelukast, zafirlukast) work?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Leukotr.back: They block the cysteinyl leukotriene (CysLT1) receptor, preventing leukotriene-driven bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, eosinophilic airway inflammation and vascular leak.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Leukotr.front: A patient with asthma is started on montelukast. What form does this drug take and how does that differ from most asthma preventers?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Leukotr.back: Montelukast is an ORAL tablet, not an inhaler. It is used as an add-on preventer, in contrast to inhaled preventers (e.g. inhaled corticosteroids) which are delivered directly to the airways via a device.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Leukotr.front: In which patient groups is an LTRA such as montelukast especially useful in asthma?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Leukotr.back: Allergic asthma, exercise-induced asthma, and aspirin/NSAID-exacerbated asthma. It is also helpful when there is concurrent allergic rhinitis, and it is an option in children.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Leukotr.front: A patient is prescribed montelukast. What is the standard dosing schedule and when in the day should it be taken?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Leukotr.back: Montelukast 10 mg once daily, taken in the EVENING/at night. Lower doses are used in children (e.g. 5 mg age 6-14; 4 mg granules for younger children).

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Leukotr.front: What is the key MHRA safety warning you must counsel a patient (or parent) about before starting montelukast?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Leukotr.back: Neuropsychiatric side effects: sleep disturbance, vivid dreams/nightmares, agitation, mood or behaviour changes, and rarely suicidal ideation. Counsel patients/parents to watch for these and seek review; stop the drug if they occur.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Leukotr.front: A child on montelukast is brought to clinic for asthma follow-up. What specific symptoms should you actively ask about?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Leukotr.back: Ask about mood, sleep and behaviour changes (e.g. nightmares, agitation, low mood) because of the MHRA neuropsychiatric warning. This is especially important in children.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Leukotr.front: Montelukast is generally well tolerated, but which rare, serious condition is it associated with, and in what setting?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Leukotr.back: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss syndrome), presenting with eosinophilia and vasculitis. It is often unmasked as oral corticosteroids are weaned down.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Leukotr.front: How does the mechanism of an oral LTRA differ from that of an inhaled corticosteroid preventer in asthma?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Leukotr.back: An LTRA is a tablet that specifically blocks leukotriene receptors to reduce one inflammatory pathway. An inhaled corticosteroid is a device-delivered drug with broad anti-inflammatory action on the airway. Because the LTRA is oral it is convenient (useful in poor inhaler technique or with allergic rhinitis) but is generally less effective than ICS as a preventer.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Leukotr.front: Zafirlukast is prescribed for a patient also taking warfarin. What must you watch for?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Leukotr.back: Zafirlukast can raise the INR and increase bleeding risk -> monitor INR closely. It also requires LFT monitoring.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: What are biologics for asthma, and where do they fit in management?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: Injectable monoclonal antibodies used as SPECIALIST add-on therapy for SEVERE asthma that remains uncontrolled despite high-dose inhaled therapy (high-dose ICS/LABA). Started by a severe-asthma MDT, not in primary care. They are maintenance/preventer treatments — NOT for acute attacks.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: How is the choice of asthma biologic guided?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: By phenotype. Allergic phenotype (raised IgE + sensitisation to a perennial allergen) points to anti-IgE (omalizumab). Eosinophilic/type-2 phenotype (raised blood eosinophils +/- raised FeNO) points to anti-IL-5/IL-5R or anti-IL-4Rα drugs. Tezepelumab (anti-TSLP) works across phenotypes, including low-eosinophil asthma.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: What are the main clinical benefits of asthma biologics?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: Fewer exacerbations and an oral-corticosteroid-sparing effect (allowing the maintenance oral steroid dose to be reduced or stopped). This reduces cumulative steroid toxicity. They do not replace inhaled preventers and are not used for acute attacks.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: How do biologics differ from inhaled/oral corticosteroids in asthma?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: Corticosteroids are broad anti-inflammatory agents (inhaled or oral). Biologics are TARGETED monoclonal antibodies against a specific cytokine/pathway, given by injection (usually subcutaneous), and are STEROID-SPARING — a key aim is to cut down oral steroid exposure and its side effects.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: Why are asthma biologics 'specialist-only' medicines?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: They are reserved for severe asthma meeting strict criteria (e.g. eosinophil thresholds, exacerbation frequency, steroid dependence), approved via NICE technology appraisals, are expensive, require phenotyping and response review, and must be initiated and monitored by a specialist severe-asthma service/MDT.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: What is the target and mechanism of omalizumab?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: Anti-IgE monoclonal antibody. It binds FREE (circulating) IgE, lowering free IgE and downregulating FcεRI receptors on mast cells/basophils, blocking the allergic cascade. It does NOT bind IgE already bound to cells, so it does not trigger degranulation.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: Which asthma phenotype is omalizumab used for, and how is it given?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: Severe persistent ALLERGIC asthma — raised IgE plus sensitisation to a perennial allergen — uncontrolled on high-dose ICS/LABA. Given subcutaneously every 2-4 weeks, with dose based on body weight and baseline IgE level.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: What key safety point must you remember with omalizumab dosing?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: Risk of anaphylaxis, particularly after the early doses — patients should be observed after injections. It is not for acute asthma exacerbations, and is contraindicated after previous anaphylaxis to the drug.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: Besides asthma, what other condition is omalizumab used for?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: Chronic spontaneous urticaria. (It is also the asthma biologic with the most pregnancy safety data, so is generally preferred if a biologic is needed in pregnancy.)

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: What do mepolizumab, reslizumab and benralizumab target?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: The IL-5 pathway, which drives eosinophils. Mepolizumab and reslizumab bind IL-5 itself (the ligend); benralizumab binds the IL-5 receptor (IL-5Rα). All cause profound eosinophil depletion → fewer eosinophilic exacerbations.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: Which asthma phenotype do the anti-IL-5/IL-5R biologics treat?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: Severe EOSINOPHILIC asthma — raised blood eosinophils with frequent exacerbations and/or oral-corticosteroid dependence. They are strongly steroid-sparing. Mepolizumab is also used in EGPA and hypereosinophilic syndromes.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: How are the anti-IL-5 biologics given, and which one is different?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: Mepolizumab and benralizumab are given subcutaneously every 4-8 weeks. Reslizumab is the exception — given by IV infusion (weight-based, 3 mg/kg every 4 weeks), and carries a specific anaphylaxis risk during/shortly after infusion, so patients must be observed.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: What is monitored to guide anti-IL-5 asthma biologic therapy?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: Blood eosinophil count and exacerbation frequency, with a formal response review — continue only if there is benefit (fewer exacerbations, reduced oral steroids). Watch for unmasking of a pre-existing parasitic (helminth) infection.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: What is the target and mechanism of dupilumab?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: Blocks the shared IL-4 receptor alpha subunit (IL-4Rα), inhibiting BOTH IL-4 and IL-13 signalling — the core of type-2 inflammation. Blocking IL-13 reduces eosinophil migration into tissues, which can cause a transient rise in BLOOD eosinophils (redistribution, not overproduction).

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: Which asthma phenotype is dupilumab used for, and how is it given?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: Severe TYPE-2 asthma — raised eosinophils and/or raised FeNO, or maintenance oral-steroid-dependent asthma. Given subcutaneously every 2 weeks after an initial loading dose.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: Besides asthma, what other conditions is dupilumab used for?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) and chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps — reflecting its broad action across type-2 inflammatory disease.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: What characteristic side effect is associated with dupilumab?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: Conjunctivitis (and sometimes keratitis) — characteristic, especially in patients with eczema. It can also cause a transient blood eosinophilia. Injection-site reactions and headache also occur.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: What is the target of tezepelumab, and why is it distinctive?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: Blocks TSLP (thymic stromal lymphopoietin), an epithelial 'alarmin' released on exposure to allergens, viruses or pollutants. Because TSLP sits UPSTREAM of the whole inflammatory cascade, tezepelumab works across BOTH type-2 and non-type-2 asthma.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: When is tezepelumab particularly useful, and how is it given?
