pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: It is the broadest-acting asthma biologic — effective irrespective of eosinophil count or allergic status, making it useful in severe asthma with LOW eosinophils where other biologics are less suitable. Given subcutaneously every 4 weeks.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: A patient with severe asthma has a high blood eosinophil count but no raised IgE or perennial allergy — which biologic class fits?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: An eosinophilic phenotype favours an anti-IL-5/IL-5R biologic (mepolizumab, reslizumab or benralizumab) or anti-IL-4Rα (dupilumab). Anti-IgE (omalizumab) would be less appropriate as it targets the ALLERGIC/IgE phenotype. Tezepelumab is also an option across phenotypes.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.front: What general safety precautions apply to ALL asthma biologics?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Biologi.back: Treat any pre-existing helminth (parasitic) infection first; avoid live vaccines during treatment and keep immunisations up to date; do NOT stop corticosteroids abruptly; and never use them for acute asthma attacks. Assess response formally and continue only if benefit is seen.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH): what are the three drug pathways targeted, and where must this be managed?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: PAH is managed in specialist pulmonary hypertension centres using pulmonary vasodilators that act on three pathways: the nitric oxide/cGMP pathway, the endothelin pathway, and the prostacyclin (cAMP) pathway. Therapy is often started as upfront combination across pathways rather than single-agent.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: Before starting targeted PAH drugs, what must be confirmed, and why can these drugs be harmful in the wrong patient?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: Diagnosis must be confirmed on right heart catheterisation. Targeted therapies are for Group 1 PAH (and riociguat for Group 4 CTEPH). They can be harmful in Group 2 (left heart disease) and Group 3 (lung disease) pulmonary hypertension, where vasodilation can worsen pulmonary oedema or V/Q mismatch.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: Which PAH patients are treated with high-dose calcium channel blockers rather than targeted therapy?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: The small minority who are acute vasoreactive responders on right heart catheterisation testing. These patients get high-dose CCBs. Everyone else needs pathway-targeted pulmonary vasodilators.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: Sildenafil and tadalafil in PAH: what is the mechanism?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: They inhibit phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE5), preventing breakdown of cGMP in pulmonary vascular smooth muscle (the NO to soluble guanylate cyclase to cGMP pathway). This causes sustained pulmonary vasodilation and reduced remodelling. Tadalafil has a longer half-life, allowing once-daily dosing.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: Where else would a medical student recognise sildenafil and tadalafil, and what is their role in PAH?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: Sildenafil is the classic erectile dysfunction drug; tadalafil is also used in ED and in benign prostatic hyperplasia. In PAH they are a first-line agent on the NO/cGMP pathway, given in a specialist centre and usually as part of upfront combination therapy.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: What is the absolute contraindication of PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil/tadalafil), and why?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: Never combine with nitrates or nicorandil. Both increase cGMP/nitric oxide signalling, so together with a PDE5 inhibitor they cause additive vasodilation and profound, potentially fatal hypotension. Also contraindicated with riociguat for the same reason.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: What are the common side effects of PDE5 inhibitors, and the classic visual one with sildenafil?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: Headache, flushing, dyspepsia, nasal congestion and hypotension. Sildenafil classically causes transient blue-tinged vision (from cross-inhibition of retinal PDE6). Rare but serious: sudden vision loss (NAION), sudden hearing loss, and priapism lasting over 4 hours.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: Endothelin receptor antagonists (the "-sentans": bosentan, ambrisentan, macitentan): what do they block?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: They block endothelin-1, a potent endogenous vasoconstrictor and pro-fibrotic mediator, at endothelin receptors. This produces pulmonary vasodilation and reduces vascular remodelling. Bosentan and macitentan are dual receptor blockers; ambrisentan is ETA-selective. They are oral agents used in Group 1 PAH.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: What is the headline hepatic safety issue with endothelin receptor antagonists, and how is it monitored?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: Hepatotoxicity, most notably with bosentan (dose-related rise in transaminases). Liver function tests must be monitored, classically monthly, on bosentan. Ambrisentan is less hepatotoxic (but causes more peripheral oedema).

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: Why are endothelin receptor antagonists contraindicated in pregnancy, and what is required in women of childbearing potential?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: They are highly teratogenic. Pregnancy is contraindicated, and mandatory effective contraception plus regular (monthly) pregnancy testing is required. A Pregnancy Prevention Programme applies.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: Besides hepatotoxicity and teratogenicity, what two other adverse effects should you expect with endothelin receptor antagonists?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: Fluid retention with peripheral oedema (most prominent with ambrisentan), and anaemia (monitor haemoglobin/FBC). Headache and flushing also occur.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: Why can bosentan make hormonal contraception unreliable, and what practical advice follows?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: Bosentan is an enzyme inducer that lowers levels of hormonal contraceptives (and also warfarin and sildenafil). Because these women must avoid pregnancy (teratogenicity), they need to ADD a barrier method rather than rely on hormonal contraception alone.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: Prostacyclin analogues (epoprostenol, iloprost, treprostinil): what is the mechanism?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: They mimic prostacyclin (PGI2), acting on the IP receptor to raise cAMP in pulmonary vascular smooth muscle. This causes potent pulmonary vasodilation, plus antiplatelet and anti-proliferative effects. This cAMP pathway is complementary to the NO/cGMP drugs. They are the most potent option, used for severe (WHO functional class III-IV) PAH.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: How do the routes of epoprostenol and iloprost differ?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: Epoprostenol is given as a continuous intravenous infusion via a central line (it is extremely short-acting). Iloprost is given by nebuliser/inhalation, but is short-acting so must be inhaled many times a day (roughly 6-9 times). Treprostinil can be subcutaneous, IV, inhaled or oral.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: Why must intravenous epoprostenol never be stopped abruptly?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: Its half-life is only minutes, so it is given as a continuous IV infusion. Abrupt interruption causes rebound pulmonary hypertension, which can be life-threatening. Infusion integrity must be protected and the line never simply interrupted.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: What are the key risks and side effects of prostacyclin analogues?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: Line-related complications with continuous IV therapy: catheter infection/sepsis and thrombosis. Class side effects include flushing, headache, jaw pain, diarrhoea and hypotension. The antiplatelet effect adds bleeding risk. Subcutaneous treprostinil commonly causes infusion-site pain.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: Riociguat: what is its mechanism of action?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: It is a soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC) stimulator. It raises cGMP directly, both by sensitising sGC to nitric oxide and independently of nitric oxide, causing pulmonary vasodilation. It works on the same NO/cGMP pathway as PDE5 inhibitors but at a different point.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: What indication makes riociguat notably different from the other PAH drugs?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: As well as PAH, riociguat is used in chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH, Group 4): inoperable CTEPH or persistent/recurrent CTEPH after pulmonary endarterectomy. Pulmonary endarterectomy remains the definitive treatment for operable CTEPH, so riociguat does not replace surgical assessment.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: Which two drug groups must never be combined with riociguat, and why? Any pregnancy issue?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: Never combine riociguat with nitrates OR with PDE5 inhibitors. All three raise cGMP, so the combination causes severe hypotension. Riociguat is also teratogenic, requiring effective contraception and monthly pregnancy testing.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: Name the three PAH drug pathways with one example drug for each.
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: 1) Nitric oxide/cGMP pathway: PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil/tadalafil) and the sGC stimulator riociguat. 2) Endothelin pathway: endothelin receptor antagonists (bosentan/ambrisentan/macitentan). 3) Prostacyclin/cAMP pathway: prostacyclin analogues (epoprostenol/iloprost/treprostinil).

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: Why are nitrates so dangerous with several PAH drugs, and which ones?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: Nitrates (and nicorandil) raise cGMP/NO signalling. PDE5 inhibitors and riociguat also raise cGMP, so adding a nitrate causes additive vasodilation and profound hypotension/collapse. So nitrates are contraindicated with both PDE5 inhibitors and riociguat.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.front: Which PAH drug classes are teratogenic and require a pregnancy prevention programme?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Pulmona.back: Endothelin receptor antagonists (the -sentans) and riociguat are teratogenic, needing effective contraception and regular pregnancy testing. Note bosentan additionally weakens hormonal contraception (enzyme inducer), so a barrier method must be added.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: What is dornase alfa and how does it work?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: A nebulised recombinant human DNase (enzyme). CF sputum is thick partly because dead neutrophils release lots of extracellular DNA; dornase alfa cleaves this DNA, lowering sputum viscosity so it is easier to clear.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: In which condition is dornase alfa used, and how is it given?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: Cystic fibrosis. It is a specialist-initiated, nebulised mucolytic taken regularly (2.5 mg once daily) to improve mucociliary clearance and lung function. It is a symptomatic treatment, not disease-modifying.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: Name a common side effect / practical point with dornase alfa.
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: Pharyngitis, voice change (hoarseness) and chest discomfort; occasionally a transient early dip in lung function. It is inhaled, so effects are mostly local to the airway.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: What is a CFTR modulator, and why is this class a landmark advance in cystic fibrosis?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: CFTR modulators are oral drugs that target the faulty CFTR protein itself, so they are DISEASE-MODIFYING rather than just symptomatic. They improve lung function and reduce exacerbations. Which one a patient gets depends on their CF genotype (the specific CFTR mutation).

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: What is the difference between a CFTR 'potentiator' and a 'corrector'?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: A potentiator (ivacaftor) helps CFTR channels already at the cell surface open properly. A corrector (e.g. elexacaftor/tezacaftor) helps misfolded CFTR reach the cell surface in the first place. Some genotypes need only a potentiator; the common F508del mutation needs correctors plus a potentiator.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: What is ivacaftor and what is it used for?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: An oral CFTR potentiator for cystic fibrosis patients with specific gating-type CFTR mutations (CFTR reaches the surface but won't open, so opening it is enough). Taken with fat-containing food to aid absorption.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: What is Kaftrio, and which CF patients is it for?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: Kaftrio = elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor, a combination of two correctors plus a potentiator. It is used for the common F508del mutation, meaning it is suitable for the majority of CF patients, and has been transformative, giving large gains in lung function and fewer exacerbations.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: What monitoring is needed with CFTR modulators (ivacaftor / Kaftrio)?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: Liver function tests, as they can raise transaminases (LFTs at baseline and periodically). In children, eye checks are advised because of a cataract signal. Take with fatty food.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: What are nintedanib and pirfenidone, and what do they achieve?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: Antifibrotic drugs for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). They SLOW the decline in lung function / slow disease progression, but they do NOT cure or reverse the fibrosis. Used alongside supportive measures (smoking cessation, pulmonary rehab) and transplant consideration.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: Which antifibrotic causes photosensitivity, and what advice follows?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: Pirfenidone. It commonly causes a photosensitivity rash, so patients must use sun protection (sunblock, cover up, avoid strong sun). Contrast: nintedanib's hallmark side effect is diarrhoea.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: Which antifibrotic characteristically causes diarrhoea, and how is it managed?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: Nintedanib. Diarrhoea is common; manage with hydration, loperamide and dose reduction if needed. Contrast: pirfenidone's hallmark side effect is photosensitivity.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: What monitoring do both nintedanib and pirfenidone require?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: Liver function tests, as both can derange LFTs (drug-induced liver injury). Both are also teratogenic, so effective contraception is needed. IPF treatment is initiated by a specialist ILD team.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: What is N-acetylcysteine (NAC) as a respiratory drug?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: A mucolytic that breaks disulphide bonds in mucus to thin secretions (given nebulised or orally). However, its high-yield exam use is as an antidote in a completely different setting: paracetamol overdose.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: Why is N-acetylcysteine the antidote in paracetamol overdose?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: Paracetamol's toxic metabolite (NAPQI) damages the liver once glutathione is depleted. NAC replenishes hepatic glutathione, allowing the toxic metabolite to be detoxified. Given IV, weight-based, guided by the paracetamol level taken at least 4 hours post-ingestion (or empirically for staggered/unknown-timing overdose).

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: What key adverse reaction can occur during IV N-acetylcysteine, and how is it handled?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: An anaphylactoid reaction (flushing, rash, bronchospasm) that is infusion-rate related rather than true allergy. Managed by slowing or pausing the infusion, plus an antihistamine if needed, then restarting - it is usually NOT a reason to abandon treatment.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: What is carbocisteine and when is it used?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: An oral mucolytic that reduces sputum viscosity, making it easier to cough up. Used in COPD / chronic productive cough. Trial it and continue ONLY if there is symptomatic benefit (less cough and sputum).

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: What is a key caution with carbocisteine?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: Avoid in active peptic ulceration - it can disrupt the gastric mucosal barrier and risk GI bleeding. Otherwise mainly causes GI upset. Dose is typically 750 mg three times daily, reduced once improving.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: What are palivizumab and nirsevimab, and what are they for?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: Monoclonal antibodies against the RSV fusion (F) protein. They are given to high-risk infants (e.g. prematurity, chronic lung disease, significant congenital heart disease) to prevent severe RSV bronchiolitis.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: Why are palivizumab / nirsevimab described as passive immunisation rather than a vaccine?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: They provide ready-made antibodies that neutralise RSV directly (passive immunity), giving immediate but temporary protection. A vaccine, by contrast, would prompt the infant's own immune system to make antibodies (active immunity).

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: How does the dosing of nirsevimab differ from palivizumab?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: Nirsevimab is a single intramuscular dose lasting the whole RSV season, whereas palivizumab must be given by monthly injections through the season. This convenience is why nirsevimab now underpins the broader UK national infant RSV programme.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: Contrast the two broad approaches among the 'other respiratory' drugs: mucolytics vs disease-modifying agents.
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: Mucolytics (dornase alfa, N-acetylcysteine, carbocisteine) only thin secretions to ease clearance - symptomatic. Disease-modifying agents (CFTR modulators in CF, antifibrotics in IPF) act on the underlying disease process - modifying its course rather than just symptoms.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: Which 'other respiratory' mucolytics are inhaled/nebulised vs oral?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: Dornase alfa is nebulised (CF). N-acetylcysteine can be nebulised or oral (and is given IV as the paracetamol antidote). Carbocisteine is oral (COPD/chronic productive cough).

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: Which respiratory drug is also a famous antidote, and for what?
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: N-acetylcysteine - a mucolytic in respiratory medicine, but far more commonly encountered as the IV antidote for paracetamol overdose, where it restores glutathione to detoxify the toxic metabolite. A classic crossover fact.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: Contrast the two CF drug types dornase alfa and Kaftrio.
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: Dornase alfa is a nebulised mucolytic that treats the SYMPTOM (thick sputum) by breaking down DNA in secretions. Kaftrio (a CFTR modulator) is oral and DISEASE-MODIFYING, correcting/potentiating the faulty CFTR protein, chosen by genotype. They target different levels of the disease.

pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.front: For IPF, contrast what antifibrotics achieve versus what patients often expect.
pharmacology__Respiratory Drugs__Other R.back: Nintedanib and pirfenidone slow the rate of lung-function decline; they do not reverse existing fibrosis or cure IPF. Setting this expectation matters - the goal is slower progression, alongside supportive care and considering transplant.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How do penicillins (beta-lactams) kill bacteria at a molecular level?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They bind penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases), inhibiting cross-linking of the peptidoglycan cell wall. This weakens the wall and activates autolysins -> bactericidal killing.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient reports a previous anaphylactic reaction to penicillin. Can you give any beta-lactam?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: No. A true type-1 (anaphylaxis) reaction means avoid ALL beta-lactams. There is roughly 1-2% cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins, so cephalosporins are also unsafe in true penicillin anaphylaxis.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why are penicillins as a class associated with C. difficile infection?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Like most antibiotics they disrupt normal gut flora, allowing C. difficile overgrowth -> diarrhoea/colitis. Broader-spectrum penicillins (co-amoxiclav, piperacillin-tazobactam) carry a higher risk.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why can benzylpenicillin (Pen G) only be given IV or IM, never orally?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It is acid-labile -> destroyed by stomach acid, so it is not absorbed orally. Only the acid-stable oral penicillins (e.g. phenoxymethylpenicillin, amoxicillin) can be swallowed.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the spectrum of benzylpenicillin and which infections is it used for?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Narrow spectrum: streptococci and meningococcus (Gram-positive and Gram-negative cocci). Used IV for streptococcal infections, meningococcal disease, endocarditis (with gentamicin), severe strep/clostridial infection, and syphilis (benzathine).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A GP sees a child with a non-blanching purpuric rash and suspected meningococcal disease. What penicillin is given before transfer to hospital?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IM/IV given immediately in the community before transfer. Give early -- do not delay for investigations.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the mechanism of phenoxymethylpenicillin (Pen V) and how does it differ from benzylpenicillin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Same penicillin-binding-protein / cell-wall mechanism as benzylpenicillin, but it is acid-stable so it is absorbed orally (though less potent). It is the oral narrow-spectrum penicillin.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: When should phenoxymethylpenicillin be prescribed for a sore throat?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Only when the score suggests bacterial (group A strep) infection: FeverPAIN 4-5 or Centor 3-4. Most sore throats are self-limiting and need no antibiotic.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which penicillin is used for long-term antibiotic prophylaxis in asplenia/post-splenectomy and sickle cell disease?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Phenoxymethylpenicillin (Pen V), taken long-term/lifelong to prevent overwhelming encapsulated-organism infection (e.g. pneumococcus) in asplenia, post-splenectomy, and sickle cell disease.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What makes flucloxacillin different from benzylpenicillin, and what does it treat?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Flucloxacillin is penicillinase-resistant -> its side chain blocks staphylococcal beta-lactamase, so it is active against MSSA (and streptococci). It is the go-to anti-staph penicillin for cellulitis, skin/soft-tissue infection, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, and staph endocarditis.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why does flucloxacillin (and other standard beta-lactams) fail against MRSA?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: MRSA has an altered, low-affinity penicillin-binding protein that beta-lactams cannot bind effectively, so all standard beta-lactams fail. MRSA needs an alternative agent (e.g. vancomycin).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How should flucloxacillin be taken in relation to food, and why?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Take it 1 hour before food (on an empty stomach). Food impairs its absorption, reducing effectiveness.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the signature/most characteristic adverse effect of flucloxacillin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Cholestatic hepatitis / jaundice. It is characteristic and can appear up to 2 months AFTER stopping the drug, especially in patients over 55 or with courses longer than 2 weeks.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient develops jaundice weeks after a course of flucloxacillin has finished. Is this consistent with the drug?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Yes. Flucloxacillin-induced cholestatic hepatitis can present delayed -- up to about 2 months after stopping -- particularly in older patients or after prolonged courses. Check LFTs. A previous episode is a contraindication as it can recur.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What metabolic disturbance can occur with high IV doses of flucloxacillin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Hypokalaemia (low K+) -- monitor U&Es/K+ with high IV doses.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why can flucloxacillin combined with paracetamol cause a metabolic problem, and what is it?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Together (especially in malnourished, elderly, or renally impaired patients) they can cause a high anion gap metabolic acidosis (pyroglutamic/5-oxoproline acidosis). Consider this in an unexplained high anion gap acidosis on this combination.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why must flucloxacillin be used with caution alongside methotrexate?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It reduces methotrexate excretion -> raised methotrexate levels -> methotrexate toxicity.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What are amoxicillin and ampicillin, and what advantage do they have over benzylpenicillin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They are broad-spectrum aminopenicillins -- an added amino group lets them penetrate Gram-negative porins, giving extended Gram-negative cover. However they are still destroyed by beta-lactamases.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which oral penicillin is first-line for community-acquired pneumonia?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Amoxicillin (a broad-spectrum aminopenicillin) is first-line for CAP. It is also used for otitis media, sinusitis, and dental/odontogenic infection.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Between amoxicillin and ampicillin, which is preferred orally and why?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Amoxicillin -- it is better absorbed orally than ampicillin, giving more reliable blood levels.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What extra organisms do amoxicillin/ampicillin cover that many other penicillins miss?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Listeria and enterococci -- amoxicillin/ampicillin are used for Listeria infection and enterococcal infection/endocarditis.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is amoxicillin's role in Helicobacter pylori eradication?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It forms part of PPI-based triple therapy (a PPI plus two antibiotics, one usually amoxicillin) to eradicate H. pylori.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient with glandular fever (EBV) is given amoxicillin and develops a widespread maculopapular rash. What is this?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: The classic EBV-amoxicillin (aminopenicillin) rash -- a widespread maculopapular rash triggered by giving an aminopenicillin during EBV/infectious mononucleosis. It is NOT a true penicillin allergy, but avoid aminopenicillins in suspected glandular fever.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the interaction between amoxicillin and warfarin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Amoxicillin can enhance the anticoagulant effect of warfarin, raising the INR. Monitor INR.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which drug, if co-prescribed with amoxicillin/ampicillin, notably increases the risk of a rash?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Allopurinol -- co-prescription increases the risk of a rash. (Amoxicillin also interacts with methotrexate -> toxicity, and warfarin -> raised INR.)

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is co-amoxiclav made of and what does the clavulanate add?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid, a beta-lactamase inhibitor. Clavulanate protects amoxicillin from beta-lactamases, broadening cover to include beta-lactamase-producing Gram-negatives, anaerobes, MSSA, and H. influenzae.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What are the typical indications for co-amoxiclav rather than plain amoxicillin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Defined indications needing broader cover: human/animal bites, aspiration or hospital pneumonia, intra-abdominal and biliary infection, and diabetic foot infection. It is a reserved/stewardship agent, not a routine broad-spectrum default.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which component of co-amoxiclav is the commonest cause of drug-induced (cholestatic) liver injury?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Clavulanate. Co-amoxiclav-associated cholestatic hepatitis/jaundice is the commonest cause of drug-induced liver injury, more common in men and those over 65, and may be delayed. A previous episode contraindicates re-use.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Does co-amoxiclav cover ESBL- or carbapenemase-producing organisms?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: No. Co-amoxiclav does not cover ESBL, AmpC, or carbapenemase producers -- these need a carbapenem (or other agent).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is co-amoxiclav considered a reserved antibiotic on stewardship grounds?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Its broad spectrum carries a higher risk of C. difficile infection and of cholestatic liver injury, so it is reserved for defined indications rather than used as a routine broad-spectrum default.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) and what key organism does it cover that most penicillins do not?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: An extended-spectrum penicillin (piperacillin, the anti-pseudomonal component) plus tazobactam (a beta-lactamase inhibitor), giving very broad cover including Pseudomonas, other Gram-negatives, and anaerobes. IV only.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A neutropenic patient on chemotherapy becomes febrile and septic. Which broad-spectrum IV penicillin is typically chosen, and why?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin), because neutropenic sepsis needs broad Gram-negative cover including anti-Pseudomonal activity. It is also used for hospital-acquired pneumonia and intra-abdominal sepsis.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What electrolyte and renal effects should be watched with piperacillin-tazobactam?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Hypokalaemia and a sodium load; it can also raise creatinine. Monitor renal function/U&Es. It can additionally give a false-positive Aspergillus galactomannan test.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is caution needed when giving piperacillin-tazobactam together with vancomycin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: The combination has additive nephrotoxicity -> increased risk of acute kidney injury. Monitor renal function and vancomycin levels.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: After starting broad-spectrum piperacillin-tazobactam empirically, what stewardship step should follow?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: De-escalate according to culture and sensitivity results -- narrow the antibiotic once the organism is known, to reduce C. difficile risk and resistance.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which penicillins carry the highest C. difficile risk and why does this matter clinically?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: The broad-spectrum agents co-amoxiclav and piperacillin-tazobactam. Their heavy disruption of gut flora makes C. difficile-associated diarrhoea/colitis more likely, which is a key reason to use them only when indicated and de-escalate promptly.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the mechanism of action of cephalosporins, and are they bactericidal or bacteriostatic?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They are beta-lactams: they bind penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) and inhibit bacterial cell-wall synthesis, making them bactericidal. Killing is time-dependent, so regular dosing matters.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which organisms do standard cephalosporins fail to cover?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Enterococci, Listeria, MRSA (except ceftaroline) and atypicals are not covered by standard cephalosporins.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Explain the cephalosporin generation concept in terms of spectrum.
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: 1st gen = good Gram-positive cover; higher generations progressively gain broader Gram-negative cover; 4th gen adds anti-Pseudomonal activity while keeping broad Gram-positive; 5th gen (ceftaroline) uniquely covers MRSA.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Cephalosporins are one of the '4C' high-risk antibiotics for C. difficile. What are the other three, and why does this matter?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: The 4Cs are cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav, clindamycin and ciprofloxacin. They are classic C. difficile inducers and are restricted in primary care to reduce C. difficile risk.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient develops profuse watery diarrhoea after a course of a cephalosporin. What complication should you suspect?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: C. difficile infection. Cephalosporins are classic C. difficile culprits (one of the '4C' antibiotics); stop the offending antibiotic and treat the C. difficile.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Is penicillin allergy an absolute contraindication to all cephalosporins?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: No. Cross-reactivity is low and side-chain-dependent, not class-wide. Avoid mainly in severe/anaphylactic penicillin allergy where the cephalosporin shares a side chain with the penicillin.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which cephalosporin shares a side chain with amoxicillin/ampicillin, so should be avoided in severe penicillin allergy?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Cefalexin (and cefadroxil) share their side chain with amoxicillin/ampicillin, so avoid them in severe/anaphylactic amoxicillin/ampicillin allergy.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the spectrum and main clinical niche of a 1st-generation cephalosporin like cefalexin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Good Gram-positive (staph/strep) cover with limited Gram-negative activity. It is oral and used for lower UTI and as a penicillin-allergy alternative in skin infection.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: When would you use oral cefalexin for a UTI, including in pregnancy?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Cefalexin is an option for lower UTI (a second-line choice) and is a useful oral option in pregnancy.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient with cellulitis cannot take flucloxacillin because of a mild penicillin allergy. What oral cephalosporin is an appropriate alternative?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Cefalexin. Flucloxacillin is first-line for cellulitis, but cefalexin is a reasonable penicillin-allergy alternative (cross-reactivity is low).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the typical oral dose of cefalexin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Cefalexin 500 mg BD to TDS.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Cefalexin can cause false-positive results on which two bedside/lab tests?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It can give a false-positive direct Coombs test and a false-positive urinary glucose (Benedict's/Clinitest).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the main clinical use of a 2nd-generation cephalosporin like cefuroxime?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Mainly surgical prophylaxis. It has broader Gram-negative cover than 1st gen while retaining some Gram-positive activity.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: In colorectal surgical prophylaxis, what is often added to cefuroxime and why?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Metronidazole is added to cover anaerobes, since cephalosporins do not reliably cover anaerobic bowel flora.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Name three 3rd-generation cephalosporins and the key property that distinguishes this generation.
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Ceftriaxone, cefotaxime and ceftazidime. They have extended Gram-negative cover plus good CNS penetration.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the first-line empirical antibiotic class for bacterial meningitis, and which agents are used?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: A 3rd-generation cephalosporin, ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, given empirically because of their extended Gram-negative spectrum and good CNS penetration.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: In a patient over 50, immunocompromised, pregnant or a neonate with suspected meningitis, what must you add to the cephalosporin and why?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Add amoxicillin (or ampicillin) to cover Listeria monocytogenes, which cephalosporins do not treat.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: When treating severe community-acquired pneumonia with a 3rd-generation cephalosporin, what should you pair it with and why?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Pair it with a macrolide, because cephalosporins do not cover atypical organisms.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the first-line treatment for gonorrhoea, and how is it given?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM as a single dose, now given as monotherapy (BASHH guidance).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which 3rd-generation cephalosporin is anti-Pseudomonal, and what is its weakness?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Ceftazidime is anti-Pseudomonal but has weak Gram-positive cover.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Besides meningitis, name two other severe infections a 3rd-generation cephalosporin is used for.
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Pyelonephritis and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (also severe CAP and gonorrhoea).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Heavy use of 3rd-generation cephalosporins selects for which resistant organisms, and how should confirmed ESBL infection be treated?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It selects for ESBL/AmpC producers and C. difficile. ESBLs hydrolyse 3rd-gen cephalosporins, so confirmed ESBL infection needs a carbapenem.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is ceftriaxone avoided in neonates, and what is used instead?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Ceftriaxone displaces bilirubin (risking kernicterus) and forms fatal ceftriaxone-calcium precipitates in the lungs/kidneys. Use cefotaxime in neonates instead.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why must ceftriaxone never be mixed or co-administered with IV calcium?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Ceftriaxone and calcium form insoluble precipitates that can be fatal (lung/kidney deposition, MHRA warning), especially in neonates. Never mix or co-give them via the same line.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What benign biliary side effect can ceftriaxone cause?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Biliary sludge / pseudolithiasis (ceftriaxone precipitating in bile), which can mimic gallstones and usually resolves after stopping.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How often is ceftriaxone dosed, and what dose is used in meningitis?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Once daily (long half-life) — typically 1-2 g IV OD. In meningitis, 2 g BD or 4 g OD is used.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the spectrum of the 4th-generation cephalosporin cefepime?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Broad Gram-positive AND anti-Pseudomonal Gram-negative cover, and it is stable to chromosomal AmpC (though still hydrolysed by ESBLs).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: In what clinical settings is cefepime used?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Severe hospital infections, neutropenic sepsis, and hospital-acquired pneumonia where broad cover is needed.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient on cefepime develops new confusion, myoclonus and seizures. What is the likely cause and who is at risk?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Cefepime neurotoxicity/encephalopathy (confusion, myoclonus, seizures, non-convulsive status epilepticus). It occurs especially in renal impairment; suspect it with any new confusion or reduced consciousness on treatment.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How do you reduce the risk of cefepime neurotoxicity?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Adjust the dose to renal function (CrCl) and monitor closely, since accumulation in renal impairment drives the encephalopathy.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which cephalosporin uniquely covers MRSA, and how?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Ceftaroline (5th generation). It binds the altered penicillin-binding protein of MRSA, so it works where standard beta-lactams fail.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Is ceftaroline anti-Pseudomonal, and what is its main clinical use?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: No, ceftaroline is not anti-Pseudomonal. It is used (specialist-only) for MRSA skin/soft-tissue infection and CAP.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What blood test should be monitored on prolonged ceftaroline courses?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: FBC — ceftaroline can cause neutropenia/agranulocytosis on prolonged use (also monitor renal function; it may cause a positive direct Coombs).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How do cephalosporins interact with warfarin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They can enhance anticoagulation and raise the INR, so monitor INR when co-prescribed.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the risk of combining a cephalosporin with an aminoglycoside?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Additive nephrotoxicity — monitor renal function when they are used together.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What class of antibiotic are meropenem, imipenem and ertapenem, and how do they kill bacteria?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Carbapenems — beta-lactam antibiotics. They bind penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) and inhibit cell-wall synthesis, making them bactericidal.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why are carbapenems described as the 'broadest-spectrum' beta-lactams?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They cover Gram-positive AND Gram-negative bacteria, anaerobes, and Pseudomonas (meropenem/imipenem) in a single agent — the widest cover of any beta-lactam class.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient has a confirmed ESBL-producing Gram-negative bloodstream infection. Why is a carbapenem the agent of choice?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Carbapenems are stable to ESBL (extended-spectrum beta-lactamase) and AmpC enzymes, so they remain effective when penicillins and cephalosporins are hydrolysed. They are the go-to for confirmed ESBL infection.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How can bacteria become resistant to carbapenems?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: By producing carbapenemase enzymes that hydrolyse the drug — giving carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE). These infections are very difficult to treat and are a major stewardship concern.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: In what clinical situations would a carbapenem typically be started?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Severe or resistant infections: hospital-acquired sepsis, intra-abdominal infection, ESBL-producing Gram-negatives, and febrile neutropenia — when very broad Gram-positive, Gram-negative, anaerobic and (with meropenem) Pseudomonal cover is needed.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why are carbapenems kept as 'last-line' reserved antibiotics rather than used routinely?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Antimicrobial stewardship — overuse drives carbapenem resistance (CRE), for which few treatment options remain. Once cultures return, therapy should be de-escalated to a narrower agent.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Can a carbapenem be given to a patient with a penicillin allergy?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Cross-reactivity exists but is lower than historically thought, so a carbapenem can often be used with caution. However, they must be AVOIDED in a patient with true anaphylaxis to a penicillin or carbapenem.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which important gut-related infection can carbapenems precipitate, like other broad-spectrum antibiotics?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) colitis — presents with diarrhoea, often after broad-spectrum use. Their very wide spectrum makes this a real risk.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: List the key adverse effects of carbapenems a student should know.
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: C. difficile infection, hypersensitivity reactions, thrombophlebitis at the infusion site, and seizures (lowered seizure threshold).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient on a carbapenem develops seizures. Which carbapenem is most implicated, and who is at greatest risk?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Imipenem — it lowers the seizure threshold most. Risk is higher with renal impairment, high doses, and pre-existing CNS disease (e.g. epilepsy, meningitis).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient with epilepsy is on sodium valproate and needs a carbapenem. What is the dangerous interaction?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Carbapenems dramatically LOWER valproate levels, causing loss of seizure control and breakthrough seizures. The combination should be avoided — use an alternative antibiotic or alternative seizure control.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which carbapenem is preferred for CNS infections such as meningitis, and why?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Meropenem — it has the broadest spectrum (including Pseudomonas) and a lower seizure risk than imipenem, making it safer and effective in CNS infection. Dosing is increased (e.g. 2 g IV in meningitis).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is imipenem always given combined with cilastatin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Cilastatin blocks a kidney enzyme that would otherwise break down imipenem in the renal tubules, so it protects the drug and maintains effective levels. Meropenem and ertapenem do not need it.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How does ertapenem differ from meropenem in terms of dosing and spectrum?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Ertapenem is given once daily (convenient for community/OPAT), but crucially has NO Pseudomonas cover. Meropenem covers Pseudomonas and is dosed every 8 hours — used for hospital/severe infection where Pseudomonas is a concern.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Your patient with a serious Pseudomonas infection — is ertapenem an appropriate carbapenem?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: No. Ertapenem does not cover Pseudomonas (or Acinetobacter). Choose meropenem (or imipenem) when Pseudomonal cover is needed.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How are carbapenems administered, and what must be monitored during treatment?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They are given intravenously. Monitor renal function and dose-adjust in renal impairment (important as accumulation raises seizure risk, especially with imipenem).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is ertapenem's once-daily dosing clinically useful?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It suits outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy (OPAT) and community treatment, allowing a single daily IV dose — practical for patients who don't need Pseudomonal cover.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the mechanism of action of macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin, azithromycin)?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They bind the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit and inhibit protein synthesis, making them bacteriostatic.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the antibacterial spectrum of the macrolides, and in which patient group are they a particularly useful alternative?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They cover atypical organisms and Gram-positive bacteria. They are a useful alternative in patients with penicillin allergy.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: In moderate-to-severe community-acquired pneumonia, how is a macrolide typically used alongside a penicillin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: A macrolide (e.g. clarithromycin) is ADDED to amoxicillin to provide atypical cover (Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila). In penicillin allergy or low-severity CAP a macrolide can be used as monotherapy.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Name three respiratory/other infections (besides CAP) for which a macrolide is a recognised choice.
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Penicillin-allergic streptococcal infections, whooping cough (pertussis), and genital Chlamydia (azithromycin, now second-line as doxycycline is first-line). Clarithromycin is also used in H. pylori eradication.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which macrolide is used in H. pylori triple therapy?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Clarithromycin (combined with a proton pump inhibitor and a second antibiotic such as amoxicillin or metronidazole).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why might a patient with bronchiectasis or COPD be prescribed low-dose azithromycin three times a week?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: As long-term prophylaxis to reduce infective exacerbations — it is used for its anti-inflammatory effect, not just as an antibiotic course.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the standard oral dose of clarithromycin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: 500 mg twice daily (BD).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the typical azithromycin regimen for a short treatment course, and what single dose is used for genital Chlamydia?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: 500 mg once daily for 3 days for a short course. For Chlamydia it can be given as a 1 g stat dose (as a second-line agent).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How often is erythromycin dosed?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Four times a day (QDS), typically 250-500 mg.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What serious cardiac effect can all macrolides cause, and what are the key risk factors?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They prolong the QT interval and can precipitate torsades de pointes. Caution/avoid with other QT-prolonging drugs, hypokalaemia, and congenital long-QT syndrome.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What specific cardiovascular caution applies to clarithromycin (per an MHRA warning)?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Clarithromycin should be used with caution in patients with coronary artery disease, due to a signal of increased cardiovascular risk.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Besides QT prolongation, name two other important adverse effects of macrolides.
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Cholestatic hepatitis and reversible ototoxicity (at high doses). GI upset and rash also occur.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient on long-term simvastatin needs a course of clarithromycin. What is the safe practical action and why?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Stop the statin for the duration of the macrolide course. Clarithromycin (and erythromycin) inhibit the metabolism of simvastatin, raising its levels and greatly increasing the risk of rhabdomyolysis — the combination is contraindicated.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How do clarithromycin and erythromycin affect a patient taking warfarin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They inhibit the metabolism of warfarin, raising its levels and the INR, which increases bleeding risk. Monitor the INR closely.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Give three drugs (other than statins and warfarin) whose levels/toxicity rise when co-prescribed with clarithromycin or erythromycin.
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Colchicine (risk of toxicity), digoxin, and ciclosporin/tacrolimus. These macrolides inhibit the metabolism of these drugs, raising their levels.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which macrolide has the fewest drug interactions, and why is this clinically useful?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Azithromycin — it has the least effect on the metabolism of other drugs. This makes it a safer choice in patients on multiple interacting medications such as warfarin or statins.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why does erythromycin cause the most gastrointestinal upset of the macrolides, and how is this effect sometimes exploited?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Erythromycin stimulates gut motility (it is a motilin agonist), causing marked nausea and cramps. This same prokinetic action means it is sometimes used deliberately to promote gastric emptying/gut motility.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which macrolide is preferred in pregnancy, and what neonatal complication is it linked to?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Erythromycin is the macrolide of choice in pregnancy. However, in neonates it has been associated with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How does azithromycin's long duration of action affect its dosing compared with erythromycin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Azithromycin is long-acting, allowing once-daily dosing as a single dose or a short 3-day course, whereas erythromycin must be taken four times a day.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient with penicillin allergy has low-severity community-acquired pneumonia. What is a suitable antibiotic choice?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: A macrolide such as clarithromycin as monotherapy — it covers Gram-positives and atypicals and is a safe alternative in penicillin allergy.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the mechanism of action of tetracyclines (e.g. doxycycline), and are they bactericidal or bacteriostatic?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They bind the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit and block aminoacyl-tRNA binding at the A site, inhibiting protein synthesis. They are bacteriostatic.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why do tetracyclines cover atypical and intracellular organisms so well, and which agent has particularly good tissue/prostate penetration?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They are broad-spectrum and penetrate cells, covering atypicals/intracellular bugs (e.g. Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Rickettsia). Doxycycline is lipophilic, giving excellent tissue, intracellular and prostate penetration.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the first-line antibiotic for genital Chlamydia, and at what dose and duration?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days. It is also used for pelvic inflammatory disease.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Name the main clinical uses of doxycycline a UK student should know.
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Chlamydia and PID, acne and rosacea, atypical/community-acquired pneumonia (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Q fever), Lyme disease, rickettsia, brucellosis, malaria prophylaxis and COPD exacerbations.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why are tetracyclines contraindicated in pregnancy, breastfeeding, and children under 12?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They deposit in growing bone and teeth, causing permanent tooth discolouration and dental enamel hypoplasia. Avoid in pregnancy, breastfeeding and children under 12.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient on doxycycline develops a rash on sun-exposed skin. What is happening and how do you counsel them?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Photosensitivity is a recognised tetracycline side effect. Counsel on sun protection (cover up, sunscreen, avoid strong sunlight).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How should a patient take oral doxycycline to avoid oesophagitis, and why?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Take with plenty of water, while sitting or standing upright, and do not lie down for a while afterwards. Tetracyclines can cause oesophagitis/oesophageal ulceration if a tablet lodges in the oesophagus.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A young woman on doxycycline for acne complains of headache and blurred vision. What serious side effect must you consider?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Benign (idiopathic) intracranial hypertension. It presents with headache and visual disturbance; stop the drug and investigate.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which everyday substances chelate tetracyclines and reduce their absorption, and how do you manage this?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Divalent/trivalent cations: antacids, calcium, iron, magnesium, zinc, and milk/dairy. They markedly reduce absorption, so separate the doses by 2-3 hours.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the effect of doxycycline on a patient taking warfarin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It enhances the anticoagulant effect and raises the INR. Monitor INR and adjust warfarin as needed.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why should oral retinoids (isotretinoin/acitretin) not be combined with a tetracycline, and why is this clinically relevant?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Both can cause raised intracranial pressure, so the combination gives an additive risk of intracranial hypertension. It is relevant because both are used for acne, so the overlap is easy to miss.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the typical dosing of doxycycline, and of lymecycline when used for acne?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Doxycycline 100 mg once or twice daily (with a 200 mg loading dose in some indications). Lymecycline 408 mg once daily for acne.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is doxycycline the 'go-to' tetracycline?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It is well absorbed, dosed once or twice daily, and safe in renal impairment. It is used for Chlamydia, Lyme disease, malaria prophylaxis and acne.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which tetracycline is a common oral choice for acne, and at what dose?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Lymecycline 408 mg once daily.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is tigecycline, and why must it be avoided in bacteraemia and urinary tract infection?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Tigecycline is an IV glycylcycline with very broad cover (including some MRSA and ESBL organisms). It achieves low serum levels, so it should be avoided in bacteraemia and UTI due to a mortality signal in these settings.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: For what non-antibiotic indication is demeclocycline used, and by what mechanism?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate ADH). It antagonises the renal action of ADH, promoting water excretion, and is used essentially for this rather than as an antibiotic.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient with suspected Lyme disease after a tick bite needs an oral antibiotic. What is a standard choice?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Doxycycline. It is a first-line oral agent for Lyme disease (in adults and children over 12, and outside pregnancy).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which tetracycline is used for malaria prophylaxis, and why is it suitable?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Doxycycline. It is well absorbed once daily, broad spectrum, and effective for malaria prophylaxis.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A pregnant woman with a chest infection would normally receive doxycycline for atypical cover. Why can she not have it, and what does this illustrate?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Tetracyclines are contraindicated in pregnancy because they deposit in fetal bone and teeth. An alternative (e.g. a macrolide) is needed for atypical cover.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient taking iron tablets is prescribed doxycycline and told it 'isn't working'. What is the likely explanation?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Iron chelates the tetracycline and markedly reduces its absorption. The doses should be separated by 2-3 hours (the same applies to antacids, calcium, zinc and dairy).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Besides pregnancy and children, in which patient group should tetracyclines be avoided?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Patients with severe hepatic impairment, as tetracyclines can rarely cause hepatotoxicity.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the mechanism of action of the fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin)?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, preventing DNA supercoiling and replication. This makes them bactericidal, with excellent Gram-negative cover (including Pseudomonas with ciprofloxacin) and good oral bioavailability and tissue penetration.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why are fluoroquinolones considered 'reserve' antibiotics under MHRA guidance?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They carry rare but serious, sometimes irreversible and disabling side effects (tendon, aortic, neurological, mental-health). They should be reserved for when other antibiotics are unsuitable, and NOT used for mild or self-limiting infections.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient needs oral cover for a Pseudomonas infection. Which fluoroquinolone is the agent of choice, and why?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Ciprofloxacin — it has the best Gram-negative and Pseudomonas cover of the class, plus good oral bioavailability. (It is comparatively weak against pneumococcus.)

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: For which infections might ciprofloxacin be used (when other antibiotics are unsuitable)?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Complicated UTI/pyelonephritis, Pseudomonas infections, severe bacterial gastroenteritis (Campylobacter, Shigella, Salmonella — not routine self-limiting cases), intra-abdominal infection (with metronidazole), prostatitis (good prostate penetration), and anthrax prophylaxis.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why are levofloxacin and moxifloxacin called 'respiratory quinolones'?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They have good activity against Streptococcus pneumoniae and atypical organisms, so they can be used for community-acquired pneumonia and atypical infections when a penicillin is unsuitable.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient with suspected gonorrhoea asks if they will get a quinolone like ciprofloxacin. What is the current first-line treatment?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Gonorrhoea is now treated with ceftriaxone, NOT a quinolone. Quinolones are no longer used first-line due to resistance.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What serious musculoskeletal side effect is associated with fluoroquinolones, and what should you tell the patient?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Tendonitis and tendon rupture, classically the Achilles tendon. Advise the patient to stop the drug and seek help at the first sign of tendon pain. Risk is higher with corticosteroids, in the elderly, and in renal impairment.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A 70-year-old on long-term prednisolone is started on ciprofloxacin. Why does this combination worry you?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Both corticosteroids and older age markedly increase the risk of fluoroquinolone-associated tendonitis and Achilles tendon rupture. The combination is best avoided; if used, warn the patient to stop at any tendon pain.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which cardiovascular/aortic risk do fluoroquinolones carry (MHRA warning)?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They are associated with aortic aneurysm and aortic dissection (and heart-valve regurgitation). Use with particular caution in patients at risk of aortic disease.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why must fluoroquinolones be used cautiously in patients with epilepsy?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They lower the seizure threshold and can provoke seizures. Use with caution or avoid in epilepsy, and be aware NSAIDs given alongside further increase seizure risk.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why should fluoroquinolones be avoided in a patient with myasthenia gravis?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They can worsen myasthenia gravis, potentially precipitating muscle weakness and respiratory compromise.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What neurological side effect of fluoroquinolones can be irreversible, and how should it be acted on?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Peripheral neuropathy. Advise the patient to stop the drug and seek medical advice at the first neurological symptoms (e.g. pain, tingling, numbness, weakness), as it can be long-lasting or permanent.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What disabling psychiatric side effects can fluoroquinolones cause (MHRA warning)?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Disabling and potentially long-lasting mental-health reactions, which can include suicidal ideation. These can occur even after a single dose and warrant stopping the drug.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which cardiac electrical effect do fluoroquinolones share, and which agent has the greatest effect?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They prolong the QT interval. Moxifloxacin has the longest QT effect of the class. Avoid combining with other QT-prolonging drugs and check ECG/electrolytes if risk factors are present.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why are fluoroquinolones flagged as high-risk for C. difficile infection?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Ciprofloxacin is one of the '4C' antibiotics with a high risk of causing C. difficile-associated diarrhoea. This is a key reason for their restricted, reserve-only use.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What effect can fluoroquinolones have on blood glucose?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They can cause dysglycaemia — both hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia. Monitor blood glucose, particularly in diabetic patients.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Are fluoroquinolones safe in pregnancy and children?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They are generally avoided in pregnancy and children because of concerns about cartilage/joint development, but may be used when essential and no suitable alternative exists.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient taking ciprofloxacin also uses an antacid, iron tablets, and calcium supplements. What is the problem and how do you manage it?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Divalent cations (antacids, calcium, iron, zinc, milk, sucralfate) bind ciprofloxacin and reduce its absorption. Separate the doses by at least 2 hours.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is ciprofloxacin dangerous in a patient taking theophylline?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Ciprofloxacin inhibits the metabolism of theophylline, raising its level and risking theophylline toxicity. Monitor closely or avoid the combination.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is tizanidine contraindicated with ciprofloxacin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Ciprofloxacin inhibits the metabolism of tizanidine, markedly raising its levels (risking hypotension and sedation). The combination is contraindicated.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What happens to the INR when ciprofloxacin is given to a patient on warfarin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Ciprofloxacin potentiates warfarin, raising the INR and increasing bleeding risk. Monitor INR closely.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is a standard oral dose of ciprofloxacin, and of levofloxacin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily orally. Levofloxacin 500 mg once daily.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is moxifloxacin NOT used to treat urinary tract infections?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Moxifloxacin does not achieve adequate urinary concentrations, so it is ineffective for UTI. It is used for respiratory infections and has additional anaerobe cover (but the longest QT effect of the class).

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How does ciprofloxacin's spectrum differ from levofloxacin's in choosing therapy?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Ciprofloxacin gives the best Gram-negative and Pseudomonas cover (UTI, GI infections) but is weak against pneumococcus. Levofloxacin is a 'respiratory quinolone' with good pneumococcal and atypical cover, favouring community-acquired pneumonia.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What key counselling points should a patient starting a fluoroquinolone be given?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Stop the drug and seek medical help at any tendon pain or new neurological symptoms. Separate doses from antacids/calcium/iron by at least 2 hours, and be alert to mood changes. Report palpitations, and diabetics should monitor blood glucose.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides such as gentamicin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They bind the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, causing misreading of mRNA and inhibiting protein synthesis. This makes them bactericidal, with concentration-dependent killing and a prolonged post-antibiotic effect.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why are aminoglycosides given intravenously or intramuscularly rather than orally for systemic infection?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They are very poorly absorbed from the gut, so oral dosing gives no useful systemic levels. Systemic treatment must be given IV or IM. (Oral neomycin is used only for its local effect in bowel prep.)

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why are aminoglycosides ineffective against anaerobic bacteria?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Uptake of the drug into the bacterial cell is oxygen-dependent. Anaerobes cannot take the drug up, so aminoglycosides have no anaerobic cover — hence they are often combined with metronidazole for intra-abdominal sepsis.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What type of organisms do aminoglycosides cover best, and how are they used against Gram-positives?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They have excellent Gram-negative cover. Against Gram-positives they are used for synergy — combined with a cell-wall agent (e.g. a penicillin) which enhances aminoglycoside entry, as in endocarditis regimens.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What are the main clinical indications for gentamicin?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Empirical treatment of Gram-negative sepsis, pyelonephritis/complicated UTI, and biliary or intra-abdominal sepsis (with a penicillin +/- metronidazole). It is also used in divided doses for endocarditis synergy.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: In which infections is gentamicin used for 'synergy', and with what?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: In endocarditis — mainly enterococcal, selected streptococcal, and prosthetic-valve regimens — combined with a cell-wall active agent such as a penicillin. A lower divided-dose regimen is used for this purpose.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which aminoglycoside is reserved for gentamicin-resistant Gram-negative organisms, and why?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Amikacin. It resists most aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes, so it retains activity against many strains that are resistant to gentamicin.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How is tobramycin used in cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It is given nebulised (inhaled) to suppress chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection in the airways, delivering high local drug levels while limiting systemic toxicity.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What is the role of streptomycin in modern practice?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It is a second-line agent for tuberculosis, used within combination anti-TB regimens when first-line drugs cannot be used.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why is neomycin restricted to topical and bowel-preparation use rather than systemic treatment?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It is too toxic to give systemically. It is used topically or orally (poorly absorbed) for a local effect in the gut, e.g. bowel decontamination/prep.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: What are the two major dose-limiting toxicities of aminoglycosides?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Nephrotoxicity (acute tubular necrosis) and ototoxicity (cochlear hearing loss and vestibular/balance damage). Risk rises with longer duration, high trough levels, renal impairment, and other nephro-/ototoxic drugs.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Contrast the reversibility of aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Nephrotoxicity is due to acute tubular necrosis and is usually reversible once the drug is stopped. Ototoxicity — both cochlear (hearing loss) and vestibular (balance) — may be permanent, so it is the more feared toxicity.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Besides kidney and ear damage, what other important toxicity can aminoglycosides cause?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: Neuromuscular blockade — they impair neuromuscular transmission. This is especially dangerous in myasthenia gravis and can potentiate non-depolarising muscle relaxants.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: A patient reports a family history of deafness after receiving gentamicin. Why does this matter before prescribing an aminoglycoside?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It suggests a mitochondrial mutation (m.1555A>G). Carriers can develop rapid, irreversible deafness even at normal drug levels. The MHRA advises asking about a family history of aminoglycoside-induced deafness before prescribing.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why should aminoglycosides be avoided in myasthenia gravis?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They cause neuromuscular blockade, which worsens the underlying defect in neuromuscular transmission and can precipitate or worsen weakness, including respiratory compromise.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Why are aminoglycosides generally avoided in pregnancy?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: They are ototoxic to the fetus and can cause fetal hearing damage, so they are avoided unless there is a compelling indication.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: How is gentamicin normally dosed, and what is the rationale for once-daily dosing?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: It is given once daily by body weight using a nomogram (e.g. 5-7 mg/kg). Once-daily dosing exploits concentration-dependent killing and the prolonged post-antibiotic effect, maximising efficacy while reducing accumulation and toxicity.

pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.front: Which gentamicin level is monitored routinely, and how is a high result acted upon?
pharmacology__Antibiotics & Antimicrobia.back: The pre-dose (trough) level. A high trough means the drug is accumulating between doses, so you reduce the dose or extend the dosing interval. (Peak levels are checked in divided-dose/synergy regimens.)
