Anti-TNF biologics and JAK inhibitors carry more systemic infection and other risks (e.g. TB/hepatitis B reactivation, lymphoma; and for JAK inhibitors shingles, VTE and MACE).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What class of drug is ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), and how does it help in cholestatic liver disease?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: UDCA is a hydrophilic (non-toxic) bile acid. It replaces toxic hydrophobic bile acids, improves bile flow, and is cytoprotective -> slows cholestatic liver injury.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the first-line drug treatment for primary biliary cholangitis (PBC)?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA). It improves LFTs and slows disease progression, and is generally well tolerated.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Besides primary biliary cholangitis, name two other uses of ursodeoxycholic acid.
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Dissolving small cholesterol gallstones, and treating intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why is UDCA not useful for all gallstones, and when is it contraindicated?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It only dissolves small cholesterol stones — it does not work on calcified/radio-opaque or pigment stones. Avoid in complete biliary obstruction.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient with PBC also takes cholestyramine and an aluminium antacid. How should UDCA be timed?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Cholestyramine (bile-acid sequestrants) and aluminium antacids bind UDCA and reduce its absorption. Separate the doses (take UDCA a few hours apart) so it can still be absorbed.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How is response to UDCA in PBC monitored?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: By checking LFTs — improvement in liver enzymes indicates a good biochemical response. Poor response identifies patients who may need second-line therapy.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are the common side effects of UDCA?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Generally well tolerated. May cause diarrhoea, GI upset, and weight gain.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the second-line drug for PBC when the response to UDCA is inadequate or UDCA is not tolerated?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Obeticholic acid — added on to UDCA (or used alone if UDCA is not tolerated).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How does obeticholic acid work in PBC?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It reduces bile-acid synthesis in the liver, lowering the bile-acid load and slowing cholestatic injury. This mechanism also explains its tendency to raise LDL cholesterol.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the main, often dose-limiting, side effect of obeticholic acid in PBC?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Pruritus — it commonly worsens the itch of PBC and this often limits the dose. It can also raise LDL cholesterol and cause fatigue.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why must obeticholic acid be avoided in decompensated cirrhosis or portal hypertension?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It is associated with hepatic decompensation in these patients — daily dosing in cirrhosis has caused fatal decompensation (MHRA warning), so it is avoided/contraindicated.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A PBC patient with Child-Pugh B cirrhosis is starting obeticholic acid. How does the dosing differ from a patient with normal liver function?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: In cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B/C or any prior decompensation) it must be given WEEKLY, not daily. Daily dosing in cirrhosis caused fatal hepatic decompensation (MHRA safety alert).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What monitoring is required on obeticholic acid, and when should it be stopped?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Monitor LFTs (baseline, early months, and after any dose increase) and lipids (LDL rise). Stop the drug if hepatic decompensation develops.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the first-line drug to treat and prevent hepatic encephalopathy?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Lactulose. It lowers blood ammonia and is used both to treat acute episodes and to prevent recurrence.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How does lactulose lower blood ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Colonic bacteria ferment it to acids, lowering the gut pH. This traps ammonia (NH3) as ammonium (NH4+), which is non-absorbable and excreted in stool -> less ammonia enters the blood.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How is lactulose titrated when treating hepatic encephalopathy?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Titrate the dose to produce 2-3 soft stools per day.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: You are treating a patient with hepatic encephalopathy. Besides giving lactulose, what else is essential to do?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Actively seek and treat the precipitant. Common triggers: infection (including SBP), GI bleed, constipation, electrolyte disturbance, sedatives, and dehydration.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why can over-titrating lactulose paradoxically worsen hepatic encephalopathy?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Excessive stooling causes dehydration and electrolyte disturbance, which are themselves precipitants of encephalopathy. Monitor fluid status and electrolytes and aim for just 2-3 soft stools/day.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Name two contraindications to lactulose.
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Galactosaemia, and GI obstruction or perforation.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What drug is added to lactulose to prevent recurrent hepatic encephalopathy?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Rifaximin — used for secondary prevention, added on to lactulose to reduce recurrent episodes.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How does rifaximin reduce recurrence of hepatic encephalopathy?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It is a gut-restricted (barely absorbed) antibiotic that reduces the ammonia-producing bacteria in the gut, lowering ammonia production.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why is rifaximin so well tolerated in patients with hepatic encephalopathy?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It is almost entirely non-absorbed (acts within the gut lumen), so there is minimal systemic exposure. Side effects are minor (e.g. GI upset).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What class of drug is terlipressin and what is its core mechanism in variceal bleeding?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: A vasopressin (ADH) analogue. It acts on V1 receptors to cause splanchnic vasoconstriction, reducing portal inflow and portal pressure, which reduces variceal bleeding.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient with known cirrhosis presents haematemesis from suspected oesophageal varices. Which vasoactive drug should be started?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Terlipressin, given as intermittent IV boluses (e.g. 1-2 mg every 4-6 h). It causes splanchnic vasoconstriction to lower portal pressure and control the bleed.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are the key components of the acute variceal bleed 'bundle' in cirrhosis?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Resuscitation, restrictive blood transfusion (aim Hb ~70 g/L), terlipressin, prophylactic antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone), and endoscopic band ligation within 24 hours. TIPS is used as rescue if bleeding is uncontrolled.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why are prophylactic antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone) given in an acute variceal bleed?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Cirrhotic patients with a GI bleed are at high risk of bacterial infection; prophylactic antibiotics reduce infection, rebleeding and mortality. They are a standard part of the bleed bundle.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the definitive endoscopic treatment for bleeding oesophageal varices, and within what timeframe?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Endoscopic band ligation, ideally within 24 hours of presentation. Terlipressin and antibiotics are supportive measures given while awaiting endoscopy.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What blood transfusion strategy is recommended in acute variceal/upper GI bleeding in cirrhosis?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: A restrictive strategy, transfusing to a target Hb of around 70 g/L. Over-transfusion raises portal pressure and can worsen bleeding.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Besides variceal bleeding, what is terlipressin used to treat, and what must be co-administered?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS-AKI). It is given together with IV albumin — terlipressin plus albumin is the standard regimen; it raises systemic BP and improves renal perfusion.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the main class of adverse effect of terlipressin, and which patients should therefore avoid it?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Ischaemia from vasoconstriction — cardiac, mesenteric and peripheral/digital ischaemia. Avoid in ischaemic heart disease, peripheral vascular disease and uncontrolled hypertension.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Besides ischaemia, what electrolyte disturbance can terlipressin cause?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Hyponatraemia (from residual V2 receptor activity). Monitor sodium during treatment, along with BP and for signs of ischaemic complications.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What 2023 MHRA safety warning applies to terlipressin in advanced liver disease?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Risk of serious/fatal respiratory failure and worsening septic shock. Avoid in advanced acute-on-chronic liver failure (grade 3) and advanced renal failure; correct fluid overload and respiratory problems first and monitor closely.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How do non-selective beta-blockers lower portal pressure in cirrhosis?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Beta-1 blockade reduces cardiac output, and beta-2 blockade leaves unopposed alpha activity causing splanchnic vasoconstriction — both reduce portal inflow and lower portal pressure. Carvedilol adds alpha-1 blockade for extra reduction.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the role of non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol/carvedilol) in varices — acute bleeding or prophylaxis?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Prophylaxis of variceal bleeding (primary or secondary), NOT treatment of the acute bleed. They lower portal pressure over time to prevent bleeding.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Which non-selective beta-blocker is now preferred for variceal prophylaxis, and why?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Carvedilol, because it produces a greater reduction in portal pressure (it adds alpha-1 blockade). It is dosed low once daily and titrated by BP rather than heart rate.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why do cardioselective (beta-1-only) beta-blockers NOT work for lowering portal pressure?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: The splanchnic vasoconstriction that reduces portal inflow depends on beta-2 blockade (unopposed alpha). Cardioselective agents lack meaningful beta-2 effect, so they do not lower portal pressure — you must use a non-selective beta-blocker.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How is propranolol titrated when used for variceal prophylaxis?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Titrate to about a 25% drop in resting heart rate, or to a heart rate of ~55-60 bpm. Monitor heart rate and blood pressure for both efficacy and safety.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the standard regimen for SECONDARY prophylaxis of variceal bleeding (after a first bleed)?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: A non-selective beta-blocker PLUS repeated endoscopic band ligation. (Primary prophylaxis is a non-selective beta-blocker OR band ligation.)

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A cirrhotic patient with varices also has asthma — why can't you give a non-selective beta-blocker, and when else should carvedilol be withheld?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Non-selective beta-blockers cause beta-2 mediated bronchospasm, so they are contraindicated in asthma. Also withhold carvedilol if systolic BP <90 mmHg or in refractory ascites with hypotension (the 'window' where beta-blockers become harmful).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the mechanism of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) as the antidote in paracetamol overdose?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It replenishes hepatic glutathione, allowing detoxification of the toxic paracetamol metabolite NAPQI, thereby preventing or limiting hepatocellular necrosis.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How do you decide whether to treat a single-timing paracetamol overdose with NAC?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Measure the paracetamol level at least 4 hours post-ingestion and plot it on the treatment nomogram; treat with NAC if the level is above the treatment line.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: In which paracetamol overdose scenarios should NAC be started empirically without waiting for a level?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: When presentation is more than 8 hours post-ingestion, when the overdose is staggered, or when the timing of ingestion is unknown. Do not delay treatment for a nomogram level in these cases.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How is NAC administered in paracetamol overdose?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Intravenously as a weight-based regimen — the modern 2-bag regimen (first bag over 2 h, then over 10 h), which causes fewer anaphylactoid reactions than the older 3-bag regimen.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: A patient on an NAC infusion develops flushing, urticaria and wheeze. What is this and how do you manage it?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: An anaphylactoid reaction — infusion-rate related, NOT a true allergy. Pause or slow the infusion, give an antihistamine (+/- salbutamol for bronchospasm), then restart at a slower rate. Do not abandon treatment.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What are King's College Criteria used for in paracetamol-induced liver failure, and what are they?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: They identify patients needing referral to a liver transplant unit. Refer if arterial pH <7.3, OR the triad of INR >6.5 + creatinine >300 micromol/L + grade III/IV encephalopathy.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What is the stepwise drug ladder for cholestatic pruritus (e.g. in PBC)?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: First-line cholestyramine (bile-acid sequestrant) -> second-line rifampicin -> then naltrexone (opioid antagonist) or sertraline. Escalate when the itch remains troublesome.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Why must cholestyramine be dose-separated from other medications, and how?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It binds many drugs in the gut — including UDCA and obeticholic acid, warfarin, digoxin, levothyroxine and fat-soluble vitamins (A/D/E/K) — reducing their absorption. Give other drugs 1 hour before or 4-6 hours after cholestyramine.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: What safety issues accompany rifampicin when used second-line for cholestatic pruritus?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: Watch for hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs), harmless orange discolouration of body fluids, and that rifampicin is a potent enzyme inducer — it can cause contraceptive failure and reduce the effect of warfarin and many other drugs.

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: Before starting naltrexone for cholestatic pruritus, what must you check?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: That the patient is opioid-free — naltrexone is an opioid antagonist and will precipitate opioid withdrawal if the patient is taking opioids (needs to be off them for roughly 7-10 days first).

pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.front: How does naltrexone relieve the itch of cholestasis?
pharmacology__Gastroenterology & Hepatol.back: It is an opioid antagonist that blocks central opioidergic itch signalling. It sits at the top of the ladder (with sertraline as an alternative) when cholestyramine and rifampicin are insufficient.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What class of drug is metformin, and what is its main mechanism for lowering blood glucose?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: A biguanide. It mainly reduces hepatic glucose production (gluconeogenesis) and increases peripheral insulin sensitivity/glucose uptake. It does not stimulate insulin release.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which oral diabetes drug is first-line for type 2 diabetes in all patients unless contraindicated?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Metformin. It reduces hepatic glucose output and is started in every patient with T2DM unless there is a contraindication.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why does metformin not cause hypoglycaemia and stay weight-neutral as monotherapy?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: It does not stimulate insulin secretion — it lowers glucose by reducing hepatic glucose production and improving insulin sensitivity. So as monotherapy it causes no hypoglycaemia and is weight-neutral.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: A patient starting metformin also has established atherosclerotic CVD, heart failure, or high CV risk. What does NICE (2022) advise adding first-line?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Add an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven CV benefit first-line, alongside metformin (once metformin is tolerated). The SGLT2 inhibitor is added because of its cardiovascular and renal protection.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Besides type 2 diabetes, name another common condition in which metformin is used.
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)/insulin resistance.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What are the common early side effects of metformin, and how can they be managed?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: GI upset — nausea, diarrhoea, cramps, metallic taste (dose-related). Take with food, titrate slowly, and switch to a modified-release preparation before abandoning the drug.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What long-term deficiency can metformin cause, and what should be monitored?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use. Check B12 levels periodically on long-term treatment.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What rare but serious metabolic complication can metformin cause, and who is most at risk?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Lactic acidosis. Risk is highest in renal impairment, hypoxia, sepsis, and dehydration.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How is metformin dosing adjusted at eGFR 30-45 versus below 30?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: At eGFR 30-45: review and reduce the dose (and do not initiate). If eGFR falls below 30: stop metformin (lactic acidosis risk).

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: In which acute situations should metformin be withheld (sick-day rules)?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Withhold in acute kidney injury, severe illness, sepsis, and dehydration — states that raise the risk of lactic acidosis.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How should metformin be managed around IV iodinated contrast?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Hold metformin before and for 48 hours after IV iodinated contrast, because contrast-induced nephropathy can precipitate lactic acidosis. Restart once renal function is confirmed stable.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why is metformin dosing so dependent on renal function?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Metformin is not metabolised — it is renally cleared unchanged, so it accumulates as GFR falls, raising lactic acidosis risk. Monitor eGFR at least annually (more often if impaired).

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is the nephrotoxic 'triple whammy', and why does it matter with metformin?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: NSAID + ACE inhibitor/ARB + diuretic together. This combination can precipitate acute kidney injury, which in turn increases the risk of metformin accumulation and lactic acidosis.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How do sulfonylureas (e.g. gliclazide) lower blood glucose?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: They are insulin secretagogues — they close the ATP-sensitive K+ channel on pancreatic beta-cells -> depolarisation and calcium influx -> stimulate insulin secretion. They work only if there is residual beta-cell function.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is the main dangerous side effect of sulfonylureas?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Hypoglycaemia — the key risk. It can be prolonged and severe, especially in the elderly, in renal impairment, and in those who skip meals.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Besides hypoglycaemia, what other notable side effect do sulfonylureas cause?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Weight gain. They can also cause GI upset and, rarely, cholestasis or blood dyscrasias.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which sulfonylurea should be avoided in the elderly or in renal impairment, and why?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Glibenclamide — it is long-acting and has renally-cleared active metabolites, so it causes prolonged, severe hypoglycaemia. Gliclazide (inactive metabolites) is preferred in the elderly and renal impairment.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: When should gliclazide be taken, and what is a typical dose?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Take with breakfast. Typical dose is 40-80 mg once daily, up to 160 mg twice daily.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why do sulfonylureas only work in some patients with type 2 diabetes?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: They stimulate insulin release from beta-cells, so they only work if there is residual beta-cell function. They are used as an add-on, when metformin is not tolerated, or when quick control of symptomatic hyperglycaemia is needed.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which antifungal must be avoided with sulfonylureas because it causes severe hypoglycaemia?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Miconazole — avoid, as it can cause severe hypos. Other potentiators of hypoglycaemia include co-trimoxazole/trimethoprim, fluconazole, and alcohol.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What DVLA/driving advice should a patient on a sulfonylurea receive?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Carry fast-acting glucose, and check blood glucose before and while driving. Recurrent severe hypoglycaemia is notifiable to the DVLA.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How do SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g. dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) lower blood glucose?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: They block SGLT2 in the proximal renal tubule (which normally reabsorbs most filtered glucose) -> glucose is lost in the urine (glycosuria), lowering blood glucose independently of insulin.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Beyond glucose lowering, what additional benefits do SGLT2 inhibitors provide?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Cardiovascular and renal protection, plus weight and blood pressure reduction (partly via natriuresis/osmotic diuresis). They do not cause hypoglycaemia.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: When does NICE recommend an SGLT2 inhibitor first-line in type 2 diabetes?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: When there is established CVD, heart failure, or high CV risk — offer it first-line alongside metformin (or as first-line monotherapy if metformin is unsuitable), for its proven CV and renal benefit.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which SGLT2 inhibitors are licensed for use even without diabetes, and for what?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Dapagliflozin and empagliflozin are licensed for heart failure and chronic kidney disease even in patients without diabetes.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What are the most common side effects of SGLT2 inhibitors, and why do they occur?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Genital candidiasis (thrush) and urinary tract infections, caused by glucose in the urine (glycosuria) feeding infection. Volume depletion and hypotension can also occur.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is euglycaemic DKA, and why is it important with SGLT2 inhibitors?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Ketoacidosis occurring with blood glucose near-normal, so it is easily missed. If a patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor is unwell with symptoms, check ketones — do not rely on glucose. Follow sick-day rules and stop the drug when acutely unwell or perioperatively.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What are the sick-day rules for SGLT2 inhibitors?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Stop the drug when acutely unwell (and around surgery), and check ketones if the patient is unwell — because of the risk of euglycaemic DKA. Monitor renal function and volume status.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What rare but serious genital infection is associated with SGLT2 inhibitors?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Fournier's gangrene — a rare necrotising infection of the perineum/genitals. It is a surgical emergency; warn patients to report severe genital pain, swelling, or redness.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which SGLT2 inhibitor carries a signal for lower-limb amputation, and what counselling follows?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Canagliflozin. Advise on good foot care and monitor the feet.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: A patient starting an SGLT2 inhibitor shows a small early drop in eGFR. Is this concerning?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: No — the initial small eGFR dip is haemodynamic (reduced glomerular hyperfiltration) and is benign and reversible, driven by the same mechanism as the drug's renoprotection.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What interaction should be watched when combining an SGLT2 inhibitor with diuretics or ACE inhibitors/ARBs?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Additive volume depletion, hypotension, and AKI risk. Monitor volume status, blood pressure, and renal function, and consider reviewing the diuretic dose.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How do GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g. semaglutide, liraglutide) lower blood glucose?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: They mimic the incretin GLP-1 -> stimulate GLUCOSE-DEPENDENT insulin secretion (so low hypo risk), suppress glucagon, slow gastric emptying, and centrally suppress appetite -> glucose lowering with marked weight loss.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why do GLP-1 receptor agonists carry a low risk of hypoglycaemia when used alone?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Their stimulation of insulin secretion is GLUCOSE-DEPENDENT — insulin is only released when glucose is high — so they do not drive glucose below normal on their own.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Besides lowering glucose, what major additional benefits do GLP-1 receptor agonists offer in type 2 diabetes?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Marked WEIGHT LOSS (via appetite suppression and slowed gastric emptying) and cardiovascular benefit. This makes them attractive in obese patients with type 2 diabetes.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How are the main GLP-1 receptor agonists administered?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Semaglutide and dulaglutide: subcutaneous ONCE WEEKLY. Liraglutide: subcutaneous ONCE DAILY. An oral semaglutide tablet also exists (taken once daily on an empty stomach).

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Under NICE, when is a GLP-1 receptor agonist added in type 2 diabetes?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: After triple therapy has failed, typically in patients with BMI >=35 plus obesity-related problems (adjusting the threshold for ethnicity), or BMI <35 where insulin would have occupational implications.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: A patient started a GLP-1 receptor agonist 6 months ago. What response is needed to justify continuing it (NICE)?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Continue only if HbA1c has fallen by >=11 mmol/mol AND body weight has fallen by >=3%. If not, the drug is stopped.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is the most common side effect of GLP-1 receptor agonists, and how is it minimised?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Gastrointestinal upset — NAUSEA, vomiting and diarrhoea. Minimised by starting low and titrating the dose SLOWLY. It often settles with time.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: A patient on a GLP-1 receptor agonist develops severe, persistent abdominal pain. What serious side effect must you consider and what do you do?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Acute PANCREATITIS. Stop the drug and assess for pancreatitis (it should not be restarted if confirmed). Gallstones are also more common with these agents.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which family history is a contraindication to GLP-1 receptor agonists?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: A personal or family history of MEDULLARY THYROID CANCER, or MEN2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2).

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: An insulin-treated patient is started on a GLP-1 receptor agonist. What key safety warning applies to their insulin (MHRA)?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Do NOT stop or reduce insulin too quickly — abrupt reduction risks DIABETIC KETOACIDOSIS. Taper insulin gradually with close glucose monitoring.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why can starting a GLP-1 receptor agonist affect the absorption of a patient's other oral medications?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Because it slows gastric emptying, which can DELAY the absorption of concomitant oral drugs. This is relevant for drugs where timing of absorption matters.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which GLP-1-based agents are also licensed specifically for weight management?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Semaglutide and liraglutide (at their weight-management doses), and the dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist tirzepatide.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How do DPP-4 inhibitors ('gliptins', e.g. sitagliptin) lower blood glucose?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: They inhibit the enzyme that breaks down the body's own incretins -> raise incretin levels -> increased GLUCOSE-DEPENDENT insulin secretion. Effect is modest.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why are DPP-4 inhibitors a useful, safe add-on in the elderly?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: They are WEIGHT-NEUTRAL, carry a LOW risk of hypoglycaemia, are oral and very well tolerated, making them a safe option where sulfonylurea-related hypos or weight gain are undesirable.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Can DPP-4 inhibitors be used in renal impairment?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Yes, but most (e.g. sitagliptin) need dose REDUCTION in renal impairment. LINAGLIPTIN is the exception — it requires no renal dose adjustment.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How does the glucose-lowering efficacy of DPP-4 inhibitors compare to other agents?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: They have only MODEST efficacy. Their appeal is tolerability, weight-neutrality and low hypo risk rather than potency.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: A patient on sitagliptin develops tense skin blisters. What side effect must you consider and what do you do (MHRA)?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: BULLOUS PEMPHIGOID. Stop the DPP-4 inhibitor and refer/treat; it usually improves on withdrawal. Rare acute pancreatitis is also reported with this class.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which DPP-4 inhibitors carry a heart-failure caution, and why?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: SAXAGLIPTIN and ALOGLIPTIN — they are associated with a signal of increased heart-failure HOSPITALISATION. Use with caution in patients with heart failure.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How does pioglitazone lower blood glucose?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: It is a thiazolidinedione (PPAR-gamma agonist) that increases peripheral INSULIN SENSITIVITY in fat and muscle and reduces hepatic glucose output. It does not stimulate insulin secretion, so causes no hypoglycaemia.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Does pioglitazone cause hypoglycaemia?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: No — it improves insulin sensitivity rather than driving insulin secretion, so it does not cause hypoglycaemia when used alone.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why is pioglitazone contraindicated in heart failure?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: It causes FLUID RETENTION -> peripheral oedema and worsening (often diuretic-resistant) heart failure. It is contraindicated in patients with heart failure or a history of heart failure.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What malignancy signal makes pioglitazone contraindicated in certain patients?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: A BLADDER CANCER signal — it is contraindicated in active or past bladder cancer, and in uninvestigated haematuria (which should be worked up first).

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Beyond fluid retention and bladder cancer, what other adverse effects should you counsel a patient about before starting pioglitazone?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: WEIGHT GAIN, increased risk of FRACTURES (typically distal limb), and hepatotoxicity — so LFTs should be monitored. Ask about symptoms of heart failure and haematuria.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What must be monitored in a patient taking pioglitazone?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Weight and signs of oedema/heart failure, LIVER function tests (LFTs), and enquire about haematuria (bladder cancer signal).

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How does acarbose lower blood glucose, and what specifically does it target?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: It is an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor that slows intestinal breakdown/absorption of complex carbohydrates -> blunts the POST-PRANDIAL (after-meal) glucose rise.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: When should acarbose be taken?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: With the FIRST MOUTHFUL of each meal, titrated up slowly to improve tolerance.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What side effects limit the usefulness of acarbose?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: FLATULENCE, bloating and diarrhoea — caused by unabsorbed carbohydrate being fermented in the gut. These are very common and often make it poorly tolerated, so it is only a minor/adjunct agent.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: A patient on acarbose (with other agents) has a hypoglycaemic episode. Why must you treat with pure glucose rather than sucrose (table sugar)?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Acarbose BLOCKS the breakdown of sucrose, so sucrose won't be absorbed and won't correct the hypo. Use PURE GLUCOSE (e.g. glucose tablets/gel) instead.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: In which gastrointestinal conditions is acarbose contraindicated?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Inflammatory bowel disease and intestinal obstruction or hernia, because its gas-producing, carbohydrate-fermenting effects can worsen these conditions.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How does insulin lower blood glucose at the cellular level?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: It binds its receptor (a tyrosine kinase) and triggers translocation of GLUT4 transporters, driving glucose uptake into muscle and fat, plus glycogen, fat and protein synthesis.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: By what mechanism does insulin lower serum potassium, and what is this used for clinically?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Insulin stimulates the cellular Na+/K+-ATPase, shifting K+ from the blood into cells. This is the basis for using insulin (with glucose) to treat hyperkalaemia.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is the onset, peak and duration profile of rapid-acting analogues (aspart, lispro, glulisine)?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Fast on, fast off: onset ~15 min, peak ~1-3 h, duration ~2-5 h. Amino-acid substitutions reduce hexamer self-association so monomers are absorbed quickly.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is the clinical role of rapid-acting insulin analogues in a diabetic regimen?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: They provide meal-time ('bolus') cover in basal-bolus regimens and insulin pumps, and are used for correction doses. Injected just before or with food.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Can rapid-acting analogues be given after a meal, and in whom?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Yes. Because of their fast onset they can be given just before, with, or even after eating in erratic eaters and children, giving flexible meal-time timing.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How long before a meal should short-acting soluble (regular) insulin be given, and why?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: About 30 minutes before meals, because soluble insulin forms zinc hexamers that must dissociate first: onset ~30 min, peak ~2-3 h, duration ~8 h (slower than rapid analogues).

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which type of insulin is used intravenously for DKA, hyperkalaemia and perioperative sliding scales?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Short-acting soluble (regular) insulin, e.g. Actrapid. Soluble insulin is the IV insulin; rapid analogues and other formulations are not given IV for these uses.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why is NPH (isophane) insulin cloudy, and what must you do before injecting it?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: It is insulin complexed with protamine to delay absorption, which makes it cloudy. It must be gently resuspended (mixed) before injection to give a reliable dose.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is the profile of NPH insulin and its main hypoglycaemia drawback?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Onset ~1-2 h, peak ~4-8 h, duration ~12-16 h. It is a basal insulin but has a definite peak, giving more nocturnal hypoglycaemia than flat long-acting analogues.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which basal insulin does NICE (NG28) recommend first-line in type 2 diabetes, and why?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: NPH (isophane) insulin, chosen largely on cost. Switch to a long-acting analogue only if there is hypoglycaemia, a need for injection assistance, or twice-daily NPH is impractical.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How do long-acting analogues (glargine, detemir, degludec) differ from NPH in their action profile?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: They give a flat, near-'peakless' basal effect over ~24 h, so cause less nocturnal hypoglycaemia than NPH. They are clear solutions needing no resuspension.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which long-acting analogue is ultra-long-acting with flexible timing, and what is the dosing caution?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Degludec (Tresiba) forms a multihexamer depot lasting >42 h, allowing flexible timing. Avoid dosing too frequently or changing the dose too often -> accumulation and delayed hypoglycaemia (allow days between changes).

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why must long-acting analogue insulins be prescribed by exact brand?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: High-strength versions are NOT unit-for-unit interchangeable, e.g. glargine U100 (Lantus/Abasaglar) vs Toujeo U300, and degludec U100 vs U200. Prescribing by brand avoids dangerous dosing errors.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: According to NICE NG17, what is the preferred basal insulin in type 1 diabetes?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Twice-daily detemir. Once-daily glargine or degludec are alternatives. Basal is combined with a rapid-acting mealtime bolus in a basal-bolus regimen.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is a biphasic (mixed) insulin, e.g. Novomix 30 or Humalog Mix 25?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: A single pen combining a rapid/short-acting component (meal cover) with an intermediate protaminated (NPH-like) component in a fixed ratio, e.g. 30/70.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How are mixed insulins typically given, and why are they not first-line in type 1 diabetes?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Twice daily with breakfast and evening meal. They are a convenient T2DM option but the fixed ratio is inflexible; basal-bolus MDI is first-line for T1DM (NG17).

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why do mixed insulins carry hypoglycaemia risk if a meal is skipped?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: The dose is fixed and includes a rapid/short-acting component, so skipping a meal after injecting can cause hypoglycaemia between meals or at night. They are also cloudy and must be resuspended before use.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Describe the basal-bolus insulin regimen.
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: A long-acting or intermediate insulin provides continuous background ('basal') cover, plus a rapid-acting insulin ('bolus') given with each meal. It is the standard first-line regimen for type 1 diabetes.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: In DKA, what type of IV insulin infusion is used and at what rate?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: A FIXED-rate IV insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h (soluble insulin) - NOT a sliding/variable-rate scale.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: When managing DKA, when should potassium be replaced, and why?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Insulin drives K+ into cells, lowering serum K+. Replace potassium once it falls below 5.5 mmol/L and monitor it closely, because insulin can cause dangerous hypokalaemia.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: During DKA treatment, when do you add 10% glucose, and when can the fixed-rate insulin be stopped?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Add 10% glucose once blood glucose falls below ~14 mmol/L. Do not stop the fixed-rate insulin infusion until the ketones/ketosis have cleared.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What must you monitor hourly during a fixed-rate insulin infusion for DKA?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Hourly blood glucose and ketones, plus regular potassium. Add 10% glucose when glucose <14 and continue insulin until ketones clear.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How is insulin used to treat hyperkalaemia, and what must you watch for afterwards?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: IV insulin (with glucose to prevent hypoglycaemia) shifts K+ into cells. Monitor blood glucose for at least 6 hours afterwards because of the risk of delayed hypoglycaemia.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: A type 1 diabetic is unwell and not eating - should they stop their insulin?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: No. Never stop basal insulin in T1DM even if not eating (sick-day rule). Insulin requirements usually rise during illness; check ketones and continue basal insulin to prevent DKA.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What are the warning features of hypoglycaemia?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Autonomic and neuroglycopenic features: sweating, tremor, palpitations, then confusion progressing to coma if untreated. Hypoglycaemia is the universal risk of all insulins.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why are non-selective beta-blockers a concern in an insulin-treated diabetic?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: They mask the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycaemia (e.g. tremor, palpitations) and can blunt recovery, so a hypo may go unnoticed until neuroglycopenia develops.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How does alcohol affect the risk of hypoglycaemia in insulin-treated patients?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Alcohol potentiates, prolongs and masks hypoglycaemia, so a hypo can be severe, delayed and hard to recognise.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which common drugs raise blood glucose and increase insulin requirements?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Corticosteroids and thiazide diuretics raise blood glucose, so insulin doses often need to be increased when they are started.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is lipohypertrophy, and how is it prevented?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Fatty lumps at repeatedly used injection sites. Injecting into them gives erratic insulin absorption, so patients should rotate injection sites to prevent it and ensure reliable dosing.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Besides hypoglycaemia, what is a common metabolic side effect of insulin therapy?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Weight gain. Local injection-site reactions and lipohypertrophy can also occur.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why must 'units' always be written in full on an insulin prescription?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Abbreviations like 'U' or 'IU' can be misread as an extra zero (e.g. '10U' read as '100'), causing a massive overdose. Always write 'units' in full.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which insulins are cloudy and need resuspending, and which are clear?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: NPH/isophane (basal) and biphasic mixed insulins are cloudy and must be gently resuspended before injecting. Long-acting analogues and soluble insulin are clear solutions needing no mixing.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why might a long-acting analogue be preferred over NPH in a patient with troublesome nocturnal hypos?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Long-acting analogues have a flat, near-peakless ~24 h profile, so they cause less nocturnal hypoglycaemia than NPH, which has a definite peak.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is the mechanism of levothyroxine?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: It is synthetic T4 (thyroxine), a prohormone that is converted in the body to the active hormone T3, replacing thyroid hormone and normalising metabolic rate.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is the main indication for lifelong levothyroxine?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Replacement in primary hypothyroidism, and after thyroidectomy or radioiodine. It is taken lifelong.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: After changing a levothyroxine dose, when should you recheck the TSH and why?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Recheck TSH at 6-8 weeks. Levothyroxine has a long half-life so it takes ~4-6 weeks to reach steady state; checking earlier gives a misleading result. Titrate to a TSH within the reference range.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: A 78-year-old with angina needs to start levothyroxine. How do you dose it?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Start low (e.g. 25-50 mcg) and titrate slowly. In the elderly or anyone with ischaemic heart disease, full replacement can precipitate angina or AF.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: A patient has both untreated hypothyroidism and untreated adrenal insufficiency. What must you treat first before levothyroxine?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Treat the cortisol deficiency first (give steroids). Starting levothyroxine before replacing cortisol can precipitate an Addisonian crisis.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How should levothyroxine be taken in relation to food?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: On an empty stomach, 30-60 minutes before food (or at bedtime well after eating), to ensure reliable absorption.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which common medicines reduce levothyroxine absorption, and what do you advise?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Iron, calcium, antacids, PPIs and cholestyramine reduce absorption. Separate them from levothyroxine by about 4 hours.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What effect do enzyme inducers (e.g. rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine) have on levothyroxine?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: They increase levothyroxine requirements, so the dose may need to be raised.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: A woman on levothyroxine has just confirmed she is pregnant. What should happen to her dose?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Increase the dose (roughly 25-50%) as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, and monitor TFTs closely. Requirements rise in pregnancy.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: When is subclinical hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Treat if TSH is persistently >10, or offer a trial if the patient is symptomatic and under 65.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What are the features of levothyroxine over-replacement?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Hyperthyroid features: palpitations, tremor, weight loss, diarrhoea, heat intolerance. Long-term over-treatment risks atrial fibrillation and osteoporosis.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How do thionamides (carbimazole, PTU) lower thyroid hormone?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: They block thyroid peroxidase, reducing synthesis of new thyroid hormone. The effect takes weeks because pre-formed stored hormone must first be depleted.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What extra action does PTU have that makes it useful in thyroid storm?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: PTU also blocks the peripheral conversion of T4 to active T3, giving faster control of thyrotoxic symptoms.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which thionamide is first-line for Graves', and when is PTU preferred instead?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Carbimazole is first-line. PTU is preferred in the first trimester of pregnancy and in thyroid storm.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: A patient on carbimazole phones with a sore throat and fever. What is the critical action?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Suspect agranulocytosis: stop the drug and get an urgent FBC. Any sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers on a thionamide (carbimazole or PTU) must be checked immediately.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why is carbimazole avoided in the first trimester of pregnancy?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: It is teratogenic (e.g. aplasia cutis, choanal/oesophageal atresia). Use PTU in the first trimester, and women of childbearing potential need effective contraception.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which serious MHRA-flagged adverse effect of carbimazole means stopping it permanently?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Acute pancreatitis. If it occurs, stop carbimazole permanently and never restart it.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What serious adverse effect is specific to PTU, and how does it present?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Severe, potentially fatal hepatotoxicity. Warn the patient to report anorexia, nausea, dark urine or jaundice; monitor LFTs.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: For how long are thionamides typically given in Graves', and in what regimens?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: For about 12-18 months, either as 'titration' or 'block-and-replace'. They are also used to render a patient euthyroid before surgery or radioiodine.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How does radioactive iodine (I-131) treat hyperthyroidism?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: It is taken up and concentrated by the thyroid, where emitted beta particles destroy thyroid tissue over weeks, definitively reducing hormone production.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is the usual eventual outcome after radioiodine, and how is it managed?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Hypothyroidism is the common endpoint, requiring lifelong levothyroxine. Monitor TFTs lifelong as it may develop early or years later.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is now the first-line definitive treatment for Graves' disease per NICE?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Radioactive iodine (I-131), unless the patient is unsuitable (e.g. pregnancy/planning pregnancy, or active moderate-severe thyroid eye disease).

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What are the absolute contraindications to radioiodine, and what advice on future pregnancy?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Pregnancy and breastfeeding are absolute contraindications. Women should avoid pregnancy for ~6 months afterwards, and men avoid fathering a child for ~4 months.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How does radioiodine affect thyroid eye disease, and how is this managed?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: It can worsen thyroid eye disease (a relative contraindication). Corticosteroid cover is given if radioiodine is used in patients with active eye disease.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What radiation-protection advice follows a dose of radioiodine?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Avoid close, prolonged contact with others for a period, especially children and pregnant women.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why is propranolol used in thyrotoxicosis?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: It rapidly controls the adrenergic symptoms (tremor, palpitations, tachycardia, anxiety) while definitive treatment takes effect. At high dose it also reduces conversion of T4 to T3.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why must you avoid propranolol in a thyrotoxic patient with asthma?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker and can trigger bronchospasm. Avoid it in asthma.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How does high-dose (Lugol's) iodine help before thyroidectomy?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: It transiently inhibits thyroid hormone release and synthesis and reduces gland vascularity, making the gland less vascular and reducing bleeding at surgery.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How long does the effect of high-dose iodine last?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Only short-term: the thyroid 'escapes' after about 10-14 days, so it is used for brief pre-operative preparation or in thyroid storm, not long-term.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why must Lugol's iodine be given AFTER starting a thionamide in Graves'?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Giving iodine before a thionamide can worsen thyrotoxicosis (Jod-Basedow effect) by supplying substrate for hormone production. Start the thionamide first.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is the drug bundle for managing thyroid storm?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: A thionamide (PTU) + iodine (given AFTER the thionamide) + a beta-blocker (propranolol) + IV hydrocortisone, plus supportive care.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which corticosteroid is the agent of choice for physiological cortisol replacement in adrenal insufficiency, and why?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Hydrocortisone. It is a glucocorticoid with significant mineralocorticoid activity and has a short plasma half-life, so divided doses (larger on waking) can mimic the normal diurnal cortisol rhythm.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How is oral hydrocortisone replacement typically dosed through the day in adrenal insufficiency?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: About 15-25 mg/day in divided doses, with the largest dose given on waking, to reproduce the natural morning peak of the diurnal cortisol rhythm.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: A patient with known Addison's presents drowsy, hypotensive and vomiting; you suspect an adrenal (Addisonian) crisis. What are the two immediate treatments?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: IV/IM hydrocortisone 100 mg stat plus IV 0.9% saline. Treat immediately on clinical suspicion.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: In suspected adrenal crisis, should you wait for a random cortisol result before giving hydrocortisone?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: No. Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IM/IV immediately on clinical suspicion - never delay life-saving treatment to await biochemical confirmation.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: After the initial 100 mg bolus in adrenal crisis, how is hydrocortisone continued?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: 50 mg QDS IV/IM (i.e. continued regular hydrocortisone) alongside ongoing IV 0.9% saline for fluid/volume resuscitation.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is the sick-day rule for oral hydrocortisone in a patient with a febrile intercurrent illness?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Double the usual oral hydrocortisone dose for the duration of the febrile illness. Steroid must never be omitted during illness.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: A steroid-dependent patient with Addison's is vomiting and cannot keep down oral hydrocortisone. What should they do?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Self-inject IM hydrocortisone and attend hospital. Vomiting/diarrhoea means oral steroid can't be absorbed, so the injectable route and admission are needed.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What card should every patient on long-term steroid replacement carry, and what does it signal?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: The red NHS Steroid Emergency Card (2020). It alerts healthcare staff that the patient is steroid-dependent and needs steroid cover in acute illness, injury or surgery.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Hydrocortisone has notable mineralocorticoid activity - what side effects can this cause?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Sodium and fluid retention, causing oedema and hypertension, plus hypokalaemia.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What are the approximate glucocorticoid potency equivalents of hydrocortisone, prednisolone and dexamethasone?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Hydrocortisone 20 mg is roughly equivalent to prednisolone 5 mg, which is roughly equivalent to dexamethasone 0.75 mg.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Rank hydrocortisone, prednisolone and dexamethasone by mineralocorticoid (sodium-retaining) activity.
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Hydrocortisone > prednisolone >> dexamethasone (dexamethasone has negligible mineralocorticoid activity).

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which drug provides mineralocorticoid replacement in Addison's disease, and what does it do?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Fludrocortisone - a potent synthetic mineralocorticoid. It acts on the distal nephron to retain Na+ and water and excrete K+, maintaining blood pressure and volume. Given alongside hydrocortisone.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why is fludrocortisone needed in primary but not secondary adrenal insufficiency?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: In primary AI (Addison's) the whole adrenal cortex fails, so aldosterone is lost and must be replaced. In secondary AI the RAAS/aldosterone axis is intact, so mineralocorticoid replacement is not required.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What should you monitor in a patient taking fludrocortisone?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Blood pressure and U&Es (Na+/K+), plus postural symptoms. Watch for hypertension, oedema and hypokalaemia; titrate to BP, electrolytes and renin.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Besides Addison's, in what other setting is fludrocortisone sometimes used?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Postural (orthostatic) hypotension due to autonomic failure - its sodium/fluid-retaining effect expands volume and supports blood pressure.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: In which patients should fludrocortisone be used with particular caution?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Those with hypertension, heart failure or hypokalaemia, as its sodium/fluid retention and potassium loss worsen all three.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why is dexamethasone preferred when you want a strong anti-inflammatory effect without fluid retention?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: It is a potent, long-acting glucocorticoid with negligible mineralocorticoid activity, giving powerful anti-inflammatory action without significant sodium/water retention.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which corticosteroid is used for cerebral oedema from raised intracranial pressure or brain tumours?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Dexamethasone (e.g. 8-16 mg/day) - potent, long-acting and non-fluid-retaining, ideal for reducing tumour-associated cerebral oedema.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which steroid is given as a single dose for croup?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Dexamethasone - a single oral dose reduces upper-airway inflammation in croup.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which corticosteroid is used antenatally to promote fetal lung maturation?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Dexamethasone (a glucocorticoid) given to the mother to accelerate fetal surfactant/lung maturation before anticipated preterm delivery.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why is dexamethasone the steroid used in the dexamethasone suppression test for Cushing's?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: It is potent (so a tiny dose suppresses ACTH) and does not cross-react in cortisol immunoassays, so it suppresses the axis without interfering with the cortisol measurement. Classic dose: 1 mg overnight.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which oral glucocorticoid is the standard default for chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease and flares?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Prednisolone - the workhorse oral steroid for maintenance and flares of conditions like asthma/COPD, IBD, RA, PMR/GCA and vasculitis.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What dose of prednisolone is used for giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms, and why urgently?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: 60 mg daily. High-dose steroid is started immediately to prevent irreversible blindness; do not delay for biopsy. (A typical inflammatory flare uses ~40 mg.)

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: When should oral prednisolone be taken during the day, and when must it be tapered rather than stopped?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Take in the morning (mimics diurnal rhythm, reduces insomnia). Taper if used for more than about 3 weeks, because of HPA/adrenal suppression - never stop abruptly.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Give a brief summary of the main long-term harms of prednisolone to warn a patient about.
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Cushingoid habitus and weight gain, steroid-induced diabetes/hyperglycaemia, osteoporosis, hypertension, mood change/psychosis, cataracts/glaucoma, immunosuppression/infection and peptic ulcer (especially with NSAIDs). (Covered fully in the systemic corticosteroids deck.)

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How do metyrapone, ketoconazole and osilodrostat lower cortisol, and what are they used for?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: They are steroidogenesis inhibitors that block enzymes of cortisol synthesis. They are used for medical control of Cushing's syndrome - pre-operatively, while awaiting surgery/radiotherapy, or when surgery isn't possible. Doses are titrated against cortisol levels.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is the main risk if cortisol-synthesis inhibitors over-suppress cortisol production?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Iatrogenic adrenal insufficiency. Cortisol levels are monitored and the dose titrated to avoid over-suppression.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which cortisol-synthesis inhibitor causes hepatotoxicity, and what monitoring is mandatory?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Ketoconazole - mandatory LFT monitoring. (Its oral antifungal use was withdrawn in 2013; it is now used only for endocrine indications.)

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why is ketoconazole dangerous to co-prescribe with statins or warfarin?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: It strongly inhibits the metabolism of other drugs, raising their levels - statin levels rise (risk of rhabdomyolysis) and warfarin effect increases (bleeding risk).

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What specific monitoring does osilodrostat require, and why?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: ECG for QT prolongation and U&Es for hypokalaemia (it can also cause hypertension). QT effect is additive with other QT-prolonging drugs.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which drug is used specifically for adrenocortical carcinoma, and how does it work?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Mitotane - an adrenolytic agent cytotoxic to the adrenal cortex (and it inhibits steroidogenesis). Specialist adjuvant/palliative use.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why must glucocorticoid replacement be co-prescribed at roughly double the usual dose with mitotane?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Mitotane causes adrenal insufficiency by destroying the cortex, so steroid replacement is needed; it is also a potent enzyme inducer that speeds cortisol breakdown, so about double the usual glucocorticoid dose is required.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What key safety issues make mitotane a specialist-only drug?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: It is teratogenic and persists in fat for a long time (prolonged contraception needed after stopping), neurotoxic (ataxia/lethargy), and has a narrow therapeutic window requiring plasma-level monitoring.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why does a dopamine (D2) agonist like cabergoline lower prolactin?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Hypothalamic dopamine tonically INHIBITS prolactin release. A D2 agonist mimics this inhibition -> suppresses prolactin secretion and shrinks prolactinomas.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is the first-line treatment for a prolactinoma / symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: A dopamine agonist (cabergoline or bromocriptine). Medical therapy suppresses prolactin, shrinks the tumour and restores fertility, so surgery is usually avoided.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which dopamine agonist is generally preferred for a prolactinoma, and why?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Cabergoline - it is longer-acting (given twice weekly) and better tolerated than bromocriptine (which is daily).

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: A patient on cabergoline for a prolactinoma develops new gambling and compulsive shopping. What is happening and who should be counselled?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Dopamine agonists can cause impulse-control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating, compulsive shopping). Warn and counsel BOTH the patient and their family, as the patient may not recognise it; review/reduce the dose.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why are patients started on bromocriptine/cabergoline at a low dose taken at night?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: They cause postural hypotension (and nausea), especially with the first doses. Starting low and dosing at night reduces symptomatic hypotension.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What sudden neurological side effect of dopamine agonists must be discussed with drivers?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Sudden-onset sleep / excessive daytime somnolence. Warn patients of the risk when driving or operating machinery.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which serious side effect of long-term high-dose ergot-derived dopamine agonists (cabergoline/bromocriptine) requires echocardiography monitoring?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Cardiac valve fibrosis (also pulmonary and retroperitoneal fibrosis). Monitor with echocardiography, plus CXR, ESR and creatinine during long-term therapy.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which class of drug directly opposes the therapeutic effect of a dopamine agonist and can itself raise prolactin?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Dopamine antagonists - metoclopramide, prochlorperazine and antipsychotics. They block D2 receptors, opposing the agonist and raising prolactin.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How do somatostatin analogues (octreotide, lanreotide) work?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: They mimic somatostatin -> suppress growth hormone (and IGF-1) release, plus many gut hormones and splanchnic blood flow.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: When are somatostatin analogues used in acromegaly?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: To control GH/IGF-1 when surgery has been incomplete or is unsuitable. Lanreotide is a depot every 4 weeks; octreotide is short-acting SC or a long-acting depot.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: A patient with carcinoid syndrome has disabling flushing and diarrhoea. Which drug controls these symptoms?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: A somatostatin analogue (octreotide or lanreotide). They suppress the hormones released by neuroendocrine tumours, controlling flushing and diarrhoea.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Besides endocrine tumours, what acute GI emergency is octreotide used in?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Acute variceal (upper GI) bleeding - it reduces splanchnic blood flow and portal pressure.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which two important side effects should you monitor for in a patient on long-term octreotide/lanreotide?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Gallstones/biliary sludge (reduced gallbladder contraction -> gallbladder USS) and altered glucose control - they suppress both insulin and glucagon, so glucose can go up or down. Also GI upset/steatorrhoea and bradycardia.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How does pegvisomant work in acromegaly?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: It is a growth-hormone RECEPTOR antagonist - it binds the GH receptor and blocks its activation -> lowers hepatic IGF-1 production.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: When is pegvisomant indicated?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Acromegaly that is resistant to, or intolerant of, surgery and somatostatin analogues - it normalises IGF-1 in most patients. Given SC once daily.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: On pegvisomant, should you titrate the dose to GH or to IGF-1, and why?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Titrate to IGF-1, NOT GH. Measured GH actually RISES on pegvisomant (loss of IGF-1 feedback), so GH is misleading; IGF-1 reflects true disease control.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What blood test must be monitored on pegvisomant because of its main serious toxicity?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: LFTs - pegvisomant can cause deranged LFTs/hepatotoxicity. Caution in hepatic impairment.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Does pegvisomant shrink the pituitary tumour, and what does this mean for follow-up?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: No - it blocks GH action peripherally but does not shrink the tumour. Continue pituitary MRI surveillance to monitor tumour size.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: A diabetic patient starting pegvisomant is at risk of what, and what should you do?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: It increases insulin sensitivity -> risk of hypoglycaemia. Reduce insulin / oral antidiabetic doses and monitor glucose.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is desmopressin (DDAVP) and how does it concentrate urine?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: A synthetic ADH/vasopressin analogue that is V2-selective (no V1 pressor effect). It acts on renal collecting-duct V2 receptors -> water reabsorption -> concentrated urine.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why does desmopressin work in cranial diabetes insipidus but NOT nephrogenic DI?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Cranial DI is a deficiency of ADH, which desmopressin replaces. In nephrogenic DI the kidney cannot respond to ADH, so giving more (desmopressin) has no effect.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Aside from concentrating urine, what haemostatic effect does desmopressin have and where is it used?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: It releases factor VIII and von Willebrand factor from endothelium, boosting their levels. A single dose helps mild haemophilia A and von Willebrand disease (e.g. before procedures).

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is the most dangerous side effect of desmopressin and how is it prevented?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Hyponatraemia / water intoxication (headache, confusion, seizures). Restrict fluids around the dose, monitor serum sodium, and (MHRA) WITHHOLD during vomiting, diarrhoea or intercurrent illness.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: When prescribing desmopressin for childhood nocturnal enuresis, what practical fluid advice is essential?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Restrict fluids from about 1 hour before until 8 hours after the dose, to avoid hyponatraemia/water intoxication.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Which drugs increase the risk of hyponatraemia when combined with desmopressin?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Drugs that potentiate SIADH/water retention - SSRIs/TCAs, carbamazepine, NSAIDs and chlorpropamide. Be extra vigilant with sodium.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: How do terlipressin and vasopressin act, and what are they used for?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: They act on V1 receptors -> vasoconstriction. Uses: acute variceal bleeding (terlipressin reduces portal pressure), hepatorenal syndrome, and vasopressin as a vasopressor in refractory shock. (See vasoactive drugs for detail.)

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is the main hazard of terlipressin/vasopressin?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Ischaemia from potent vasoconstriction - cardiac, mesenteric and peripheral/digital. Avoid in ischaemic heart disease and peripheral/mesenteric vascular disease; also causes hyponatraemia.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: Why is hydrocortisone used in secondary adrenal insufficiency / hypopituitarism?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: To replace the cortisol that a failing pituitary (low ACTH) cannot drive. Typical dose ~15-25 mg/day in divided doses, with sick-day rules and a steroid card. (Full profile under adrenal drugs.)

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: In combined pituitary failure needing both thyroxine and steroid, which is given first and why?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Give hydrocortisone (the STEROID) BEFORE levothyroxine. Starting thyroxine first raises metabolic demand and can precipitate an adrenal crisis. Note: fludrocortisone is usually NOT needed in secondary AI, as aldosterone is renin-driven and preserved.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What is somatropin and what is it used for?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Recombinant human growth hormone. It replaces GH to stimulate linear growth (via IGF-1). Used for proven GH deficiency (NICE-restricted) - in children (GHD, Turner, Prader-Willi, etc.) and in severe adult GHD - NOT for idiopathic short stature. Given SC once daily, titrated to IGF-1/growth.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: What are the key side effects of growth hormone (somatropin)?
pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.back: Fluid retention (oedema, carpal tunnel syndrome, arthralgia), impaired glucose tolerance, benign intracranial hypertension, and slipped upper femoral epiphysis in children.

pharmacology__Endocrinology & Diabetes D.front: In which situations is growth hormone contraindicated?
