pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus - the kidney becomes insensitive to ADH, so it cannot concentrate urine. This gives dilute polyuria and compensatory thirst.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which endocrine glands are affected by long-term lithium?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: The thyroid (hypothyroidism and goitre) and the parathyroids (hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcaemia). This is why thyroid function and calcium are monitored.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What renal harm can chronic lithium cause besides diabetes insipidus?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Chronic kidney impairment (a progressive decline in renal function). Renal function must be checked before starting and monitored during treatment.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is lithium avoided in pregnancy?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is teratogenic, classically causing Ebstein's anomaly (a cardiac defect). It is contraindicated/avoided in pregnancy and in those planning to conceive.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What must you check before starting lithium, and what is monitored long-term?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Check renal and thyroid function before starting. Long-term, monitor lithium levels plus U&Es, thyroid function and calcium roughly every 6 months.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why should lithium always be prescribed by a consistent brand?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Different preparations have differing bioavailability, so switching brand can change the serum level and risk toxicity or loss of effect. Patients also receive the lithium information pack (purple booklet and alert card).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the role of valproate in bipolar disorder?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is an anti-manic mood stabiliser used for acute mania and maintenance (an antipsychotic is usually first-line for acute mania). It is also an antiepileptic for generalised and absence seizures.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is valproate so strongly restricted in people of childbearing potential?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is highly teratogenic, causing neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental disorders. It must not be used in anyone of childbearing potential except under a Pregnancy Prevention Programme.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What does the valproate Pregnancy Prevention Programme require?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Effective contraception, annual review by a specialist, and a signed Risk Acknowledgement Form confirming the patient understands the risks in pregnancy.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What did the MHRA 2024 advice change about starting valproate?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It must not be started in any new patient under 55 (either sex) unless two independent specialists agree there is no suitable alternative. Men face fertility and offspring risks, so the restriction applies to both sexes.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which two common cosmetic side effects should you warn a patient starting valproate about?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Weight gain and hair loss - the hair typically regrows curly. A fine tremor is also common.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which serious organ toxicities can valproate cause?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Hepatotoxicity and pancreatitis. LFTs are checked before starting and during the first 6 months, and pancreatitis should be considered in a patient with abdominal pain and vomiting.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What haematological side effect of valproate is monitored with an FBC?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Thrombocytopenia (a low platelet count). FBC is checked as part of monitoring alongside LFTs.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on valproate becomes drowsy and confused but their LFTs are normal - what should you consider?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Hyperammonaemic encephalopathy. Valproate can raise ammonia and cause encephalopathy even when LFTs are normal - check an ammonia level.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What happens to lamotrigine levels when valproate is co-prescribed, and what must you do?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Valproate is an enzyme inhibitor and raises lamotrigine levels, increasing the risk of serious rash. The lamotrigine dose must be halved.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why should carbapenem antibiotics be avoided in a patient on valproate?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Carbapenems dramatically lower valproate levels, risking loss of seizure or mood control. The combination should be avoided.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which pole of bipolar disorder is lamotrigine particularly useful for?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: The depressive pole - it is a mood stabiliser best for preventing bipolar depression. It is weight-neutral, well tolerated, and a safer option than valproate in women of childbearing age.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the most dangerous adverse effect of lamotrigine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A serious rash - Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) or DRESS. Any rash should prompt stopping the drug.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How is lamotrigine dosed to reduce the risk of a serious rash?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Start low and titrate slowly - rapid dose escalation is a major risk factor for Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN. Patients are told to report any rash immediately.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is the lamotrigine dose halved when combined with valproate?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Valproate raises lamotrigine levels, which increases the risk of a serious rash. Halving the dose offsets this interaction.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What effect do enzyme inducers and the combined oral contraceptive have on lamotrigine levels?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Both lower lamotrigine levels. With the combined pill, levels fall during active pills and rise again in the pill-free week, which can affect seizure/mood control.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the first-line drug for trigeminal neuralgia?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Carbamazepine, a sodium-channel blocker. It is also used for focal epilepsy and, on a specialist basis only, for bipolar disorder.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why can carbamazepine cause contraceptive failure?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is a potent enzyme inducer that lowers levels of many drugs including hormonal contraceptives. Women need a reliable non-affected contraceptive method; it also reduces the effect of warfarin, DOACs and other antiepileptics.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is 'auto-induction' with carbamazepine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Carbamazepine induces its own metabolism, so clearance rises over the first weeks of treatment. It is started low and titrated up to account for this.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What electrolyte disturbance does carbamazepine cause, and how does this contrast with lithium?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Hyponatraemia (an SIADH-like effect). This is the opposite of lithium, which causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Sodium is monitored via U&Es.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which haematological and skin reactions should prompt caution with carbamazepine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Blood dyscrasias (leucopenia, aplastic anaemia) and serious rash including Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN. Warn patients to report rash, fever or bruising, and monitor FBC.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which patients should be screened for HLA-B*1502 before starting carbamazepine, and why?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Patients of South-East Asian ancestry. Carrying HLA-B*1502 markedly increases the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN with carbamazepine.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What monitoring is required for a patient on carbamazepine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: FBC (blood dyscrasias), U&Es for sodium (hyponatraemia), and LFTs (hepatotoxicity). It is also teratogenic, causing neural tube defects.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do benzodiazepines act at the GABA-A receptor at the level of the chloride channel?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They bind an allosteric site on the GABA-A receptor and increase the FREQUENCY of chloride channel opening (they need endogenous GABA to work). This enhances GABA-mediated inhibition -> sedation, anxiolysis, muscle relaxation and anticonvulsant effects.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why are benzodiazepines safer than barbiturates in overdose?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Benzodiazepines require endogenous GABA to act (they increase the frequency of channel opening), which gives a ceiling effect. Barbiturates increase the duration of channel opening and can act without GABA, so they have no ceiling and are far more dangerous in overdose.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why should benzodiazepines only be used short-term (about 2-4 weeks)?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Regular use causes tolerance and dependence. They are therefore for short-term crises only and are NOT appropriate for routine treatment of generalised anxiety or insomnia.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the main clinical indications for benzodiazepines?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Status epilepticus/seizures, alcohol withdrawal, acute agitation and procedural sedation, and muscle spasm - all short-term. They are not for routine long-term anxiety or insomnia.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which benzodiazepines are used for status epilepticus/acute seizures, and by what route?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: IV lorazepam (in hospital), buccal midazolam, or rectal diazepam (useful in the community/children).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which drugs are used for alcohol withdrawal, and why is a benzodiazepine appropriate?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Chlordiazepoxide or diazepam. Alcohol acts on GABA, so a benzodiazepine substitutes and is tapered down, preventing withdrawal seizures and delirium tremens.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is diazepam a poor choice in the elderly or in liver disease?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Diazepam is long-acting because it has an active metabolite that accumulates, prolonging sedation and increasing falls/confusion risk. This accumulation is worse in the elderly and in hepatic impairment.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which benzodiazepines are preferred in liver disease and the elderly, and why?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: The 'LOT' drugs - Lorazepam, Oxazepam and Temazepam. They have no active metabolite, so they do not accumulate and are safer where clearance is impaired.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the key side effects of benzodiazepines?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Sedation and drowsiness, falls (especially the elderly), anterograde amnesia, respiratory depression, and paradoxical agitation. Tolerance and dependence develop with regular use.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on regular benzodiazepines stops them abruptly. What is the danger and how should they be stopped?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Abrupt withdrawal can cause seizures and delirium due to rebound hyperexcitability. Benzodiazepines must be tapered slowly, not stopped suddenly.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is co-prescribing a benzodiazepine with an opioid dangerous?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: There is additive CNS depression -> profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death (MHRA warning). Avoid the combination or use the lowest possible doses with close monitoring.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the antidote for benzodiazepine overdose and what is the caution with its use?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Flumazenil (a benzodiazepine receptor antagonist). Use cautiously - in a dependent patient it can precipitate seizures, and its short duration may mean re-sedation.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: In which conditions are benzodiazepines contraindicated or used with great caution?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Respiratory depression, severe respiratory disease and sleep apnoea; myasthenia gravis; and severe hepatic impairment. Caution in the elderly due to falls and confusion.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do Z-drugs (zopiclone, zolpidem, zaleplon) work, and how does this differ from benzodiazepines?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They act at the same benzodiazepine site on the GABA-A receptor but are hypnotic-selective, so they promote sleep with less anxiolytic/muscle-relaxant effect. They carry the same dependence risk as benzodiazepines.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the correct place in therapy for Z-drugs?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Short-term insomnia only (about 2-4 weeks), after sleep hygiene and CBT for insomnia have been tried. They are not used for anxiety, and there is no clear advantage over short-acting benzodiazepines.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which Z-drug classically causes a bitter/metallic taste?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Zopiclone.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the key safety concerns with Z-drugs in practice?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Next-day driving impairment (especially zopiclone/higher-dose zolpidem), falls in the elderly, dependence/tolerance, rebound insomnia on stopping, and complex sleep behaviours.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on zolpidem reports episodes of sleep-walking and sleep-driving. What must be done?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Stop the Z-drug permanently (MHRA advice on complex sleep behaviours). Warn patients to avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants which increase the risk.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How does buspirone produce anxiolysis, and how does this differ from benzodiazepines?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist that works without any action on GABA. So it causes no sedation, no dependence and no muscle relaxation - unlike benzodiazepines.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is buspirone used for and why is it useless for acute or PRN anxiety?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is used for generalised anxiety disorder. It takes about 2 weeks to work and must be taken regularly, so it is ineffective for acute or as-needed anxiety relief.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What advice about food/drink and other drugs should you give with buspirone?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Avoid grapefruit (it can raise buspirone levels - levels also rise with certain enzyme inhibitors). Avoid MAOIs (risk of hypertension) and use caution with other serotonergic drugs.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the main advantage of buspirone over benzodiazepines for anxiety?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: No dependence and no sedation. The trade-off is slow onset (about 2 weeks) and the need for regular dosing.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What type of drug is hydroxyzine and what is it used for?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A sedating antihistamine (H1 antagonist) with anxiolytic and antipruritic effects. It is used for short-term anxiety and for pruritus/urticaria, and is non-dependence-forming.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the key cardiac safety concern with hydroxyzine, and what are the dose limits?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: QT prolongation. To limit this (MHRA), the maximum is 100 mg/day in adults and 50 mg/day in the elderly. Avoid in patients with a long QT or on other QT-prolonging drugs.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Besides QT prolongation, what side effects limit hydroxyzine use, especially in the elderly?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Sedation and antimuscarinic effects (dry mouth, urinary retention, worsening glaucoma). Use caution in the elderly and in prostatism/glaucoma.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do pregabalin and gabapentin work?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They bind the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing the release of excitatory neurotransmitters. This gives anxiolytic, anticonvulsant and neuropathic-pain effects.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the main indications for pregabalin/gabapentin, and where does pregabalin sit for GAD?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Neuropathic pain (e.g. diabetic, post-herpetic), adjunct in focal epilepsy, and generalised anxiety disorder. For GAD, pregabalin is third-line, after an SSRI then an SNRI.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why are prescriptions of pregabalin and gabapentin now more tightly controlled?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They are controlled drugs because of misuse, diversion and dependence potential. They can also produce euphoria.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How should pregabalin/gabapentin dosing be adjusted in renal impairment, and why?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: The dose must be reduced because they are renally cleared, so they accumulate if renal function is poor - increasing sedation and respiratory-depression risk.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the notable side effects of pregabalin/gabapentin?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Sedation, dizziness, weight gain and peripheral oedema. Pregabalin also carries a signal for congenital malformations in pregnancy (MHRA).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is combining a gabapentinoid with an opioid dangerous?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Additive CNS/respiratory depression can cause serious respiratory depression (MHRA warning), particularly in the elderly and those with renal or respiratory disease. The same caution applies with alcohol and benzodiazepines.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How does propranolol help anxiety, and what symptom does it NOT treat?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker that blocks the physical/somatic adrenergic symptoms of anxiety - tremor, palpitations, tachycardia and sweating. It does not treat the psychological component.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: For which type of anxiety is propranolol most useful, and how is it dosed?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Situational/performance anxiety (e.g. exams, public speaking), where somatic symptoms dominate. It is given as 10-40 mg, taken PRN before the stressor (or regularly). It causes no dependence.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why must propranolol be avoided in asthma, and what other caution applies in diabetes?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Being non-selective, it can cause bronchospasm and is contraindicated in asthma. In diabetes it can mask the warning signs of hypoglycaemia (e.g. tremor, tachycardia).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the mechanism of action of sodium valproate?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Broad-spectrum: increases GABA activity, and blocks Na+ channels and T-type Ca2+ channels (the latter underlies its action in absence seizures). This wide mechanism covers essentially all seizure types.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient has generalised tonic-clonic seizures and separately a diagnosis of absence epilepsy. Which single AED is first-line for both?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Sodium valproate is first-line for both generalised tonic-clonic and absence seizures (broad-spectrum) - but only if the patient is not of childbearing potential, because it is highly teratogenic.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is sodium valproate avoided in women and girls of childbearing potential?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is highly teratogenic - causing neural-tube defects and neurodevelopmental disorders in the child. It is used only under a Pregnancy Prevention Programme; lamotrigine or levetiracetam are preferred alternatives.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What does the MHRA 2024 rule say about starting sodium valproate in a new patient?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Do not start valproate in ANY new patient under 55 (either sex) unless two independent specialists agree there is no effective alternative. Men are also counselled about a possible fertility/offspring risk.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Name the characteristic side effects of sodium valproate.
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Weight gain, hair loss (which regrows curly), tremor, GI upset, plus serious effects: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, thrombocytopenia, and hyperammonaemic encephalopathy. It is also teratogenic.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on sodium valproate becomes drowsy and confused with NORMAL liver function tests. What complication should you consider and how is it confirmed?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Hyperammonaemic encephalopathy - check the serum ammonia level. LFTs can be normal; it relates to the urea cycle/carnitine, and L-carnitine may be used in management.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Is sodium valproate an enzyme inducer or inhibitor, and what is the key consequence for lamotrigine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is an enzyme INHIBITOR. It raises lamotrigine levels, so the lamotrigine dose must be halved because of the increased risk of a serious rash (Stevens-Johnson syndrome). It also raises phenytoin levels.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why must carbapenem antibiotics be avoided in a patient taking sodium valproate?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Carbapenems dramatically LOWER valproate levels, causing loss of seizure control. The combination should be avoided.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What baseline and ongoing monitoring is needed for sodium valproate?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Monitor LFTs and FBC. Ensure pregnancy prevention is in place, and check ammonia if the patient becomes drowsy or encephalopathic. Drug levels are less useful than clinical seizure control.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the mechanism of action of carbamazepine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels, stabilising neuronal membranes. It is also a potent enzyme inducer and auto-induces its own metabolism over the first few weeks.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the first-line drug treatment for trigeminal neuralgia?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Carbamazepine is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia. It is also used as an alternative agent in focal epilepsy and in bipolar disorder.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why should carbamazepine be avoided in a patient with generalised epilepsy (absence or myoclonic seizures)?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Carbamazepine can WORSEN absence and myoclonic seizures, so it is avoided in generalised epilepsy. It is appropriate for focal epilepsy.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Carbamazepine is a potent enzyme inducer. What clinically important consequences does this have?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It lowers levels of many co-prescribed drugs - causing hormonal contraceptive failure, reduced effect of warfarin and DOACs, and reduced levels of other AEDs. It also auto-induces its own metabolism.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on carbamazepine develops confusion and low sodium. What adverse effect is likely?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Hyponatraemia due to SIADH is a recognised effect of carbamazepine. Check U&Es; other dose-related effects include dizziness, ataxia and diplopia.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which serious haematological and skin reactions must you warn about with carbamazepine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Blood dyscrasias - leucopenia and aplastic anaemia (warn re fever, bruising, infection) - and serious rash progressing to Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN. It can also cause hepatotoxicity.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which genetic screening test is recommended before starting carbamazepine in patients of South-East Asian origin, and why?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Screen for HLA-B*1502. Carriers, more common in South-East Asian populations, are at high risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN with carbamazepine.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is carbamazepine started at a low dose and titrated up over weeks?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Because it auto-induces its own metabolism, clearance rises over the first weeks, so it is started low and titrated to maintain effective levels. It is also a Category 1 drug - keep the patient on the same brand.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the mechanism of action of lamotrigine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels, giving broad-spectrum anticonvulsant activity. It is weight-neutral and non-sedating.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: For which seizure types and which mood disorder is lamotrigine used?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Both focal and generalised epilepsy (broad-spectrum), and bipolar depression. It is a preferred option in women of childbearing age.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is lamotrigine often preferred over valproate in women of childbearing age, and what caveat applies in pregnancy?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It has a lower teratogenic risk than other AEDs. It is not 'safe' - its levels fall during pregnancy, so levels and seizure control must be monitored and the dose adjusted.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the key danger of lamotrigine and how do you reduce the risk?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A serious rash - Stevens-Johnson syndrome, TEN or DRESS. Reduce risk by titrating the dose slowly, and stop the drug immediately at any sign of rash.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient is on sodium valproate and lamotrigine is being added. How does this change lamotrigine dosing?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Valproate (an enzyme inhibitor) raises lamotrigine levels, so the lamotrigine dose must be halved to reduce the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What effect do enzyme inducers (e.g. carbamazepine, oestrogen-containing contraceptives) have on lamotrigine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They lower lamotrigine levels, which may reduce seizure control and require dose adjustment.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which cardiac caution applies to lamotrigine, and which seizure type can it worsen?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: An MHRA warning advises caution in structural/underlying heart disease due to arrhythmia/Brugada-type risk. It can also worsen myoclonic seizures.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the mechanism of action of levetiracetam?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It binds the synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, modulating neurotransmitter release, giving broad-spectrum anticonvulsant activity.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is levetiracetam considered very practical to prescribe?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It has few drug interactions, no enzyme induction, IV and oral doses are equivalent (IV=PO), and it is renally cleared. This makes it useful in status, in patients on many medications, and it is relatively pregnancy-friendly.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How should levetiracetam dosing be adjusted in renal impairment?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is renally cleared, so the dose must be reduced in renal impairment. It is typically started around 250-500 mg twice daily and titrated.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Where does levetiracetam sit in the management of status epilepticus?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is given IV as a second-line agent, after benzodiazepines have been used first.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the signature adverse effect of levetiracetam, and how should patients be counselled?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Neuropsychiatric effects - irritability, aggression, mood change and depression. Counsel patients (and relatives) to report any behavioural or mood change, or suicidal ideation. Caution with a prior psychiatric history.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the mechanism of action of phenytoin?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels in a use-dependent manner. It has zero-order (saturable) kinetics and a narrow therapeutic index, and is a potent enzyme inducer.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the main clinical uses of phenytoin?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Status epilepticus (given IV after benzodiazepines) and focal/generalised epilepsy (an older agent). It can worsen absence and myoclonic seizures.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why do small dose changes of phenytoin cause large jumps in blood level, and what does this mean practically?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Because it has zero-order (saturable) kinetics with a narrow therapeutic index, small dose increases can cause disproportionate rises in level. Therefore drug levels must be monitored (target total level 10-20 mg/L).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Phenytoin is heavily protein-bound. How does low albumin affect interpretation of its level?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: With low albumin (or uraemia) the total measured level underestimates the active free drug, so you must correct the level for albumin or follow the free phenytoin level.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How must IV phenytoin be administered in status epilepticus?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: By slow infusion - maximum 50 mg/min (25 mg/min in the elderly or those with cardiac disease) - with ECG and BP monitoring, because of the risk of arrhythmia and hypotension.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the signs of dose-related (acute) phenytoin toxicity?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A progression of nystagmus -> ataxia -> slurred speech -> confusion (cerebellar/CNS signs) as the level rises.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: List the chronic side effects of phenytoin.
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Gum hypertrophy, hirsutism, coarse facies, acne, folate deficiency/megaloblastic anaemia, peripheral neuropathy and osteomalacia. Long-term dental and bone review is advised.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the two acute IV-related dangers of phenytoin?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Cardiac arrhythmia and purple glove syndrome (a limb-threatening reaction at the infusion site). Give slowly with cardiac monitoring.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How does phenytoin's enzyme induction affect other drugs, and what is its risk in pregnancy?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: As a potent enzyme inducer it lowers levels of the contraceptive pill, warfarin and DOACs, causing treatment failure. It is teratogenic, causing fetal hydantoin syndrome.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What class-wide MHRA warning applies to all antiepileptic drugs?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: All AEDs carry a small increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviour. Counsel patients to report any mood change, low mood or suicidal ideation.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How does phenobarbital act on the GABA-A receptor, and how does this differ from a benzodiazepine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Phenobarbital is a barbiturate that increases the DURATION of chloride-channel opening at GABA-A -> strong CNS depression/anticonvulsant. Benzodiazepines instead increase the FREQUENCY of channel opening.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why has phenobarbital been largely superseded as an epilepsy treatment, and where is it still used?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Superseded because of marked sedation and its strong enzyme-inducing interactions. Still used in refractory status epilepticus (later-line, IV loading) and in neonatal seizures.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A woman on the combined oral contraceptive pill is started on phenobarbital. What must you counsel her about?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Phenobarbital is a potent enzyme inducer -> reduces contraceptive efficacy (risk of pill failure). Advise an alternative or additional non-hormonal contraception; the same applies to warfarin (reduced effect).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why must phenobarbital never be stopped abruptly?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It causes dependence, and abrupt withdrawal is dangerous -> withdrawal seizures. It has a narrow therapeutic index, so withdraw gradually. It is also a Category 1 AED -> keep the patient on the same brand.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What behavioural side effect can phenobarbital cause in children?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Paradoxical hyperactivity (behavioural/cognitive effects). Other important effects are marked sedation, respiratory depression, dependence and rarely Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Clobazam and clonazepam are used in epilepsy - what is their mechanism and their role?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They are benzodiazepines that enhance GABA-A -> broad anticonvulsant effect. They are used as ADJUNCTS (add-on), including in syndromes such as Lennox-Gastaut, because tolerance limits long-term monotherapy.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which benzodiazepine AED is particularly used for myoclonic seizures?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Clonazepam. Clobazam is typically used as an add-on for focal/generalised epilepsy.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What limits the long-term usefulness of clobazam/clonazepam in epilepsy?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Tolerance and dependence, plus sedation and behavioural effects. Abrupt cessation risks withdrawal seizures, so they are best reserved as adjuncts.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the danger of combining a benzodiazepine AED with opioids or alcohol?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Additive CNS and respiratory depression -> risk of dangerous sedation and respiratory depression. Also avoid in sleep apnoea/pre-existing respiratory depression.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: By what mechanisms does topiramate work as a broad-spectrum antiepileptic?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Multiple actions: sodium-channel block, GABA enhancement, glutamate/AMPA block and carbonic anhydrase inhibition -> broad-spectrum anticonvulsant (focal and generalised).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Besides epilepsy, what is a key licensed use of topiramate?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Migraine prophylaxis. (It also tends to cause weight loss.)

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is topiramate subject to a Pregnancy Prevention Programme, and what does this require?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is teratogenic -> oral clefts plus neurodevelopmental disorders/growth restriction (MHRA 2024). Women of childbearing potential need highly effective contraception under a full PPP; it is contraindicated for migraine prophylaxis in pregnancy.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on topiramate for epilepsy also uses the combined pill. What interaction must you counsel on?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Topiramate at doses above 200 mg/day reduces combined-contraceptive efficacy -> counsel and consider an alternative/additional contraception (especially important given its teratogenicity).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What characteristic side effects should you warn a patient starting topiramate about?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Weight loss, paraesthesia (tingling), cognitive slowing/word-finding difficulty, renal stones, acute angle-closure glaucoma and metabolic acidosis. Titrate slowly to limit cognitive effects; in children watch for reduced sweating/heat intolerance.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on topiramate develops sudden painful red eye with blurred vision. What must you exclude?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Acute angle-closure glaucoma - a recognised topiramate reaction needing urgent ophthalmology assessment and drug withdrawal.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the mechanism of gabapentin and pregabalin, and which seizure type do they treat?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They bind the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels -> reduced excitatory neurotransmitter release. They are ADJUNCTS for FOCAL epilepsy only; they are ineffective and can worsen generalised/absence seizures.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why are gabapentin and pregabalin now controlled drugs, and why does this matter?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Because of misuse and diversion (Class C / Schedule 3 controlled drugs). This affects prescribing/dispensing requirements and means dependence must be considered.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How must gabapentin/pregabalin dosing be adjusted in renal impairment, and why?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They are renally cleared, so dose-reduce in renal impairment to avoid accumulation and toxicity (sedation, dizziness).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the risk of prescribing pregabalin or gabapentin with opioids?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Additive respiratory depression (MHRA warning - especially in the elderly and those with renal or respiratory disease) -> risk of dangerous/ fatal respiratory depression.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What common side effects should you warn about when starting gabapentin/pregabalin?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Sedation, dizziness, weight gain and peripheral oedema. Pregabalin also carries an MHRA congenital-malformation signal in pregnancy.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the first-line drug for absence seizures when valproate is unsuitable, and how does it work?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Ethosuximide - it blocks T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons, suppressing the 3-Hz spike-and-wave of absence seizures. It is the drug of choice, e.g. in girls/women where valproate is avoided.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A child has both absence AND tonic-clonic seizures. Why is ethosuximide alone inadequate?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Ethosuximide is narrow-spectrum and has no effect on tonic-clonic seizures. Cover the tonic-clonic seizures too (e.g. add valproate if both types are present).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What side effects are associated with ethosuximide?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: GI upset/nausea, drowsiness and headache; rarely blood dyscrasias and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do oxcarbazepine and eslicarbazepine work, and what are they used for?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They are sodium-channel blockers (carbamazepine relatives) used for FOCAL epilepsy, often better tolerated than carbamazepine. They can worsen absence/myoclonic seizures.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Compared with carbamazepine, what electrolyte disturbance is MORE common with oxcarbazepine/eslicarbazepine, and how do you monitor it?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Hyponatraemia (SIADH-type) is more common than with carbamazepine. Monitor serum sodium, especially if symptomatic (confusion, drowsiness, seizures).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Do oxcarbazepine/eslicarbazepine still affect hormonal contraception despite being weaker enzyme inducers than carbamazepine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Yes - they induce enzymes less than carbamazepine but still enough to lower hormonal contraceptive efficacy -> counsel and consider alternative/additional contraception.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which patients should be screened for HLA-B*1502 before oxcarbazepine, and why?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Patients of South-East Asian ancestry - a positive HLA-B*1502 test predicts a higher risk of severe skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome). There is also some rash cross-reactivity with carbamazepine.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the role and mechanism of brivaracetam in epilepsy?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: An adjunct for focal seizures; it binds SV2A (like levetiracetam but higher affinity) with fewer behavioural/psychiatric effects - an option if levetiracetam causes behavioural problems.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why must cenobamate be titrated very slowly?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: To reduce the risk of DRESS/serious skin reactions. It is a potent adjunct for drug-resistant focal epilepsy but also has significant drug interactions with other AEDs.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How does primidone exert its anticonvulsant effect?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is a prodrug metabolised to phenobarbital, so it acts as a barbiturate at GABA-A -> anticonvulsant. It shares phenobarbital's cautions (sedation, dependence, enzyme induction).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Aside from epilepsy, what is primidone used for today?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Essential tremor - a licensed option alongside propranolol. Its use in epilepsy is now largely historical.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What practical cautions apply when starting and managing primidone?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Start very low and titrate (marked sedation, ataxia, nausea, especially initially). It is a Category 1 AED (keep the same brand) and an enzyme inducer -> contraceptive failure; withdraw gradually due to dependence.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the most effective symptomatic treatment for Parkinson's disease, and who is it first-line for?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Levodopa (given with a peripheral dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor, e.g. co-careldopa/co-beneldopa). NICE recommends it first-line where motor symptoms impair quality of life, regardless of the patient's age.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is levodopa given as a large neutral amino acid rather than as dopamine itself?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, but levodopa can. Once in the brain, levodopa is converted by dopa-decarboxylase into dopamine, replacing the deficient neurotransmitter.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is levodopa combined with carbidopa or benserazide?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They are peripheral dopa-decarboxylase inhibitors that do NOT cross the blood-brain barrier. They block conversion of levodopa to dopamine in the periphery -> less nausea and postural hypotension, and more levodopa reaches the brain.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How should levodopa doses be timed in Parkinson's disease, and why does this matter for inpatients?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Give on time, every time — missed doses cause rigidity/akinesia. Inpatients must not miss doses; if nil-by-mouth, use a patch or nasogastric route rather than omitting it.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why should levodopa be taken away from protein-rich meals?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Dietary protein (and iron) competes with levodopa for absorption, reducing its effect. Separating it from protein gives a more reliable response.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What can happen if levodopa is stopped abruptly?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Acute akinesia and a neuroleptic-malignant-like syndrome. Levodopa must never be stopped suddenly.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the common EARLY side effects of levodopa?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Nausea and postural hypotension.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What long-term MOTOR complications develop after years of levodopa treatment, and why?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Wearing-off (end-of-dose loss of effect), on-off fluctuations, and dyskinesias. Its short duration of action gives pulsatile (rather than continuous) dopamine receptor stimulation, driving these complications.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What neuropsychiatric side effects can levodopa cause?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Hallucinations, confusion, and impulse-control disorders (e.g. gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive shopping/eating), along with dopamine dysregulation syndrome.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which antiemetics must be AVOIDED in a patient on levodopa for Parkinson's, and why?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Metoclopramide and prochlorperazine — they are central dopamine antagonists that worsen Parkinsonism. Non-selective MAOIs must also be avoided (hypertensive crisis).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do the non-ergot dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine) work?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They directly stimulate dopamine D2/D3 receptors, mimicking dopamine. Being longer-acting, they give more continuous (less pulsatile) stimulation -> less dyskinesia but more impulse-control disorders and somnolence.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the place of dopamine agonists in Parkinson's therapy?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: An option in early PD (not first-line over levodopa) where motor symptoms don't yet affect quality of life, and as adjuncts to levodopa for motor fluctuations.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which dopamine agonist is a transdermal patch, and when is that formulation especially useful?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Rotigotine. The patch is useful when a patient is nil-by-mouth and cannot take oral Parkinson's medication.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the two signature harms of dopamine agonists that you must counsel about?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Impulse-control disorders (pathological gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating, compulsive shopping) — warn patient AND family — and sudden-onset sleep / excessive daytime somnolence (caution with driving).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why are dopamine agonists used cautiously in elderly patients?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They cause more confusion and hallucinations in the elderly.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What happens if a dopamine agonist is stopped abruptly?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A dopamine-agonist withdrawal syndrome can occur — they should not be stopped suddenly.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why are the older ergot-derived dopamine agonists (bromocriptine, cabergoline, pergolide) now rarely used, and what monitoring do they require?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They cause fibrosis — cardiac valve, pulmonary, and retroperitoneal. Patients need monitoring such as echocardiography, inflammatory markers, renal function, and chest X-ray.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline, rasagiline, safinamide) treat Parkinson's disease?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They inhibit monoamine oxidase-B, reducing dopamine breakdown and prolonging its action. Used in early mild disease (modest benefit, delays levodopa) or as an adjunct to reduce end-of-dose 'off' time.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the key dangerous drug interaction with MAO-B inhibitors?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs — SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, tramadol and pethidine (pethidine is contraindicated). A washout is needed when switching (e.g. after a long-acting SSRI).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which MAO-B inhibitor commonly causes insomnia, and how do you manage this?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Selegiline. Advise taking it early in the day to reduce insomnia.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do COMT inhibitors (entacapone, tolcapone) help in Parkinson's disease, and what is the crucial limitation?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They inhibit catechol-O-methyltransferase, blocking breakdown of levodopa to prolong its plasma level and 'on' time. They only work WITH levodopa — they have no effect given alone.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: When are COMT inhibitors added to levodopa?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: For end-of-dose 'wearing-off' motor fluctuations — they extend the duration of each levodopa dose.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient started on entacapone reports reddish-brown urine. What is your response?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Reassure them — this is a harmless discolouration of the urine caused by entacapone and needs no action.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which COMT inhibitor is hepatotoxic, and what does this mean for its use?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Tolcapone. It is restricted to second-line use with regular liver function test monitoring, and is stopped if transaminases rise.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Besides urine discolouration, what side effect is increased by adding a COMT inhibitor to levodopa?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Enhanced dopaminergic effects, especially dyskinesia (also nausea, hypotension and diarrhoea).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the main modern use of amantadine in Parkinson's disease?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: To reduce levodopa-induced dyskinesias. It has combined dopaminergic and NMDA-antagonist actions and a mild anti-parkinsonian effect.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What two characteristic side effects should make you think of amantadine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Livedo reticularis (a mottled skin appearance) and ankle oedema.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What should you consider before prescribing amantadine in an elderly patient or one with renal impairment?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It can cause hallucinations and confusion (worse in the elderly), and it is renally cleared so the dose must be reduced in renal impairment. It should not be stopped abruptly.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do anticholinergics (procyclidine, trihexyphenidyl) work in Parkinson's disease, and which symptom do they mainly help?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They are antimuscarinics that rebalance the dopamine-acetylcholine relationship in the striatum (relatively too much acetylcholine in PD). They mainly help tremor, with little effect on bradykinesia.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is a key use of procyclidine outside idiopathic Parkinson's disease?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Drug-induced parkinsonism and acute dystonia — procyclidine (given IV/IM) reverses an antipsychotic-induced acute dystonic reaction.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why should anticholinergics be avoided in elderly Parkinson's patients?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They cause confusion and cognitive impairment, which is worse in the elderly. Their antimuscarinic effects also cause dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention and constipation, with cautions in glaucoma and prostatism.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How is apomorphine given, and for which patients?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Subcutaneously — as rescue injections or a continuous pump. It is used in advanced Parkinson's with severe motor fluctuations / 'off' periods when oral therapy no longer controls symptoms, bypassing the gut.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why must apomorphine be pre-treated with an antiemetic, and which one is used?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is very emetogenic (severe nausea and vomiting). Pre-treat with domperidone, a peripheral dopamine antagonist that doesn't cross the blood-brain barrier. Never use metoclopramide or prochlorperazine — they worsen Parkinsonism.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What precautions surround the FIRST dose of apomorphine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is given under supervision with lying and standing blood pressure checks, because of first-dose postural hypotension.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What monitoring do apomorphine and its antiemetic domperidone share?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Both prolong the QT interval, so check an ECG and electrolytes and avoid other QT-prolonging drugs.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What local and neuropsychiatric side effects occur with apomorphine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Injection-site nodules, plus (as with other dopamine agonists) sedation, hallucinations and impulse-control disorders.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Despite its name, what does apomorphine have to do with opioids?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Nothing — apomorphine is a potent non-selective dopamine agonist and has no opioid/morphine activity despite the name.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) work in dementia?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They block the breakdown of acetylcholine, raising cholinergic transmission to counter the cholinergic deficit of Alzheimer's. This modestly slows cognitive decline but is symptomatic only - it does not reverse or cure the disease.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Do acetylcholinesterase inhibitors reverse dementia?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: No. They are symptomatic treatments that modestly slow cognitive decline. They do not halt, reverse or cure the underlying neurodegeneration.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which drug class is first-line for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors - donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine, any of the three as monotherapy. Started on specialist advice but may be initiated in primary care.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which dementia drugs are used for Lewy body dementia?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors - donepezil or rivastigmine are used for dementia with Lewy bodies.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which acetylcholinesterase inhibitor is used for Parkinson's disease dementia?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Rivastigmine.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: In which dementias are acetylcholinesterase inhibitors NOT effective?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Pure vascular dementia and frontotemporal dementia - they should not be used for these. Their benefit is in Alzheimer's, and (for donepezil/rivastigmine) Lewy body and Parkinson's disease dementia.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the characteristic side-effect profile of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Cholinergic effects: nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, anorexia with weight loss, bradycardia and syncope (causing falls), peptic ulcer/GI bleed, muscle cramps, vivid dreams/insomnia and urinary frequency.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why can acetylcholinesterase inhibitors cause falls in the elderly?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Their cholinergic action slows the heart (vagotonic effect at the SA/AV node), causing bradycardia and syncope. This, together with dizziness, increases the risk of falls.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: An elderly patient on a cholinesterase inhibitor develops black stools and abdominal pain. What complication should you consider?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Peptic ulceration and GI bleeding - a recognised cholinergic effect of acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, which increase gastric acid secretion. They are cautioned/contraindicated in active peptic ulcer disease.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which cardiac conditions contraindicate or require caution with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Significant bradycardia, heart block and sick sinus syndrome - the drugs are vagotonic and slow the heart, risking syncope. Check pulse and consider an ECG before starting.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why are acetylcholinesterase inhibitors used with caution in asthma or COPD?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Their cholinergic action can increase bronchial secretions and bronchoconstriction, potentially worsening reactive airways disease.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the standard dosing schedule for donepezil in Alzheimer's disease?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Start 5 mg at night, then titrate up to 10 mg at night. Given once daily (nocte).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the key MHRA safety warning about the rivastigmine patch?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Remove the old patch before applying a new one, and only ever use one patch at a time. Fatal overdoses have occurred when multiple patches were applied without removing the previous one.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on galantamine develops a widespread skin rash. What should you do?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Stop galantamine immediately. It can cause serious skin reactions (e.g. Stevens-Johnson syndrome), so treatment must be discontinued at the first sign of a rash.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do bradycardic drugs interact with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Beta-blockers, digoxin, rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers and amiodarone add to the cholinergic slowing of the heart, causing additive bradycardia and heart block. Check the pulse and be cautious when co-prescribing.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why should anticholinergic drugs like oxybutynin or amitriptyline be reviewed in a patient on an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They antagonise the cholinergic benefit - directly opposing the drug's mechanism. They should be deprescribed where possible to avoid cancelling out the treatment (and adding to cognitive impairment).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor is going for surgery. What must the anaesthetist know?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: These drugs prolong the action of suxamethonium (a depolarising muscle relaxant), so the anaesthetist should be informed before surgery.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What monitoring is appropriate for a patient started on an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Check pulse (and ECG if cardiac risk) for bradycardia, monitor weight given the risk of anorexia/weight loss, and review cognitive response at follow-up.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How does memantine work in Alzheimer's disease?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is an NMDA-receptor antagonist that blocks the pathological glutamate-driven excitotoxic calcium influx, while sparing normal physiological signalling. The benefit is symptomatic.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: When is memantine indicated in Alzheimer's disease?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: For moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease. It can be used in moderate disease if an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor is unsuitable, and in severe disease.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Can memantine be combined with an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Yes. Because it works by a different mechanism (NMDA antagonism rather than boosting acetylcholine), it can be added to an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor across moderate-to-severe disease.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How does memantine's tolerability compare with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Memantine is generally well tolerated - mainly dizziness, headache and constipation, with far fewer cholinergic and cardiac (bradycardia/syncope) effects than the acetylcholinesterase inhibitors.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why does memantine require dose adjustment in renal impairment?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is renally cleared, so it accumulates when renal function is reduced. The dose must be lowered in renal impairment to avoid toxicity.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What effect can memantine have on seizure risk?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It can lower the seizure threshold, so it should be used with caution in patients with a history of seizures.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do the anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies lecanemab and donanemab work?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They are monoclonal antibodies that bind and clear amyloid-beta from the brain. They are the first disease-modifying drugs for Alzheimer's, modestly slowing decline.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What makes lecanemab and donanemab different from all previous Alzheimer's drugs?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They are the first disease-modifying treatments - they target the underlying amyloid pathology rather than just symptoms. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are symptomatic only.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which patients are eligible for anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Those with early Alzheimer's disease - mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia - with confirmed amyloid pathology. They are specialist-initiated and not used for vascular or frontotemporal dementia.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How are lecanemab and donanemab administered?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: As intravenous infusions every few weeks, under specialist care, with MRI surveillance.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Are the anti-amyloid antibodies available on the NHS?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: No. Lecanemab and donanemab are MHRA-licensed but NICE declined NHS funding because they were not judged cost-effective, so they are currently available privately only.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is ARIA, the defining risk of anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Amyloid-Related Imaging Abnormalities - brain oedema (ARIA-E) and microhaemorrhages (ARIA-H) seen on MRI, arising from amyloid clearance. It requires serial MRI monitoring to detect.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which genetic factor increases ARIA risk with anti-amyloid antibodies?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Carrying APOE e4 - risk rises with e4 copy number, and APOE e4 homozygotes have the highest risk. Genotyping is used to stratify risk before treatment.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is anticoagulation important to consider in patients on anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Anticoagulants increase the risk of ARIA-related haemorrhage. This raises the chance of serious or fatal bleeding, so bleeding risk must be assessed and monitored.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on lecanemab presents with an acute ischaemic stroke. Why must the stroke team be alerted to the antibody?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Thrombolysis (tPA) in a patient on an anti-amyloid antibody carries a high risk of serious/fatal intracerebral haemorrhage. The antibody use must be flagged to the stroke team so bleeding risk is weighed.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What monitoring is essential during anti-amyloid antibody treatment?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Serial MRI scans to detect ARIA (oedema and microhaemorrhage), APOE genotyping to stratify risk beforehand, and regular neurological review.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the mechanism of action of triptans (e.g. sumatriptan) in aborting a migraine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They are 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonists. 5-HT1B activation causes cranial vasoconstriction and 5-HT1D activation inhibits release of trigeminal CGRP (a key migraine mediator), together aborting the attack.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the recommended first-line drug regimen for an acute migraine attack?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A triptan PLUS an NSAID (or triptan plus paracetamol), with an antiemetic (e.g. metoclopramide or prochlorperazine) added even if the patient is not vomiting, as it aids symptom control and drug absorption.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient with a history of ischaemic heart disease asks for sumatriptan for migraine. Why is this contraindicated?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Triptans are vasoconstrictors (5-HT1B agonists) and are contraindicated in ischaemic heart disease, coronary or peripheral vascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension and previous stroke/TIA because of the risk of precipitating ischaemia/coronary vasospasm.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient starting a triptan reports chest and throat tightness, tingling and flushing after a dose. What are these and how should they be interpreted?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: These are 'triptan sensations' — usually benign and self-limiting, but they mimic angina. In a patient without cardiovascular risk they can be reassured, but genuine cardiac causes and rare coronary vasospasm must be considered.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is subcutaneous sumatriptan preferred over oral for a severe migraine attack with vomiting?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Oral sumatriptan has low bioavailability (~14%) and is unreliable if the patient is vomiting. The subcutaneous route has high bioavailability and the fastest onset, making it best for severe attacks, vomiting, and for cluster headache.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which acute migraine drug is given subcutaneously for cluster headache?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Subcutaneous sumatriptan.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which triptans are preferred for menstrual mini-prophylaxis, and why?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: The longer-acting triptans frovatriptan and zolmitriptan, because their longer duration of action allows short-term scheduled dosing around the predictable perimenstrual window.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How soon after taking ergotamine (or another triptan) can a triptan be given, and why?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Not within 24 hours. Triptans and ergots are both vasoconstrictors, so combining them (or giving them close together) risks additive/prolonged vasospasm — they must be separated by at least 24 hours.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why must triptans be avoided in patients taking MAOIs?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: MAOIs impair breakdown of several triptans, raising their levels and the risk of excessive serotonergic effects; triptans are contraindicated with MAOIs and within 2 weeks of stopping them.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the risk of combining a triptan with an SSRI or SNRI, and what should the patient be told?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Serotonin syndrome (agitation, tremor, hyperreflexia, autonomic instability). The MHRA advises counselling patients on the symptoms; the combination is often used but requires awareness and caution.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How often can triptans be used before medication-overuse headache becomes a risk, and what is the limit?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Frequent use causes medication-overuse headache. Acute migraine drugs including triptans should generally be limited to no more than 10 days per month.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What assessment should be done before first prescribing a triptan?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A cardiovascular risk assessment, because triptans are vasoconstrictors and contraindicated in significant cardiovascular, cerebrovascular or peripheral vascular disease and uncontrolled hypertension.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the mechanism of ergotamine/dihydroergotamine in migraine, and why have triptans superseded them?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They are non-selective agonists at serotonin, alpha-adrenergic and dopamine receptors causing potent, prolonged vasoconstriction. They are poorly selective and toxic (including a fibrosis risk), so triptans, which are more selective and safer, have largely replaced them.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is ergotism, and how does it present?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Ergotism is severe, prolonged peripheral vasoconstriction caused by ergot drugs, presenting with cold, painful, ischaemic extremities that can progress to gangrene.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which class of interacting drugs can precipitate ergotism when combined with ergotamine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Drugs that inhibit ergotamine's metabolism — notably macrolide and azole antibiotics and HIV protease inhibitors — raise ergot levels and can trigger severe vasoconstriction (ergotism).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What serious complication can occur with chronic ergotamine use, besides ergotism?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Fibrosis (e.g. retroperitoneal or cardiac fibrosis), related to its non-selective serotonergic activity.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: In which patients is ergotamine contraindicated?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Patients with cardiovascular or peripheral vascular disease, and in pregnancy (also avoid in sepsis and hepatic/renal impairment) — largely because of its potent vasoconstrictor toxicity.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Can ergotamine be combined with a triptan for a resistant migraine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: No. Both are vasoconstrictors, so combining them causes additive vasospasm; they must be separated by at least 24 hours.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the mechanism of gepants such as rimegepant and atogepant?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They are oral small-molecule CGRP-receptor antagonists that block calcitonin gene-related peptide, a key migraine mediator, aborting/preventing attacks without causing vasoconstriction.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why are gepants particularly useful in a patient with ischaemic heart disease who cannot take triptans?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Gepants work by CGRP-receptor blockade and do not cause vasoconstriction, so they are safe in cardiovascular disease and are an option when triptans are contraindicated or ineffective.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which gepant is licensed for both acute treatment and prevention of migraine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Rimegepant — used orally for the acute attack and, on an every-other-day schedule, for prevention. (Atogepant is used once daily for prevention.)

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the common side effects of gepants, and do they cause medication-overuse headache?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They are generally well tolerated, with nausea and somnolence being most common. They have no medication-overuse-headache signal and, importantly, no vasoconstriction.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What dose and hepatic considerations apply to gepants?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Atogepant requires renal dose adjustment, and gepants should be avoided in severe hepatic impairment. Strong metabolic enzyme inhibitors and inducers should also be avoided.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the mechanism of lasmiditan, and how does it differ from a triptan?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Lasmiditan is a selective 5-HT1F receptor agonist (a 'ditan') that aborts migraine through a neuronal, non-vascular mechanism. Unlike triptans it causes no vasoconstriction, so it is an option in cardiovascular disease.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What key safety advice must be given to a patient taking lasmiditan for an acute migraine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Do not drive or perform tasks needing alertness for 8 hours after a dose, because lasmiditan is highly CNS-penetrant and causes marked sedation, dizziness and drowsiness.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is lasmiditan classed as a controlled drug?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It has CNS effects that can produce euphoria and a potential for misuse, so it is a controlled drug.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the main cautions with lasmiditan regarding other drugs?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Additive sedation with alcohol and other CNS depressants, and a risk of serotonin syndrome when combined with serotonergic drugs (SSRIs/SNRIs/triptans).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the difference between acute (abortive) and prophylactic migraine treatment?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Acute treatment (triptans, NSAIDs, gepants, lasmiditan, antiemetics) is taken at the onset of an attack to abort it. Prophylaxis (e.g. propranolol, topiramate, amitriptyline) is taken daily to reduce attack frequency and is offered when attacks are frequent or disabling — it does not treat the acute attack.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the first-line options for migraine prophylaxis?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Propranolol or topiramate are first-line, with amitriptyline as an off-label alternative. Non-drug options such as acupuncture and riboflavin 400 mg/day may also be considered.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why should propranolol be avoided as migraine prophylaxis in a patient with asthma?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: As a non-selective beta-blocker it can cause bronchospasm and is contraindicated in asthma. It also masks the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycaemia.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is topiramate contraindicated for migraine prophylaxis in a woman who could become pregnant?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Topiramate is teratogenic (cleft lip/palate risk), so it is contraindicated for migraine prophylaxis in pregnancy and is only used within a Pregnancy Prevention Programme in women of childbearing potential.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the characteristic side effects of topiramate, and its interaction with the combined oral contraceptive pill?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Cognitive slowing, weight loss and paraesthesia. At doses above 200 mg/day it reduces the efficacy of the combined oral contraceptive pill.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is valproate avoided for migraine prophylaxis in women of childbearing potential?
