pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Valproate is highly teratogenic. Under MHRA 2024 guidance it should not be started in anyone under 55 (either sex) without sign-off from two specialists, so it is avoided in women of childbearing potential.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the typical dosing and main risks of amitriptyline used for migraine prophylaxis?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: 10-25 mg taken at night. It causes antimuscarinic effects and sedation and is dangerous in overdose (cardiotoxic).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Candesartan is used for migraine prophylaxis — what monitoring and pregnancy caution apply?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: As an ARB it requires monitoring of U&Es and potassium (risk of hyperkalaemia and hypotension). It is fetotoxic and must be avoided in pregnancy.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: When are CGRP monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab) used, and how are they given?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They are specialist-initiated for prevention, reserved (along with gepants) for patients in whom at least 3 standard preventive drugs have failed. They are given by monthly subcutaneous injection.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How does erenumab differ mechanistically from fremanezumab and galcanezumab?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Erenumab blocks the CGRP receptor, whereas fremanezumab and galcanezumab bind the CGRP ligand itself (mnemonic: erEnumab = rEceptor).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the notable side effects of the CGRP monoclonal antibodies?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Injection-site reactions with all of them, and constipation particularly with erenumab.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which type of MS disease activity do disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) target, and who initiates them?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: DMTs are used for ACTIVE (relapsing) MS. They are specialist-initiated. They do NOT benefit non-active progressive MS.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on a DMT presents with an acute MS relapse. Does increasing or switching the DMT treat the relapse?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: No. DMTs reduce relapse frequency over time but do NOT treat an acute relapse. An acute relapse is treated with high-dose methylprednisolone (steroids).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the first-line treatment for an acute multiple sclerosis relapse?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: High-dose methylprednisolone (corticosteroids). DMTs do not treat the acute attack; they are for reducing future relapses in active disease.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What class of drug are the beta-interferons, and how are they given for MS?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: An immunomodulatory, injectable (SC/IM) first-generation platform DMT for active relapsing-remitting MS. Modest efficacy but a long, strong safety record.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Simply, how do beta-interferons reduce MS relapses?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They shift the immune response away from inflammatory (Th1) towards a less inflammatory (Th2) pattern and reduce leakiness of the blood-brain barrier, so fewer immune cells enter the CNS. This lowers relapse frequency.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Where do beta-interferons sit among DMTs in terms of effectiveness?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They are only modestly effective (an older moderate-efficacy platform therapy), often now superseded by more effective oral or monoclonal agents. Their advantage is a long safety record.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Can beta-interferon be used or continued in pregnancy for a woman with active relapsing-remitting MS?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Yes. Beta-interferons are regarded as safe in pregnancy and may be continued, making them a relatively pregnancy-friendly DMT option.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient reports fever, muscle aches and malaise a few hours after every beta-interferon injection. What is this, and how is it managed?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Flu-like symptoms — the hallmark, very common side effect of beta-interferons. Pre-treat with paracetamol around the time of injection; they typically settle with continued use.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Besides flu-like symptoms, name common local and blood/liver side effects of beta-interferon.
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Injection-site reactions, deranged LFTs, and leucopenia (low white cells). Beta-interferon can also cause depression/suicidal ideation, so mood must be monitored.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why must mood be monitored in a patient started on beta-interferon for MS?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Beta-interferon can cause depression and suicidal ideation. Ask about mood at review; severe depression is a caution to its use.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on beta-interferon develops new hypertension, a low platelet count and worsening renal function. What serious MHRA-flagged reaction is this, and what do you do?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Thrombotic microangiopathy (TTP/HUS) — new hypertension, thrombocytopenia and renal failure. It is a medical emergency and beta-interferon must be stopped. Can occur weeks to years after starting.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which two MHRA-flagged reactions to beta-interferon both require stopping the drug?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Thrombotic microangiopathy (TTP/HUS) and nephrotic syndrome. Both mandate discontinuation of beta-interferon.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What routine blood monitoring is needed on beta-interferon?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: FBC and LFTs (for leucopenia and deranged liver function), plus monitoring of mood for depression/suicidal ideation.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why should beta-interferon be used cautiously with other hepatotoxic or myelosuppressive drugs?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Additive effects can worsen LFT derangement and lower blood counts (leucopenia). Monitor bloods more closely if such drugs are co-prescribed.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What kind of drug is glatiramer acetate and how does it work in MS, at a simple level?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: An injectable (SC) immunomodulator made of a peptide mixture that mimics myelin. It drives the immune system towards a regulatory/anti-inflammatory (Th2) response, reducing relapses in relapsing-remitting MS.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Where does glatiramer acetate fit in MS treatment and how is it tolerated?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A well-tolerated injectable platform therapy for relapsing-remitting MS, and relatively pregnancy-friendly. Modest efficacy but a good safety profile.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Minutes after a glatiramer acetate injection, a patient develops flushing, chest tightness and palpitations. What is this and what should you do?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A characteristic benign, transient post-injection systemic reaction. It is self-limiting and harmless — reassure the patient; no specific treatment or drug cessation is needed.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What local side effects can occur with glatiramer acetate?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Injection-site reactions and lipoatrophy (loss of fat at injection sites). Rotating injection sites helps.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What kind of DMT is dimethyl fumarate and where does it sit in MS therapy?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: An ORAL, moderately effective first-line DMT for relapsing-remitting MS, taken twice daily. It is immunomodulatory, reducing relapse frequency.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient starting dimethyl fumarate complains of flushing. How is this managed?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Flushing is common. Advise taking the dose with food to reduce it; aspirin taken beforehand can also help. It usually improves over the first weeks.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the common gastrointestinal and liver-related effects of dimethyl fumarate?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: GI upset (nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal pain) is common, and it can cause deranged LFTs. Taking with food helps GI symptoms; monitor liver function.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the key haematological risk of dimethyl fumarate, and how is it monitored?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Lymphopenia (low lymphocyte count). Check FBC before starting, then every 3 months. Interrupt treatment if lymphocytes fall too low (confirmed on repeat).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why does severe or prolonged lymphopenia on dimethyl fumarate matter?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Severe/prolonged lymphopenia raises the risk of PML (progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy), a serious brain infection. This is why the lymphocyte count is monitored and the drug interrupted if it drops too far; PML has occurred even after stopping.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on dimethyl fumarate has a lymphocyte count that is persistently very low. What is the correct action?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Interrupt dimethyl fumarate (confirm the low count on repeat first). Do not restart while severe/prolonged lymphopenia persists, because of the PML risk.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What kind of drug is natalizumab and what is its target?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: A highly effective monoclonal antibody, anti-alpha-4-integrin. It blocks lymphocytes from crossing the blood-brain barrier into the CNS, sharply reducing relapses.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which patients with MS is natalizumab used for, and how is it given?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Highly active relapsing-remitting MS, where high efficacy is needed. Given by IV infusion every 4 weeks.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the defining serious danger of natalizumab?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: PML (progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy) from reactivation of the JC virus — an often fatal brain infection. It is the treatment-limiting risk.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is JC virus antibody status checked before and during natalizumab treatment?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It stratifies the risk of PML. Risk rises with a higher JCV antibody index, treatment duration over 2 years, and prior immunosuppression. A JCV-positive patient is at high PML risk.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient stops natalizumab. Can they relax about PML surveillance straight away?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: No. PML risk carries over for up to about 6 months after stopping. Continue MRI surveillance during this period to detect PML early.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Besides PML, what other adverse effects should you watch for with natalizumab?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Infusion reactions and hepatotoxicity. Monitor LFTs, alongside JC virus antibody status and MRI surveillance for PML.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How does alemtuzumab work in MS?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is an anti-CD52 monoclonal antibody that depletes circulating T and B lymphocytes. These then repopulate with a less autoreactive profile, making it a highly effective 'immune reconstitution' therapy given as short courses.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is alemtuzumab described as an 'immune reconstitution' therapy rather than a continuous drug?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is given as brief annual IV courses (5 days, repeated at 12 months) rather than ongoing dosing. Depleting the lymphocyte pool lets the immune system repopulate in a less autoreactive way, giving lasting benefit off-treatment.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Where does alemtuzumab now sit in the MS treatment pathway after the 2019/20 MHRA restriction?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is restricted to second-line use: only for highly active relapsing-remitting MS despite a full adequate course of at least one other DMT, or for rapidly-evolving severe RRMS.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the signature delayed adverse effect of alemtuzumab, and when does it appear?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Secondary autoimmune disease appearing months to years after treatment: autoimmune thyroid disease (~40%, especially Graves'), immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), and anti-GBM (Goodpasture) nephritis. It arises because B cells return before regulatory T cells, giving imbalanced reconstitution.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient develops new easy bruising and a low platelet count a year after alemtuzumab. What is the likely diagnosis?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) — one of the delayed secondary autoimmune complications of alemtuzumab. This is why platelet counts are monitored for years after treatment.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient develops haematuria and a rising creatinine after alemtuzumab. What serious complication must be excluded?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Anti-GBM (Goodpasture) nephritis, a delayed autoimmune complication. Urinalysis and creatinine are monitored monthly to catch it early, as it can cause rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What acute reactions can occur within 1-3 days of an alemtuzumab infusion?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Serious cardiovascular and haemorrhagic events including stroke, cervicocephalic arterial dissection, MI and pulmonary haemorrhage. Blood pressure must be monitored before, during and after the infusion.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What routine monitoring is required after alemtuzumab, and for how long?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Monthly FBC, creatinine and urinalysis, plus 3-monthly thyroid function tests, continued until 48 months after the last dose — to detect ITP, anti-GBM nephritis and thyroid disease.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What infection prophylaxis and counselling accompany alemtuzumab?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Aciclovir prophylaxis from day 1 (for at least a month), and counselling to avoid Listeria (undercooked meats and soft cheeses) around infusions.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: In which situations is alemtuzumab contraindicated?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Active infection, HIV, and uncontrolled hypertension. Caution is also needed given the risk of triggering autoimmune disease.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do ocrelizumab and ofatumumab work in MS?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They are anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies that deplete B cells, which are pathogenic in MS. This makes them highly effective for relapsing MS. Plasma cells lack CD20 and are spared, so serum IgG is initially preserved.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is unique about ocrelizumab's licensed indication compared with other DMTs?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is the first DMT proven and licensed for primary progressive MS (in patients with inflammatory/imaging activity). However, NICE did not recommend it for PPMS (TA585), so it is not NHS-funded for that indication.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How are ocrelizumab and ofatumumab administered?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Ocrelizumab is given by IV infusion every 6 months. Ofatumumab is a monthly subcutaneous injection that patients self-administer at home.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What must be screened for before starting an anti-CD20 antibody, and why?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Hepatitis B — because depleting B cells can reactivate the virus. Screening is done before the first dose.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the main adverse effects of anti-CD20 antibodies in MS?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Infusion/injection reactions, infections (especially respiratory and urinary), hepatitis B reactivation, hypogammaglobulinaemia developing after repeated dosing, and a small malignancy signal.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How should vaccination be timed around anti-CD20 therapy for MS?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Give required vaccines before starting — especially live/live-attenuated vaccines at least 4-6 weeks beforehand. Live vaccines should not be given during B-cell depletion.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How do S1P modulators (fingolimod, siponimod, ozanimod) reduce MS relapses?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They are sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators that trap lymphocytes in lymph nodes and prevent their egress. Fewer lymphocytes therefore reach the CNS, reducing relapses. They are taken orally.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which MS patients are S1P modulators used for?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Fingolimod for highly active relapsing-remitting MS (a high-efficacy option, not plain first-line), and siponimod for active secondary-progressive MS. All are oral therapies.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why does the first dose of fingolimod require cardiac monitoring?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: S1P modulators can cause first-dose bradycardia and heart block. The first dose requires ECG/heart rate monitoring for about 6 hours to detect this.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on a beta-blocker is due to start fingolimod. Why is this a concern?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Bradycardic and QT-prolonging drugs (beta-blockers, diltiazem, verapamil, antiarrhythmics) add to the first-dose bradycardia/AV block risk of S1P modulators. This needs careful assessment and cardiac monitoring.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on an S1P modulator reports blurred central vision. What complication should you consider?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Macular oedema — a recognised effect of S1P modulators. Eye examination/OCT screening is used to monitor for it.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What infection risks accompany S1P modulators, and what pre-treatment check is needed?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They cause lymphopenia and infections including VZV (varicella/zoster), cryptococcal infection and PML. Check VZV serology and vaccinate non-immune patients before starting; live vaccines are contraindicated during and for about 2 months after treatment.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What must be confirmed regarding pregnancy before starting an S1P modulator?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They are teratogenic, so a negative pregnancy test and effective contraception are required before starting, continued during treatment.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What can happen if an S1P modulator is stopped in MS?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Disease rebound — a severe return of MS activity on stopping. This must be considered when discontinuing, for example when planning pregnancy.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What extra pre-treatment test does siponimod specifically require?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: CYP2C9 genotype testing before starting. It is contraindicated in poor metabolisers, and the dose is adjusted in certain intermediate genotypes.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Besides cardiac and eye effects, what longer-term monitoring do S1P modulators need?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Skin surveillance for basal cell carcinoma, plus monitoring of blood pressure and liver function tests. FBC is also checked for lymphopenia.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How does cladribine work in MS?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is an oral purine analogue that selectively and durably depletes B and T lymphocytes, acting as an 'immune reconstitution' therapy. Short oral courses give lasting benefit even off-treatment.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How is cladribine dosed in MS?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: As short oral courses of a few days per year over 2 years (year 1 and year 2), typically followed by years of continued benefit without further treatment. It is used for highly active RRMS.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the key adverse effects of cladribine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Lymphopenia with increased infection risk (notably herpes zoster), headache, nausea, and a small malignancy signal. It is also teratogenic.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What screening and prophylaxis are needed before starting cladribine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Check VZV serology and vaccinate if antibody-negative, screen for HIV, hepatitis and TB, and monitor FBC (lymphocytes). Effective contraception is arranged.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the contraception requirements for cladribine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is teratogenic, so effective contraception is required in BOTH sexes during treatment and for at least 6 months after the last dose.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: In which situations is cladribine contraindicated?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Active malignancy, active infection or HIV, and pregnancy.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the mechanism of riluzole and why does it help in motor neurone disease?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It inhibits presynaptic glutamate release, antagonises postsynaptic glutamate (NMDA/kainate) receptors and inactivates voltage-gated Na+ channels -> reduces glutamate excitotoxicity -> modestly slows disease progression.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is riluzole used for and who initiates it?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is the principal disease-modifying drug in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis / motor neurone disease (per NICE TA20), specialist (neurologist)-initiated.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How much does riluzole actually change the course of MND?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It prolongs survival only modestly (a few months) and does NOT reverse existing disability — it slows progression, it is not a cure.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the standard dose of riluzole?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: 50 mg twice daily (BD).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which two blood-monitored toxicities are the key risks of riluzole?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Hepatotoxicity (raised transaminases — monitor LFTs) and neutropenia/agranulocytosis. Nausea, asthenia and dizziness also occur.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient on riluzole develops a febrile illness — what must you do?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Stop the riluzole and check an FBC urgently, because riluzole can cause neutropenia/agranulocytosis and a febrile illness may be the presenting sign.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How are LFTs monitored on riluzole, and when do you stop for liver toxicity?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Check ALT at baseline, then regularly (monthly for the first 3 months, 3-monthly for the rest of year 1, then periodically). Stop if transaminases rise above 5x the upper limit of normal.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What MHRA-flagged lung problem should prompt investigation in a patient on riluzole?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Interstitial lung disease — investigate any new cough or breathlessness.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why can smoking reduce the effectiveness of riluzole?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Smoking induces the enzyme that metabolises riluzole, lowering riluzole blood levels.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the mechanism of acetazolamide?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor -> reduces CSF and aqueous-humour production and causes renal bicarbonate loss producing a hyperchloraemic (normal-anion-gap) metabolic acidosis with mild diuresis -> lowers intracranial and intraocular pressure.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the first-line medical treatment for idiopathic intracranial hypertension?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Acetazolamide — the carbonic anhydrase inhibitor reduces CSF production and lowers intracranial pressure (alongside weight loss).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: List the main uses of acetazolamide.
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (first-line medical Rx), glaucoma, altitude sickness prophylaxis, and some seizures.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why does acetazolamide help prevent altitude sickness?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: The metabolic acidosis it induces stimulates ventilation, offsetting the hypoxic respiratory alkalosis of altitude.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient with a sulfonamide allergy is prescribed acetazolamide — what is the concern?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Acetazolamide is a sulfonamide, so there is class cross-reactivity — avoid it (risk of rash and, rarely, severe reactions such as SJS/TEN or blood dyscrasias).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Is acetazolamide safe in pregnancy?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: No — it is teratogenic and should be avoided, especially in the first trimester.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the characteristic side effects of acetazolamide?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Paraesthesia (tingling fingers, toes and lips — very common), metabolic acidosis, hypokalaemia, altered taste (fizzy drinks taste odd), renal stones, and drowsiness.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What monitoring is needed for acetazolamide in idiopathic intracranial hypertension?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: U&Es (watch potassium and bicarbonate) and visual fields (to detect worsening intracranial hypertension).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why should salicylates (e.g. high-dose aspirin) be avoided with acetazolamide?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: They cause mutual toxicity — a severe metabolic acidosis and increased salicylate toxicity.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the mechanism of pyridostigmine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor -> increases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction -> improves transmission across antibody-blocked ACh receptors -> improves muscle strength in myasthenia gravis.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the role of pyridostigmine in myasthenia gravis?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: First-line SYMPTOMATIC treatment — it improves strength but does not modify the disease; disease-modifying immunosuppression (e.g. steroids/azathioprine) is a separate treatment.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why does pyridostigmine act only peripherally and not in the brain?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is a charged (quaternary amine), lipid-insoluble molecule so it does not cross the blood-brain barrier — its action is confined to the periphery/neuromuscular junction.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What side effects would you warn a patient starting pyridostigmine about?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Muscarinic/cholinergic effects — abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, salivation, sweating and bradycardia.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is a cholinergic crisis and how does it relate to pyridostigmine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is caused by over-dosing with an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor -> weakness that mimics a myasthenic crisis. It is distinguished by muscarinic excess (SLUDGE features: salivation, lacrimation, diarrhoea, miosis, bradycardia, fasciculations), whereas a myasthenic crisis is from undertreatment.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A myasthenic patient on pyridostigmine is going to theatre — what must the anaesthetist know?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Pyridostigmine prolongs the action of suxamethonium and antagonises non-depolarising blockers (e.g. rocuronium/vecuronium) — inform the anaesthetist so neuromuscular blockade is managed appropriately.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is pyridostigmine used with caution in asthma?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Its cholinergic action can cause bronchospasm and increased secretions, worsening asthma.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Name the three antispasticity muscle relaxants and their differing mechanisms.
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Baclofen = GABA-B agonist (spinal, oral or intrathecal); tizanidine = central alpha-2 agonist; dantrolene = acts directly on skeletal muscle, blocking the ryanodine receptor to stop calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: In which conditions are antispasticity relaxants used?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Spasticity from MS, spinal cord injury, cerebral palsy and stroke (baclofen and tizanidine orally; intrathecal baclofen for severe cases).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the specific drug treatment for malignant hyperthermia?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Dantrolene — it blocks the ryanodine receptor, stopping the uncontrolled calcium release from muscle. It is also used in neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why must oral baclofen never be stopped abruptly?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Abrupt withdrawal causes severe rebound spasticity, seizures and autonomic instability — it must be tapered.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: A patient with an intrathecal baclofen pump becomes acutely unwell with high fever, rigidity and rhabdomyolysis — what is the concern?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Intrathecal baclofen withdrawal from pump/catheter failure -> a rapid, life-threatening withdrawal syndrome that mimics NMS or sepsis (fever, rhabdomyolysis, multi-organ failure) and needs urgent baclofen replacement.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the common dose-limiting side effects of the antispasticity relaxants?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Sedation, weakness (too much drug -> floppiness) and hypotension.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which two antispasticity relaxants are hepatotoxic and require LFT monitoring?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Tizanidine and dantrolene — monitor liver function tests.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is tizanidine contraindicated with ciprofloxacin or fluvoxamine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: These enzyme-inhibiting drugs markedly raise tizanidine levels -> dangerous hypotension, sedation and bradycardia.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the two acute treatments for a cluster headache attack?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Subcutaneous (or intranasal) sumatriptan for rapid onset, PLUS high-flow 100% oxygen at 12-15 L/min via a non-rebreathe mask (patient seated).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Why is oral sumatriptan not used for cluster headache?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Cluster attacks peak quickly, so oral triptans are too slow — subcutaneous (6 mg) or intranasal sumatriptan is needed for rapid onset.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How does sumatriptan work?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is a 5-HT1B/1D agonist -> causes cranial vasoconstriction and inhibits trigeminal neuropeptide (CGRP) release.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is first-line prophylaxis for cluster headache, and what monitoring does it need?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Verapamil — it needs a baseline and serial ECGs (especially at higher doses) because it can cause PR prolongation and heart block.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What are the vascular contraindications to sumatriptan?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Ischaemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, peripheral vascular disease and uncontrolled hypertension (same cautions as migraine triptans) — reflecting the risk of coronary vasospasm.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How long must you separate a triptan from an ergot derivative?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: At least 24 hours apart, because both are vasoconstrictors and combining them risks excessive vasoconstriction.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the mechanism of tetrabenazine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: It is a VMAT2 inhibitor -> depletes presynaptic dopamine (and other monoamines) in the CNS -> reduces excess involuntary movements in hyperkinetic disorders.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is tetrabenazine used for?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Chorea of Huntington's disease and other hyperkinetic movement disorders (e.g. hemiballismus, tardive dyskinesia).

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: What is the key safety risk of tetrabenazine and when is it contraindicated?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Depression and suicidality (from dopamine depletion) — it is contraindicated in active suicidality or uncontrolled depression, and mood must be monitored.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Besides depression, what other adverse effects does tetrabenazine carry?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Parkinsonism and sedation, QT prolongation, and (like antipsychotics) a risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: Which drug class is absolutely contraindicated with tetrabenazine?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: MAOIs (and reserpine) — additive monoamine depletion.

pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.front: How is tetrabenazine dosing affected by certain antidepressants?
pharmacology__Neurology & Psychiatry Dru.back: Antidepressants such as fluoxetine and paroxetine inhibit its metabolism, so the maximum tetrabenazine dose must be reduced when they are co-prescribed.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Where does paracetamol sit on the WHO analgesic ladder, and what kind of pain is that ladder for?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Step 1 (non-opioid). The WHO ladder is for acute and cancer pain. NICE (NG193) advises AGAINST starting paracetamol, NSAIDs or opioids for chronic PRIMARY pain.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How does paracetamol's mechanism and side-effect profile differ from an NSAID?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Paracetamol acts CENTRALLY (weak central COX inhibition plus descending serotonergic/endocannabinoid modulation), giving analgesia and antipyresis but MINIMAL anti-inflammatory effect and minimal GI/renal harm - so it is very well tolerated at normal doses.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the maximum daily oral dose of paracetamol in a healthy adult, and the usual regimen?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: 1 g QDS orally, maximum 4 g/day.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: In which patients should you REDUCE the paracetamol dose, and why?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Reduce if body weight <50 kg, malnourished, hepatic impairment, or chronic high alcohol intake. These patients have lower glutathione reserves, so they are more prone to hepatotoxicity.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How should IV paracetamol be dosed in an adult weighing under 50 kg?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Dose by weight: 15 mg/kg per dose (max 60 mg/kg/day), NOT a flat 1 g. This avoids fatal ~10-fold dosing errors in small/underweight patients.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the mechanism of liver injury in paracetamol overdose?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: In overdose the toxic metabolite NAPQI accumulates; once glutathione stores are depleted, NAPQI binds hepatocytes -> hepatotoxicity and acute liver failure.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the antidote for paracetamol overdose and how does it work?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: N-acetylcysteine - it replenishes glutathione, allowing the toxic metabolite NAPQI to be safely neutralised before it damages hepatocytes.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient took paracetamol in a staggered pattern over several hours, or the timing is uncertain. Can you use the treatment nomogram?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: No. The nomogram only applies to a SINGLE acute ingestion timed at least 4 hours after ingestion. For a staggered overdose, therapeutic excess, or uncertain timing, give N-acetylcysteine regardless of the level.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which patient factors increase the hepatotoxicity risk in paracetamol overdose?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Enzyme-inducing drugs (e.g. carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin) and chronic alcohol excess - both increase production of the toxic metabolite NAPQI. Malnutrition/low weight also lower glutathione and add risk.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What blood tests do you monitor in a paracetamol overdose?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Paracetamol level (plotted on the nomogram for single acute ingestions), LFTs, INR (clotting), and renal function.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How do NSAIDs produce analgesia, and what does blocking prostaglandins cost you?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They inhibit COX-1 and COX-2 -> reduced prostaglandin synthesis -> analgesic, anti-inflammatory and antipyretic. But loss of PROTECTIVE prostaglandins causes the harms: GI, renal and cardiovascular effects.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What are the THREE major harms of NSAIDs a prescriber must weigh?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: 1) GI ulceration/bleeding, 2) acute kidney injury and fluid retention, 3) increased cardiovascular/thrombotic risk.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How do you protect the stomach when prescribing an NSAID to an at-risk patient?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Co-prescribe a PPI. Also use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time and take with food.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the 'triple whammy' and why is it dangerous?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: NSAID + ACE inhibitor/ARB + diuretic taken together. All three compromise renal perfusion/autoregulation -> high risk of acute kidney injury.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which NSAID has the LOWEST cardiovascular risk, and which have the highest?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Naproxen (at 1 g/day or less) has the lowest CV/thrombotic risk. Diclofenac and high-dose ibuprofen (2.4 g/day or more) carry the highest CV risk.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: In which cardiovascular patients is diclofenac specifically contraindicated (per the MHRA)?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Established ischaemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, peripheral arterial disease, and heart failure - because of its increased thrombotic risk.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why can NSAIDs trigger a severe reaction in some asthmatics?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: In aspirin/NSAID-sensitive asthma, blocking COX shunts arachidonic acid down the leukotriene pathway -> bronchospasm. Avoid NSAIDs in these patients.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: In which situations should NSAIDs be avoided altogether?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Active peptic ulcer/GI bleeding, severe heart failure, significant renal impairment, and aspirin-sensitive asthma. Also avoid in later pregnancy.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why are NSAIDs avoided in pregnancy from around 20-28 weeks onward?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They can cause fetal renal dysfunction with oligohydramnios and, later, premature closure of the ductus arteriosus.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How do NSAIDs affect lithium and methotrexate levels?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They reduce renal excretion of both -> raised plasma levels and risk of lithium toxicity or methotrexate toxicity. Avoid the combination or monitor closely.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why should ibuprofen doses be separated from low-dose aspirin taken for cardioprotection?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Ibuprofen competes at COX-1 and can block aspirin's antiplatelet/cardioprotective effect. Separate the doses (take aspirin first, or space them apart).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How does a COX-2 selective inhibitor (e.g. celecoxib, etoricoxib) differ from a traditional NSAID for the gut?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Selective COX-2 inhibition spares COX-1, so there are FEWER GI ulcers and bleeds than with non-selective NSAIDs.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the main trade-off that limits COX-2 inhibitor use?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Their cardiovascular/thrombotic risk remains, or is higher, than traditional NSAIDs. So they are useful where GI risk is high but should be AVOIDED in established cardiovascular disease.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Do COX-2 inhibitors avoid the renal problems of other NSAIDs?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: No. They still cause the same renal effects, fluid retention and hypertension. Avoid in renal impairment and uncontrolled hypertension.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: When would you choose a COX-2 inhibitor over a traditional NSAID?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: When a patient needs anti-inflammatory analgesia and has HIGH GI risk but LOW/acceptable cardiovascular risk.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How does codeine produce its analgesic effect?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Codeine is a PRODRUG converted to morphine, which is a mu-opioid agonist. It is a weak opioid at step 2 of the WHO ladder, used for mild-to-moderate pain.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Codeine and dihydrocodeine are activated by an enzyme with genetic variation. What happens in ultra-rapid versus poor metabolisers?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Ultra-rapid metabolisers convert too much codeine to morphine -> excess morphine and dangerous respiratory depression. Poor metabolisers make little morphine -> little/no analgesia.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why is codeine contraindicated in children under 12 and after tonsillectomy?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Unpredictable conversion to morphine (ultra-rapid metabolisers) risks fatal respiratory depression. It is also avoided in breastfeeding, as excess morphine can pass to the infant.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Besides pain, what other uses does codeine have?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It is an antitussive (cough suppressant) and an antidiarrhoeal, in addition to analgesia (often given as co-codamol with paracetamol).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What should you ALWAYS co-prescribe with a weak opioid such as codeine, and why?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: A laxative - opioids reliably cause constipation. Also warn about nausea and drowsiness.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What happens if a weak opioid is combined with benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids or alcohol?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Additive sedation and respiratory depression - a dangerous combination (MHRA warning). Prescribe with caution and warn the patient.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How does tramadol differ mechanistically from codeine?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Tramadol is a weak mu-opioid agonist that ALSO inhibits serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake -> dual analgesic action, with some benefit in neuropathic pain.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What TWO extra risks does tramadol carry compared with other opioids?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: 1) It LOWERS the seizure threshold (avoid in epilepsy), and 2) it can cause serotonin syndrome when combined with serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, TCAs, MAOIs).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How do tramadol's constipation and respiratory depression compare with classic opioids?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Tramadol tends to cause LESS constipation and less respiratory depression than classic opioids, but it can still cause dependence and is a controlled drug.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient on an SSRI is prescribed tramadol and becomes agitated, tremulous, hyperthermic with clonus. What is the likely diagnosis?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Serotonin syndrome - the result of additive serotonergic effect from tramadol plus the SSRI. Stop the offending drugs and give supportive care.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Where do morphine, oxycodone and hydromorphone sit on the WHO analgesic ladder, and what is their mechanism?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They are strong opioids (step 3), acting as full mu-opioid receptor agonists -> potent analgesia (with euphoria, sedation and respiratory depression).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient with severe cancer pain needs regular opioid analgesia. What is the NICE first-line strong opioid and how is it given?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Oral morphine is first-line for cancer pain (NICE CG140): a modified-release preparation for background pain plus immediate-release morphine for breakthrough pain.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: For which type of chronic pain are strong opioids NOT recommended?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Chronic primary pain (NG193) — there is little evidence of long-term benefit and a real risk of dependence, so opioids should not be started for it.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Besides moderate-to-severe and cancer pain, name a palliative-care symptom (other than pain) that morphine is used to relieve.
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Breathlessness in palliative care. Morphine (and diamorphine) reduces the sensation of breathlessness; it is also used for acute MI and pulmonary oedema.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which opioid side effect is universal and mandates a co-prescription every single time?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Constipation — it is universal (opioids do not develop tolerance to it), so ALWAYS co-prescribe a regular laxative when starting a strong opioid.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient started on morphine is nauseated and vomiting in the first few days. How do you manage this?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Prescribe an antiemetic initially — opioid-induced nausea/vomiting is usually transient and settles within days, so the antiemetic can often be stopped later (unlike the laxative, which is continued).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What are the three features of the classic opioid overdose triad, and what reverses it?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Pinpoint (constricted) pupils = miosis, respiratory depression, and coma/reduced consciousness. Reverse with naloxone, the competitive mu-opioid antagonist.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which is the most dangerous acute side effect of strong opioids, and how is it monitored?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Respiratory depression. Monitor respiratory rate and sedation level; a falling respiratory rate is the key warning sign of toxicity.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why should morphine be avoided in renal impairment, and how does it present?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Its active metabolites accumulate when renal clearance falls, causing excessive sedation and respiratory depression, plus neuroexcitation (myoclonus/twitching and seizures).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which strong opioids are the safest choices in significant renal impairment, and why?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Fentanyl and alfentanil — they have no active metabolites that accumulate. Morphine should be avoided; oxycodone also accumulates and needs caution/dose reduction.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A palliative patient takes 60 mg of oral morphine over 24 hours. What is an appropriate breakthrough (PRN) dose?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: One-sixth (1/6) of the total daily oral morphine = 10 mg immediate-release morphine PRN for breakthrough pain.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: When converting a patient from oral to parenteral (subcutaneous/IV) morphine, roughly what conversion ratio is used?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Oral to parenteral is roughly 2:1 — i.e. the parenteral dose is about half the oral dose (e.g. 60 mg oral over 24 h -> about 30 mg subcutaneous over 24 h in a syringe driver).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which common co-prescribed drug classes cause dangerous additive respiratory depression with opioids?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids (gabapentin/pregabalin — MHRA warning), and alcohol/other CNS depressants — all add to opioid-induced respiratory depression.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How potent is fentanyl relative to morphine, and what class of opioid is it?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Fentanyl is a potent, lipophilic synthetic mu-opioid agonist, roughly 100 times more potent than morphine.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the only appropriate indication for a fentanyl transdermal patch, and who should NOT receive one?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Stable, severe chronic or cancer pain in a patient already on opioids. It is NOT for acute or unstable pain, nor for opioid-naive patients, because of its slow onset and slow offset.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why is a fentanyl patch unsuitable for rapid dose titration or acute pain?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It takes about 12-24 hours to reach effect and just as long to wear off; a depot of drug persists in skin and fat after the patch is removed, so effects are delayed and prolonged.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why is fentanyl a good opioid choice in a patient with renal impairment?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It has no active metabolites that accumulate, so it is safe in renal impairment (unlike morphine).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How does external heat affect a fentanyl patch, and what is the clinical danger?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Heat (fever, hot bath, heat pad) increases absorption of fentanyl from the patch -> risk of overdose and respiratory depression. Warn patients to avoid heat sources over the patch.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What MHRA safety point applies to disposing of used fentanyl patches?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Used patches still contain significant drug. Accidental transfer to another person or child (skin contact) can be fatal, so patches must be folded (sticky sides together) and disposed of safely.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How often is a fentanyl transdermal patch changed?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Every 72 hours (every 3 days).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which drugs raise fentanyl levels and risk respiratory depression?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Certain enzyme-inhibiting drugs (e.g. clarithromycin, azole antifungals, ritonavir, grapefruit) raise fentanyl levels -> toxicity/respiratory depression. Enzyme-inducing drugs reduce its effect.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How does buprenorphine differ mechanistically from morphine, and what safety advantage does this give?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Buprenorphine is a partial mu-opioid agonist (and kappa-antagonist), so it has a ceiling effect on respiratory depression, making it comparatively safer in overdose.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What are the two main clinical uses of buprenorphine?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Chronic pain (transdermal patch or sublingual) and opioid-dependence substitution therapy (sublingual, often combined with naloxone as 'Suboxone' to deter injection/misuse).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why can buprenorphine precipitate withdrawal if given too early to someone dependent on a full agonist?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Its high receptor affinity displaces the full agonist from the mu-receptor but only partially activates it -> abrupt drop in opioid effect. Delay the first dose until the patient shows objective early withdrawal.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why is buprenorphine-induced respiratory depression harder to reverse with naloxone?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Buprenorphine binds the mu-receptor with very high affinity, so naloxone struggles to displace it — higher and/or repeated naloxone doses (or an infusion) may be needed.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Is buprenorphine safe to use in renal impairment?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Yes — buprenorphine is considered safe in renal impairment.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is methadone's mechanism, and what property makes its dosing hazardous?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It is a long-acting full mu-opioid agonist (also an NMDA antagonist). Its long, variable half-life means it accumulates, so overdose risk is highest early in treatment.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What are the two main clinical uses of methadone?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Opioid-dependence substitution therapy (a single daily supervised dose) and some complex/neuropathic or cancer pain.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What cardiac adverse effect must be monitored with methadone, and how?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: QT prolongation, which can cause torsades de pointes. Do a baseline and on-treatment ECG, and avoid combining with other QT-prolonging drugs (e.g. amiodarone, antipsychotics, ondansetron, macrolides, quinolones).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: When during methadone treatment is the risk of fatal accumulation/overdose greatest, and why?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: In the first 1-2 weeks of induction. The long half-life means the drug outlasts its analgesic effect and accumulates -> titrate slowly with supervised consumption.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How do enzyme-inducing and enzyme-inhibiting drugs affect a patient stable on methadone?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Enzyme-inducing drugs (e.g. rifampicin, some antiepileptics) lower methadone levels -> withdrawal. Enzyme-inhibiting drugs raise levels -> toxicity, respiratory depression and torsades risk.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is naloxone and what is its principal indication?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: A competitive mu-opioid receptor antagonist — the antidote for opioid overdose / opioid-induced respiratory depression. Given IV/IM/intranasal, including take-home kits for at-risk users.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: When giving naloxone in overdose, what clinical endpoint should you titrate to and why not aim for full alertness?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Titrate in small increments to restore adequate breathing, not full consciousness — over-reversal can precipitate severe acute opioid withdrawal (agitation, pain, tachycardia, hypertension, pulmonary oedema).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why must a patient be monitored after naloxone reverses an overdose, and when is this especially important?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Naloxone's half-life is shorter than most opioids, so re-sedation (re-narcotisation) can occur as it wears off. Repeat doses or an infusion are needed, especially with long-acting/high-affinity opioids (methadone, buprenorphine, modified-release morphine).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is naltrexone and what is it used for?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: A long-acting oral opioid antagonist used to maintain abstinence — relapse prevention in opioid dependence after detox, and in alcohol dependence to reduce craving/reward. It is NOT an acute overdose antidote.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Before starting naltrexone for relapse prevention, what must be true of the patient?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They must be opioid-free for about 7-10 days (longer after methadone), otherwise naltrexone precipitates acute withdrawal. This is sometimes confirmed with a naloxone challenge.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient on naltrexone needs surgery/acute pain relief. What is the problem and how is it managed?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Naltrexone blocks all opioid analgesia, so standard opioids won't work. Plan ahead — stop it in advance and use non-opioid analgesia or specialist high-dose strategies.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What organ toxicity requires monitoring in patients taking naltrexone?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Dose-related hepatotoxicity — monitor LFTs; avoid in acute hepatitis or liver failure.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Contrast naloxone and naltrexone in role and duration of action.
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Naloxone is a short-acting antagonist for emergency reversal of opioid overdose (restores breathing, but risks re-sedation). Naltrexone is a long-acting oral antagonist for maintaining abstinence in opioid/alcohol dependence — NOT for acute overdose.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the general mechanism and speed of onset of conventional synthetic DMARDs (csDMARDs)?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They are slow-acting disease-modifiers that suppress inflammation and slow joint/tissue damage. Benefit takes weeks to months to appear, so short-term 'bridging' steroids may be used while waiting for effect.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Who initiates csDMARDs and what practical safety requirements do they share?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They are specialist-initiated (usually under shared-care arrangements) and require regular blood monitoring (typically FBC/LFTs/U&Es). Live vaccines are contraindicated in patients taking them.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the anchor (first-line) DMARD for rheumatoid arthritis?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Methotrexate. It slows joint damage and is first-line, often combined with other DMARDs or biologics using a treat-to-target approach. It is also used in psoriatic arthritis, psoriasis and Crohn's disease.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: In simple terms, how does methotrexate work as a DMARD?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It is an antifolate that reduces inflammation and dampens the immune response, slowing disease progression. It is renally excreted, so it accumulates in acute kidney injury.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How is methotrexate dosed in rheumatoid arthritis, and why is the schedule critical?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It is given ONCE WEEKLY (never daily). Accidental daily dosing can be fatal. The weekly rule is a key safety point.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient starting methotrexate asks why they are also given folic acid. What do you tell them, and when is it taken?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Folic acid 5 mg reduces methotrexate side effects such as mouth ulcers, GI upset and marrow toxicity. It must be taken on a DIFFERENT day from the methotrexate dose.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What are the MHRA safety recommendations for prescribing/dispensing methotrexate?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Prescribe and dispense as once-weekly, specifying both the dose AND the specific day. Use only one tablet strength (2.5 mg) to avoid confusion, and issue the patient a booklet/alert card.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient on methotrexate develops a new dry cough and breathlessness. What complication does this suggest and what do you do?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Pneumonitis. Stop the methotrexate and investigate. Patients should be warned to report any cough or breathlessness.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What are the key toxicities of methotrexate to monitor and warn about?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Bone-marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity/liver fibrosis, pneumonitis, mucositis/mouth ulcers (folate-responsive), GI upset, and teratogenicity.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why must methotrexate be stopped before conception, and what advice is given to couples?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It is teratogenic and abortifacient. Stop it around 3-6 months before conception in BOTH partners (men and women), and use reliable contraception until then.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: In a patient with acute methotrexate toxicity or overdose, what is the antidote/rescue treatment?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Folinic acid (leucovorin) rescue. It bypasses the folate-blocking effect of methotrexate to protect the bone marrow and other tissues.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why should trimethoprim or co-trimoxazole be avoided in a patient on methotrexate?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Both are also antifolates, so combining them gives an additive antifolate effect that can cause severe bone-marrow suppression. Avoid this combination.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which common drugs can reduce methotrexate excretion and precipitate toxicity, especially in renal impairment?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: High-dose NSAIDs, penicillins and PPIs reduce renal excretion of methotrexate, raising levels and toxicity risk. This is worse in renal impairment because methotrexate is renally cleared.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What routine blood monitoring is required on methotrexate?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: FBC, LFTs and U&Es every 2 weeks until the dose is stable (and after any dose increase), then every 2-3 months. A baseline chest X-ray is done before starting.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A woman on methotrexate for RA is planning pregnancy. How is her treatment changed?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Stop methotrexate around 3 months before conception (both partners), and switch to a pregnancy-safe DMARD such as sulfasalazine or hydroxychloroquine.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What type of drug is hydroxychloroquine and how does it act as a DMARD?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It is an antimalarial with mild immunomodulatory action, giving a mild disease-modifying effect. It is among the safest DMARDs, with no marrow, liver or pregnancy toxicity.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: In which conditions is hydroxychloroquine a cornerstone of treatment?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Systemic lupus erythematosus (both cutaneous and joint disease) and Sjögren's syndrome, plus mild rheumatoid arthritis. It is often combined with other DMARDs.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which DMARD is safe to continue in pregnancy and is particularly important to continue in lupus?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Hydroxychloroquine. It is safe in pregnancy and is continued in lupus patients.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the key long-term toxicity of hydroxychloroquine and how is it screened for?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Irreversible retinopathy ('bull's-eye' maculopathy) with long-term use. Patients have baseline retinal screening then annual retinal/OCT screening (typically from about 5 years of therapy).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How is hydroxychloroquine dosed to minimise retinopathy risk?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Keep the dose at or below 5 mg/kg/day (actual body weight).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Besides retinopathy, what serious cardiac risk is associated with hydroxychloroquine (MHRA)?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: QT prolongation and cardiomyopathy. Discontinue if cardiotoxicity develops; risk is worse with hypokalaemia or other QT-prolonging drugs.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why is caution needed when giving hydroxychloroquine to a patient with G6PD deficiency?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It can precipitate haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why is safe storage of hydroxychloroquine especially important in households with children?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It is dangerous in overdose - just a few tablets can be fatal to a small child. Advise safe storage out of reach.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How is sulfasalazine handled in the gut, and what does it split into?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Gut bacteria split it into 5-ASA, which stays in the bowel lumen and acts in ulcerative colitis, and sulfapyridine, which is absorbed and drives the rheumatoid arthritis effect and most of the toxicity.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: In which conditions is sulfasalazine used as a DMARD, and is it safe in pregnancy?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis (and ulcerative colitis). It is a well-established DMARD and is safe in pregnancy.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What are the two key contraindications to sulfasalazine?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Sulfonamide (sulfa) allergy and G6PD deficiency (risk of haemolysis).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient on sulfasalazine develops a sore throat, fever and easy bruising. What is the concern and what do you do?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Blood dyscrasia such as agranulocytosis or aplastic anaemia. Get an urgent FBC. Patients should be told to report these symptoms promptly.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What are the important side effects of sulfasalazine to counsel about?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: GI upset, headache and rash; blood dyscrasias; hepatotoxicity; severe skin reactions (DRESS/SJS); folate malabsorption; reversible oligospermia; and harmless orange discolouration of urine and contact lenses.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A man on sulfasalazine is worried about fertility. What do you tell him?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Sulfasalazine can cause reversible oligospermia (reduced sperm count), leading to reversible male infertility. It resolves after stopping the drug.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient reports their urine and soft contact lenses have turned orange on sulfasalazine. Is this harmful?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: No - orange discolouration of urine and contact lenses is a harmless, expected effect. Reassure the patient.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why is folate supplementation advised in a pregnant woman taking sulfasalazine?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Sulfasalazine causes folate malabsorption, so supplementation is needed in pregnancy to prevent deficiency.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What monitoring is needed on sulfasalazine?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: FBC and LFTs, especially in the first few months. Advise the patient to report symptoms of infection (e.g. sore throat/fever).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How does leflunomide work and what is it used for?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It blocks pyrimidine synthesis in proliferating lymphocytes, giving an immunosuppressive DMARD effect. It is used in rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis, as an alternative anchor DMARD when methotrexate is not tolerated.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why does leflunomide's active metabolite matter, and how is it removed if needed?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Its active metabolite teriflunomide has a very long half-life (persisting up to ~2 years via enterohepatic recirculation). A cholestyramine 'washout' is used to remove it rapidly, e.g. before pregnancy or in toxicity.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A woman on leflunomide wants to conceive. What must happen first?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Leflunomide is teratogenic. Because of the long half-life, do a cholestyramine washout and confirm plasma levels are low before conception. This applies to both men and women.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What distinctive cardiovascular side effect is associated with leflunomide?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Hypertension. Blood pressure should be monitored during treatment.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What are the serious toxicities of leflunomide to monitor for?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Hepatotoxicity (which can be fatal), bone-marrow suppression, interstitial lung disease (MHRA - report new/worsening cough or dyspnoea), plus diarrhoea, weight loss and peripheral neuropathy.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why does INR need checking when leflunomide is started in a patient on warfarin?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Leflunomide potentiates warfarin, raising the INR and bleeding risk. Monitor INR closely.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What monitoring is required for a patient on leflunomide?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Blood pressure, FBC and LFTs (frequently early on, e.g. every 2 weeks for the first 6 months, then periodically). Avoid other hepatotoxic drugs and alcohol. Live vaccines are contraindicated.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Before starting ANY biologic DMARD, what infection screen must be done?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Screen for latent TB, hepatitis B and C, HIV, and check VZV (chickenpox) immunity. Treat any active infection first. If latent TB is positive, start TB chemoprophylaxis before the first dose.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why are live vaccines contraindicated during biologic therapy, and what should be done about them?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Biologics are immunosuppressive, so a live vaccine risks disseminated infection. Give any needed live vaccines beforehand, before starting the biologic.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Can two biologics, or a biologic plus a JAK inhibitor, be combined?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: No. Combining them gives additive immunosuppression and serious infection risk with no added benefit. Only one targeted agent at a time.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: When are biologic DMARDs added in rheumatoid arthritis, and why is methotrexate often co-prescribed?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They are generally added after conventional DMARDs (e.g. methotrexate) have failed. Combining the biologic with methotrexate reduces formation of anti-drug antibodies, keeping the biologic effective.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the mechanism of anti-TNF agents (etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab, certolizumab, golimumab)?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They neutralise TNF-alpha, a central pro-inflammatory cytokine -> potent control of inflammatory arthritis and other immune-mediated disease.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which anti-TNF agent does NOT work in inflammatory bowel disease, and why?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Etanercept. It is a soluble TNF-receptor-Fc fusion protein, not a monoclonal antibody, and does not work in IBD. The monoclonals (adalimumab, infliximab, certolizumab, golimumab) do treat IBD.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: In which conditions are anti-TNF agents used?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Rheumatoid, psoriatic and axial spondyloarthritis, psoriasis, and IBD (monoclonals only). NICE recommends them for severe active RA (DAS28 >5.1) after at least 2 csDMARDs including methotrexate.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis and moderate-severe heart failure needs escalation. Why avoid an anti-TNF?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Anti-TNF agents worsen heart failure and are contraindicated/avoided in moderate-severe heart failure. Demyelinating disease is another key contraindication.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What are the key infection-related safety risks of anti-TNF therapy?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Reactivation of latent TB and of hepatitis B (screen and give prophylaxis first), plus serious and opportunistic infections. Also increased lymphoma and skin cancer risk (annual skin checks) and drug-induced lupus.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which anti-TNF is preferred in pregnancy and why?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Certolizumab. It is a PEGylated Fab with no Fc region, so placental transfer is minimal, making it the anti-TNF of choice in pregnancy.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A baby was exposed to adalimumab in later pregnancy. What vaccine advice applies?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Infants exposed to anti-TNF antibodies (other than certolizumab) late in pregnancy should avoid live vaccines for about 6 months, because the drug persists in the infant.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Give the typical routes and frequencies of etanercept, adalimumab and infliximab.
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Etanercept: subcutaneous weekly. Adalimumab: subcutaneous fortnightly. Infliximab: IV every 8 weeks. Infliximab is chimeric and more immunogenic, so give it with methotrexate.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why is infliximab in particular given together with methotrexate?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Infliximab is a chimeric antibody and more immunogenic, so it more readily provokes anti-drug antibodies. Co-prescribing methotrexate reduces these and preserves efficacy.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What extra cancer-surveillance advice do patients on anti-TNF therapy need?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: There is an increased skin cancer risk, so annual skin checks are advised. There is also an increased lymphoma risk.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the mechanism of abatacept?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Abatacept is a CTLA-4 fusion protein that blocks the co-stimulatory signal T cells need for activation -> it dampens the immune response upstream of cytokine production, a different mechanism from cytokine blockers.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Where does abatacept sit in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It is used for severe RA (DAS28 >5.1 after at least 2 csDMARDs) as a first-line biologic option, alongside anti-TNF and anti-IL-6R agents, ideally co-prescribed with methotrexate.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which comorbidity warrants particular caution with abatacept?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: COPD, because of an increased risk of respiratory infections. Standard biologic infection screening still applies (screen for TB and hepatitis).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Can abatacept be combined with an anti-TNF agent?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: No. Abatacept plus anti-TNF must be avoided because it increases serious infection risk with no added benefit.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the mechanism of rituximab?
