pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Rituximab is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody that depletes CD20-positive B cells, reducing autoantibody-driven inflammation. CD20 is absent on plasma cells and stem cells.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Where does rituximab sit in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It is used with methotrexate as second-line therapy, after anti-TNF failure.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: In which non-RA rheumatological conditions is rituximab used?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: ANCA-associated vasculitis (first-line) and SLE/lupus nephritis. In haematology it is also used for lymphoma, CLL and ITP.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How are rituximab infusion reactions prevented?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Premedicate with a steroid, an antihistamine and paracetamol before the infusion. Rituximab is given as two IV infusions two weeks apart, repeated roughly every 6-12 months by relapse.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why should vaccines be given BEFORE starting rituximab?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: B-cell depletion blunts the response to vaccines, so required (and live) vaccines should be given before starting. Existing IgG is initially preserved because plasma cells lack CD20.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What serious but rare neurological complication is associated with rituximab?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). Other important adverse effects are hepatitis B reactivation (screen first) and hypogammaglobulinaemia/late neutropenia over repeated courses.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the mechanism of tocilizumab and sarilumab?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They are anti-IL-6-receptor monoclonal antibodies that block interleukin-6, giving a strong anti-inflammatory effect.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why can anti-IL-6R agents be used as monotherapy in rheumatoid arthritis?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Tocilizumab and sarilumab are effective as monotherapy when methotrexate is not tolerated, unlike some other biologics which rely on co-prescribed methotrexate.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Besides RA, what are the key uses of tocilizumab?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Giant cell arteritis (steroid-sparing) and cytokine release syndrome (e.g. after CAR-T therapy or in severe COVID). It is also used in juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why can infection be dangerously masked in a patient on tocilizumab or sarilumab?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: IL-6 drives the acute-phase response, so blocking it suppresses CRP and fever. CRP and fever become unreliable markers, so a serious infection may not show the usual signs.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient on tocilizumab with diverticular disease develops abdominal pain. What serious complication must be considered?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: GI perforation, which is a recognised risk especially with diverticular disease. Suspicion should be high because CRP and fever are suppressed and may be misleadingly normal.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What laboratory monitoring is needed on anti-IL-6R therapy?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Monitor FBC (neutropenia/thrombocytopenia), LFTs (raised transaminases) and lipids (raised). Remember CRP is unreliable for detecting infection.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient on warfarin is started on tocilizumab. Why must the INR be watched?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Blocking IL-6 restores normal drug metabolism, lowering levels of warfarin, statins, ciclosporin and the oral contraceptive. Warfarin levels fall so the INR drops -> monitor INR and adjust dose on starting and stopping.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the mechanism of anakinra and canakinumab?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They block IL-1-driven inflammation. Anakinra is a recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist; canakinumab is an anti-IL-1-beta antibody.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: In which conditions are IL-1 blockers (anakinra, canakinumab) used?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Autoinflammatory/IL-1-driven conditions: adult-onset Still's disease, refractory gout flares and periodic fever syndromes. They are NOT standard in rheumatoid arthritis (poor efficacy).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How is anakinra administered, and what is its characteristic side effect?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Anakinra is given by subcutaneous injection daily (short half-life). It commonly causes injection-site reactions. Other effects are infections and neutropenia.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How does canakinumab dosing differ from anakinra?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Canakinumab is given subcutaneously every 8 weeks (anti-IL-1-beta antibody), whereas anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist) must be given subcutaneously every day because of its short half-life.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Can anakinra be combined with an anti-TNF agent?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: No. Anakinra plus anti-TNF must be avoided because it increases serious infection and neutropenia risk. As with all biologics, do not combine with another biologic or a JAK inhibitor.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What monitoring is specifically needed with IL-1 blockers?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Monitor FBC for neutropenia, in addition to the standard pre-biologic screen (latent TB, hepatitis B/C, HIV, VZV immunity) and avoiding active infection and live vaccines.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How do secukinumab and ixekizumab work, and how does bimekizumab differ?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: All are monoclonal antibodies that block the IL-17 axis. Secukinumab and ixekizumab block IL-17A alone; bimekizumab blocks both IL-17A and IL-17F. This axis is central to psoriatic disease and spondyloarthritis.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: For which conditions are IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab, bimekizumab) used?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis and axial spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis). They are highly effective for both skin and axial disease. Typically used in AS after >=2 NSAIDs fail, and in psoriatic arthritis after conventional synthetic DMARDs.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient on secukinumab for psoriasis develops white plaques in the mouth and soreness. What is the likely cause and why?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Mucocutaneous candidiasis. IL-17 is needed for antifungal defence, so blocking it predisposes to oral/skin/genital candida. It is a signature side effect of the whole IL-17 inhibitor class.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which IL-17 inhibitor carries the highest rate of candidiasis, and why?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Bimekizumab, because it blocks both IL-17A and IL-17F, giving broader suppression of the antifungal IL-17 axis than the IL-17A-only agents.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why should IL-17 inhibitors be avoided in a patient with coexisting inflammatory bowel disease?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: IL-17 inhibitors can trigger or worsen IBD (new-onset or flare of Crohn's/ulcerative colitis). Avoid them if IBD coexists; watch for new bowel symptoms in anyone started on them.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How are secukinumab and ixekizumab administered?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Subcutaneous injection, given as a loading regimen (initial doses) followed by regular maintenance dosing.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient with axial spondyloarthritis and psoriasis develops new bloody diarrhoea after starting secukinumab. What should you consider?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: New-onset or worsening inflammatory bowel disease triggered by the IL-17 inhibitor. Investigate for IBD and stop/reassess the biologic; an IL-17 inhibitor is the wrong choice if IBD is present.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How do IL-23 inhibitors (guselkumab, risankizumab) work?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They are monoclonal antibodies against IL-23 (the p19 subunit). IL-23 sits upstream of the IL-17 pathway, so blocking it dampens downstream IL-17-driven inflammation in psoriatic disease.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What are guselkumab and risankizumab used for?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis. They are very well tolerated and given infrequently (roughly every 8-12 weeks subcutaneously).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How does the dosing frequency of IL-23 inhibitors compare to many other biologics?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Infrequent - guselkumab and risankizumab are given subcutaneously only every 8-12 weeks once maintenance is reached, which improves convenience and adherence.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Are IL-23 inhibitors effective in axial spondyloarthritis/ankylosing spondylitis?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: No. Unlike IL-17 inhibitors, IL-23 inhibitors are NOT effective in axial spondyloarthritis/AS, so they are not used for axial disease.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Do IL-23 inhibitors carry the same IBD risk as IL-17 inhibitors?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: No. IL-23 inhibitors have no clear IBD-worsening signal, whereas IL-17 inhibitors can trigger/worsen IBD. This makes IL-23 inhibitors a safer choice when bowel disease is a concern.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What are the main side effects of IL-23 inhibitors?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Generally very well tolerated - nasopharyngitis, injection-site reactions and infections. No clear IBD-worsening signal (in contrast to IL-17 inhibitors).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Contrast IL-17 and IL-23 inhibitors on axial disease efficacy and IBD.
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: IL-17 inhibitors work for axial spondyloarthritis/AS but can trigger/worsen IBD (avoid in coexisting IBD). IL-23 inhibitors are NOT effective in axial SpA but have no IBD-worsening signal. So: axial disease -> favour IL-17; coexisting IBD -> favour IL-23.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How does belimumab work?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It is a monoclonal antibody against BAFF/BLyS (B-cell activating factor), reducing B-cell survival and autoantibody production. This targets the abnormal B-cell activity that drives systemic lupus.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is belimumab used for, and what is the key rule about how it is given?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Systemic lupus erythematosus - as an add-on for active, autoantibody-positive disease with high activity despite standard therapy. It is restricted, specialist-initiated and NEVER used as monotherapy (always added to standard treatment).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How is belimumab administered?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Intravenously monthly, or subcutaneously weekly.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which psychiatric side effect is a recognised (MHRA) safety signal with belimumab, and how do you act on it?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Depression and psychiatric effects, including suicidality. Perform a mental-health review and monitor mood; counsel the patient to report low mood or suicidal thoughts.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What are the main side effects of belimumab?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Infections, infusion/injection reactions, nausea, and a noted depression/psychiatric signal. Active severe infection is a reason to withhold it.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How does anifrolumab work?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It is a monoclonal antibody against the type-I interferon receptor (IFNAR1), blocking type-I interferon signalling. This 'interferon signature' is a key driver of lupus, so blocking it reduces disease activity.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is anifrolumab used for?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Moderate-to-severe systemic lupus erythematosus, as an add-on for active autoantibody-positive disease despite standard therapy. It is specialist-initiated and is NOT interchangeable with belimumab.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How is anifrolumab given?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Intravenous infusion every 4 weeks.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient on anifrolumab develops a painful vesicular rash in a dermatomal band. What is the likely diagnosis and why is this drug relevant?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Herpes zoster (shingles) reactivation. Type-I interferon is antiviral, so blocking IFNAR1 predisposes to viral reactivation. Herpes zoster and respiratory infections are the signature risks of anifrolumab.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What should be checked or done regarding VZV before starting anifrolumab?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Check VZV immunity and vaccinate against varicella-zoster before starting, because anifrolumab increases the risk of herpes zoster (shingles) reactivation. Note live vaccines cannot be given once immunosuppressed.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What are the characteristic infective risks of anifrolumab?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Respiratory infections and herpes zoster (shingles) reactivation, reflecting loss of the antiviral effect of type-I interferon. Infusion reactions also occur.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Contrast belimumab and anifrolumab as biologics for SLE.
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Both are specialist-initiated add-ons for active SLE despite standard therapy and are not interchangeable. Belimumab targets BAFF/BLyS (reducing autoantibody-producing B cells) and carries a depression/psychiatric signal -> mental-health review. Anifrolumab targets the type-I interferon receptor (IFNAR1) and carries a herpes zoster/respiratory infection risk -> check/vaccinate VZV first.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Beyond the standard biologic pre-screening (TB, hepatitis B/C, HIV, VZV, immunisations), why must you avoid combining these biologics with other biologics or JAK inhibitors?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Combining them causes additive immunosuppression and a higher risk of serious infection. Live vaccines are also contraindicated during treatment.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What class of drug is tofacitinib, and how does it work at a molecular level?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: An oral, small-molecule 'targeted synthetic' DMARD (tsDMARD) and a Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor. It blocks JAK enzymes so they can no longer activate the JAK-STAT intracellular signalling pathway used by many inflammatory cytokines -> broad immunosuppression.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How does the route of administration of JAK inhibitors differ from that of biologic DMARDs, and why is this an advantage?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: JAK inhibitors are taken orally (e.g. tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib, filgotinib), whereas biologics are injected antibodies given subcutaneously or IV. An oral tablet is more convenient for patients who prefer to avoid injections.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Baricitinib, upadacitinib and filgotinib all inhibit Janus kinases, but their selectivity differs. Which are JAK1-selective, and what is the clinical benefit of sparing JAK2?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Upadacitinib and filgotinib are JAK1-selective. JAK2 is involved in red-cell and platelet production, so sparing JAK2 tends to cause less anaemia. (Tofacitinib is pan-JAK; baricitinib is JAK1/2; ruxolitinib is JAK1/2 and is used for myelofibrosis.)

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis has had an inadequate response to methotrexate and other conventional DMARDs. Where do oral JAK inhibitors sit in the treatment pathway?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They are positioned after inadequate response to conventional synthetic DMARDs. They serve as an oral alternative to injected biologics, and can also be used as an option after a biologic has failed.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Besides rheumatoid arthritis, name conditions for which JAK inhibitors are used.
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Psoriatic arthritis and axial spondyloarthritis; ulcerative colitis (tofacitinib/upadacitinib); atopic dermatitis and alopecia (baricitinib); and myelofibrosis/polycythaemia (ruxolitinib).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: The MHRA has issued a major class safety warning for JAK inhibitors. What are the key serious risks it highlights?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Increased risks of serious infections and TB reactivation, herpes zoster (shingles) reactivation, venous thromboembolism (DVT/PE), major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), malignancy, and increased all-cause mortality.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Because of the MHRA class warning, JAK inhibitors should only be used 'when there is no suitable alternative' in certain higher-risk patients. Which patient groups trigger this caution?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Patients aged 65 years or over, current or past smokers, and those with cardiovascular, cancer or venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk factors. In these groups a JAK inhibitor should only be used if no other suitable treatment is available.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which viral reactivation is characteristically associated with JAK inhibitors, and how might it present?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Herpes zoster (shingles) reactivation is characteristic. It presents as a painful, dermatomal vesicular rash. This risk is why patients should ideally be vaccinated against zoster before starting.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient on a JAK inhibitor develops a swollen, painful calf and breathlessness. Which class-associated adverse effect must you urgently consider?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Venous thromboembolism (DVT/PE) - JAK inhibitors carry an increased risk of VTE. The calf swelling suggests a DVT and the breathlessness raises concern for a pulmonary embolism; assess and investigate urgently.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What did the ORAL Surveillance trial reveal about JAK inhibitors compared with anti-TNF biologics, and why does it matter?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It showed increased major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), malignancy and all-cause mortality with a JAK inhibitor versus anti-TNF therapy. This underpins the MHRA restriction to use only when no suitable alternative exists in higher-risk patients.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why do patients starting a JAK inhibitor need screening for latent infections before treatment?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: JAK inhibitors cause broad immunosuppression and increase the risk of serious infections and reactivation. Before starting, screen for TB, hepatitis B/C and varicella-zoster (VZV) status.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which zoster vaccine should be given before starting a JAK inhibitor, and which is contraindicated?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Give the non-live recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) before starting. The live zoster vaccine is contraindicated because the immunosuppression makes live vaccines unsafe.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What metabolic blood-test abnormalities can JAK inhibitors cause, and when should lipids be checked?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They can raise lipids (cholesterol) and liver function tests (LFTs). Check lipids at around 8-12 weeks after starting, and monitor LFTs on an ongoing basis.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why can JAK inhibitors cause anaemia and other cytopenias, and how is this monitored?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Inhibiting JAK2 reduces red-cell and platelet production, causing anaemia and cytopenias (JAK1-selective drugs cause less). Monitor the full blood count (FBC) on an ongoing basis.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why should JAK inhibitors be used cautiously in a patient with a history of diverticulitis?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: JAK inhibitors carry a risk of gastrointestinal perforation. A history of diverticulitis increases that risk, so they should be used with caution in these patients.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the advice regarding JAK inhibitors in pregnancy?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Avoid in pregnancy. Women of childbearing potential should use effective contraception during treatment and for a period after stopping.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How does renal or hepatic impairment affect JAK inhibitor prescribing?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Dose reduction or avoidance is needed in renal and/or hepatic impairment across the class. Baricitinib in particular is renally cleared (so accumulates in renal impairment); tofacitinib requires caution in both renal and hepatic impairment.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Conceptually, how can other medicines alter the levels of some JAK inhibitors?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Certain enzyme-inhibiting or enzyme-inducing drugs can raise or lower the levels of some JAK inhibitors, requiring dose adjustment. Because baricitinib is renally cleared, drugs affecting its renal elimination can raise its levels.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Can a JAK inhibitor be combined with a biologic DMARD for extra disease control?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: No. JAK inhibitors should not be combined with biologics or other potent immunosuppressants, as this excessively increases the risk of serious infection and other harm.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient starting a JAK inhibitor asks what ongoing blood tests they will need. What do you tell them?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Ongoing monitoring of full blood count (FBC) and liver function tests (LFTs), with lipids checked at around 8-12 weeks. Cardiovascular and VTE risk should also be reassessed.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the typical oral dosing of tofacitinib and baricitinib for rheumatoid arthritis?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Tofacitinib is usually 5 mg twice daily; baricitinib is usually 4 mg once daily. Upadacitinib and filgotinib are also taken once daily.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How do JAK inhibitors and biologic DMARDs compare in terms of type, use and safety?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: JAK inhibitors are oral small-molecule tsDMARDs; biologics are injected antibodies. Both are used after conventional DMARD failure, but JAK inhibitors carry the specific MHRA class warning of increased MACE, VTE, malignancy and all-cause mortality that leads to restrictions in higher-risk patients.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A JAK inhibitor patient's blood tests show a raised creatine kinase (CK). Is this a recognised effect?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Yes - JAK inhibitors can cause a raised CK. It is a recognised class effect and should be interpreted alongside the wider monitoring picture.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why is ruxolitinib grouped with the JAK inhibitors despite a different clinical use?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It is a JAK1/2 inhibitor working through the same JAK-STAT signalling pathway, but it is used for myelofibrosis and polycythaemia rather than for inflammatory arthritis.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient presents with an acute gout flare. What are the first-line treatment options?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: An NSAID, OR colchicine, OR a short course of oral (or intra-articular) corticosteroid. These are co-equal first-line - choose based on comorbidity (e.g. avoid NSAIDs in renal/cardiac disease, favour colchicine or steroid instead).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why should you NOT start allopurinol or febuxostat during an acute gout flare?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They are urate-lowering (preventive) therapies, not treatments for the acute attack - starting them during a flare can worsen/prolong it. They are introduced only after the flare settles.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient already established on allopurinol develops an acute gout flare. Do you stop the allopurinol?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: No. Continue the urate-lowering therapy through the flare and treat the acute attack separately (NSAID/colchicine/steroid). Only avoid STARTING it during a flare - never stop it if already established.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: An acute gout flare fails to respond to NSAIDs, colchicine and corticosteroids. What is the next option?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: IL-1 blockade - canakinumab or anakinra.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How does colchicine work in acute gout?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It binds tubulin and inhibits microtubule formation -> impairs neutrophil migration/activation and the NLRP3 inflammasome (reducing IL-1beta) -> dampens the inflammatory response to urate crystals. It does NOT lower urate.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Does colchicine lower serum urate?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: No. Colchicine is purely anti-inflammatory - it treats/prevents the flare but has no effect on urate levels. Urate lowering requires a separate agent (e.g. allopurinol).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: When is colchicine particularly useful for an acute gout flare?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: When NSAIDs are contraindicated - e.g. in renal or cardiac disease. It is also used as flare prophylaxis when starting urate-lowering therapy.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Besides acute gout, what are two other uses of colchicine?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Pericarditis and familial Mediterranean fever (FMF).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the dose-limiting side effect of colchicine, and what should the patient do if it occurs?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Diarrhoea/GI upset. It is the early signal of toxicity - the patient should stop the colchicine when it occurs (or when the flare settles).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Colchicine has a narrow therapeutic index. What happens in overdose/toxicity, and is there an antidote?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Toxicity causes bone-marrow suppression, neuropathy/myopathy and multi-organ failure, and can be fatal (often after delayed GI symptoms). There is NO antidote.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why is co-prescribing colchicine with clarithromycin, erythromycin, an azole antifungal, ciclosporin, verapamil or diltiazem dangerous?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: These enzyme/transporter-inhibiting drugs raise colchicine to toxic (potentially fatal) levels -> avoid or dose-reduce colchicine.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the risk of combining colchicine with a statin?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Increased risk of myopathy/rhabdomyolysis (worse if an enzyme-inhibiting drug is also present) -> monitor for muscle symptoms and CK.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why must colchicine be used cautiously in renal or hepatic impairment?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It accumulates -> toxicity. Significant renal or hepatic impairment is a caution/contraindication and warrants dose reduction.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How does allopurinol lower serum urate?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It inhibits xanthine oxidase, blocking conversion of purines to uric acid -> lowers serum urate -> prevents crystal formation over time. This is preventive (urate-lowering) therapy, not a treatment for the acute attack.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: According to NICE, when should urate-lowering therapy (e.g. allopurinol) be offered/discussed?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: After a first confirmed gout flare (not only recurrent disease), and especially in the presence of tophi, urate stones, CKD, or in patients on diuretics.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the treat-to-target serum urate for gout, and when is a lower target used?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Target urate <360 micromol/L; aim for <300 micromol/L if there are tophi, chronic arthropathy or severe disease.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How is allopurinol started and titrated?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Start low (100 mg once daily) and up-titrate to reach the target urate. Reduce the starting dose in renal impairment.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: When should allopurinol be started relative to a gout flare, and how do you cover initiation?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Start 2-4 weeks after the flare settles, and cover initiation with flare prophylaxis (low-dose colchicine, or low-dose NSAID/steroid) for up to 6 months, because starting it can precipitate a flare.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why does starting allopurinol sometimes trigger a gout flare?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: The fall in serum urate mobilises existing crystal deposits, which can precipitate an acute flare - hence prophylactic cover during initiation.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What severe skin reactions can allopurinol cause, and who is at higher risk?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: DRESS, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). Higher risk with the HLA-B*5801 allele, in renal impairment, and with concurrent ACE inhibitors or diuretics. Report any rash and stop the drug.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which patients should be screened for HLA-B*5801 before allopurinol, and why?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Those of Han Chinese, Korean or Thai background - HLA-B*5801 markedly increases the risk of severe cutaneous reactions (DRESS/SJS/TEN).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why is combining allopurinol with azathioprine or mercaptopurine dangerous?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Allopurinol blocks xanthine oxidase, the enzyme that breaks down these thiopurines -> massive rise in active drug -> life-threatening myelosuppression. Avoid the combination or drastically reduce the thiopurine dose.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which common cardiovascular/renal drugs increase the risk of allopurinol hypersensitivity?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: ACE inhibitors and thiazide/loop diuretics, especially in renal impairment.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What monitoring is required for a patient on allopurinol?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Serum urate (titrate to target) and renal function; advise the patient to report any rash and stop the drug if it develops.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How does febuxostat work, and how does its clearance differ from allopurinol?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It is a non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor that lowers serum urate. It is predominantly hepatically metabolised (unlike renally-cleared allopurinol), so it can be used without dose adjustment in mild-moderate renal impairment.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Where does febuxostat sit in the management of gout?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It is a first-line urate-lowering option alongside allopurinol for long-term gout prevention; hepatic clearance makes it useful in renal impairment. Choice is individualised, avoiding it in cardiovascular disease.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What important cardiovascular caution applies to febuxostat?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: There is a cardiovascular-mortality signal -> avoid/use with caution in established cardiovascular disease (e.g. ischaemic heart disease).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient had a severe hypersensitivity reaction to allopurinol. Can febuxostat be used instead?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: No - do not use febuxostat if there was prior allopurinol hypersensitivity (risk of severe cutaneous reactions such as SJS/DRESS). Do not rechallenge.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Does febuxostat share allopurinol's dangerous interaction with thiopurines?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Yes. Like allopurinol, febuxostat inhibits xanthine oxidase -> azathioprine/mercaptopurine accumulate -> life-threatening myelosuppression. The combination is avoided/contraindicated.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What monitoring/initiation measures apply to febuxostat?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Monitor serum urate, LFTs and cardiovascular risk; cover initiation with colchicine or an NSAID (it can precipitate a flare when started).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How do uricosuric agents (probenecid, benzbromarone, lesinurad) lower urate?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They increase renal excretion of uric acid by blocking its tubular reabsorption -> lower serum urate. Used in under-excreters, or as add-on to a xanthine oxidase inhibitor to reach target.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the key risk of uricosuric therapy, and how is it minimised?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Urate renal stones (increased urinary uric acid). Minimise by maintaining good hydration, with or without urinary alkalinisation.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: In which patients should uricosurics be avoided?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Those with a history of urate/renal stones, marked urate overproduction, or significant renal impairment (they are ineffective and unsafe in significant impairment).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What serious adverse effect is associated specifically with benzbromarone?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Serious hepatotoxicity - the reason it is restricted/named-patient only.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the key safety issue with lesinurad, and how must it be prescribed?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It can cause acute kidney injury (boxed warning) -> it must never be used as monotherapy, only combined with a xanthine oxidase inhibitor. It has since been withdrawn in the UK/EU.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which drug levels does probenecid raise, and why?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It blocks renal tubular secretion of other drugs -> raises methotrexate (risk of toxicity) and penicillins/beta-lactams.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why can low-dose aspirin undermine uricosuric therapy?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Low-dose aspirin/salicylates are urate-retaining and blunt the uricosuric effect.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How do uricase agents (rasburicase, pegloticase) lower urate?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They are recombinant uricase (urate oxidase) - an enzyme humans lack - which converts uric acid to soluble allantoin, producing rapid and dramatic urate lowering.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is rasburicase used for?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Prevention and treatment of tumour lysis syndrome - rapid urate lowering in high-risk chemotherapy, given with hydration.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is pegloticase used for and how is it given?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Severe refractory chronic tophaceous gout; given IV every 2 weeks.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why are uricase agents contraindicated in G6PD deficiency?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: The reaction generates hydrogen peroxide as a byproduct, which causes severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia in G6PD-deficient patients. Screen for G6PD deficiency before use.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Besides haemolysis in G6PD deficiency, what other serious reaction can uricase agents cause?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Anaphylaxis/hypersensitivity (infusion reactions).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A blood sample for urate is left at room temperature before analysis. How does this affect the result in a patient on uricase therapy?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It gives a falsely LOW urate - the enzyme keeps converting urate to allantoin in the tube. Samples should be kept/sent on ice.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why is serum urate checked before each pegloticase infusion, and what does a rising pre-infusion urate mean?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: A rising pre-infusion urate signals anti-drug antibody formation (loss of response) and predicts anaphylaxis -> stop pegloticase. Concurrent oral urate-lowering therapy is stopped because it would mask this warning sign.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How do bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate, zoledronate, ibandronate) work?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They bind to bone and are taken up by osteoclasts, causing osteoclast death -> reduced bone resorption. They are antiresorptive drugs that increase bone density and cut fracture risk.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which drug class is first-line for osteoporosis?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Bisphosphonates (antiresorptive). Oral alendronate or risedronate are first-line; IV zoledronate or denosumab are used if oral bisphosphonates are not tolerated.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How is the decision to start bone protection in osteoporosis made?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: By assessed fracture risk using a tool such as FRAX or QFracture, and/or a DXA T-score <= -2.5. Treatment is guided by risk, not age alone.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: When should bone protection be started in glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Early - start bone protection at the initiation of steroids in high-risk patients, rather than waiting. Long-term steroids markedly raise fracture risk.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Besides osteoporosis, name other conditions treated with bisphosphonates.
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Paget's disease of bone, hypercalcaemia of malignancy, and bone metastases/multiple myeloma.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How should an oral bisphosphonate (e.g. alendronate) be taken, and why?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: On an empty stomach with plenty of water, sitting upright for 30 minutes, before any food. Absorption is only ~1% and this reduces the risk of oesophagitis.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient takes alendronate with their morning milky coffee and calcium tablet. What is the problem?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Calcium, antacids, iron, milk, coffee and food abolish the drug's ~1% absorption. The bisphosphonate must be taken well before (about 30 min) any food or other medication.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What must be checked and corrected before starting a bisphosphonate?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Correct any hypocalcaemia and ensure the patient is calcium and vitamin D replete first. Also check renal function, as bisphosphonates are avoided in significant renal impairment (drug-specific, e.g. avoid if eGFR < 35).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why are bisphosphonates avoided in significant renal impairment?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They are renally handled and contraindicated below a drug-specific eGFR threshold (e.g. eGFR < 35 for alendronate/zoledronate). In renal impairment, denosumab may be preferred as it is not renally cleared.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What GI side effect are oral bisphosphonates known for, and how is it minimised?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Oesophagitis/GI upset. Minimised by taking the tablet upright with plenty of water and remaining upright for 30 minutes; avoid in oesophageal disease or if the patient cannot sit upright.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is osteonecrosis of the jaw, and how do you reduce the risk before starting a bisphosphonate?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Death of jaw bone, presenting with exposed non-healing bone/pain after dental work. Arrange a dental check and complete invasive dental work before starting, especially with IV or cancer-dose bisphosphonates.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient on long-term alendronate develops new thigh, hip or groin pain. What complication must you consider and how do you investigate?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Atypical femoral fracture. Review the drug and image BOTH femurs - these fractures are often bilateral. Consider stopping the bisphosphonate / a drug holiday.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: An MHRA warning links bisphosphonates and denosumab to osteonecrosis of which other site, and how does it present?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Osteonecrosis of the external auditory canal - presenting with ear pain or ear discharge. Consider it in patients on these drugs with persistent ear symptoms.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What acute reaction can follow the first dose of IV zoledronate?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: An acute-phase flu-like reaction (fever, myalgia, malaise), usually transient. It is most common after the first infusion.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why do bisphosphonates allow a 'drug holiday', and when is reassessment made?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They have a very long skeletal half-life and are retained in bone for years. Reassess after 5 years of oral treatment or 3 years of IV zoledronate; high-risk patients (e.g. prior hip/vertebral fracture, ongoing steroids, T-score <= -2.5 on treatment) continue rather than pause.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How does denosumab work?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It is a monoclonal anti-RANKL antibody. Blocking RANKL prevents osteoclast formation and activity -> potent antiresorptive effect.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How is denosumab given and how often?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: 60 mg by subcutaneous injection every 6 months. It must be given strictly on time.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why is denosumab useful in a patient with chronic kidney disease?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It is not renally cleared, so it can be used in CKD. It is a second-line option, or used when bisphosphonates are unsuitable (e.g. renal impairment).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What must you correct before starting denosumab, and why the extra caution in CKD?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Correct hypocalcaemia and ensure calcium/vitamin D replete first - denosumab can cause severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia, which is worse in renal impairment. Monitor calcium, especially in the first weeks.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the single most important danger of stopping or delaying denosumab?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Rapid rebound bone loss with multiple vertebral fractures. It must be given strictly on time every 6 months and never stopped without switching to a bisphosphonate.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Does denosumab share the jaw and femoral complications of bisphosphonates?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Yes - like bisphosphonates it can cause osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fractures (and osteonecrosis of the external auditory canal).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How do teriparatide and abaloparatide work, and why is the injection timing important?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They are recombinant PTH/PTHrP analogues given as an intermittent DAILY subcutaneous injection, which paradoxically builds new bone (anabolic, via osteoblasts). Continuous PTH would instead drive bone resorption - the intermittent dosing gives the anabolic effect.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which patients are teriparatide/abaloparatide reserved for?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Very-high-risk osteoporosis - e.g. a very low T-score or multiple vertebral fractures. They are an anabolic option, usually used after or instead of antiresorptives.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the maximum duration of teriparatide, and what is done afterwards?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: A maximum of 24 months lifetime. It is then followed with an antiresorptive (bisphosphonate) to maintain the bone gains.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What are the typical side effects of teriparatide?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Transient hypercalcaemia, nausea, dizziness/postural hypotension, and limb pain (also headache). Monitor serum/urinary calcium.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: In which conditions is teriparatide contraindicated?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Pre-existing hypercalcaemia, Paget's disease, unexplained raised ALP, prior bone radiotherapy, and bone malignancy/metastases.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why is teriparatide's hypercalcaemia relevant in a patient on digoxin?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Hypercalcaemia potentiates digoxin toxicity - use with caution and monitor calcium.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How does romosozumab work?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It is a monoclonal anti-sclerostin antibody with a dual effect: it increases bone formation AND decreases resorption -> strongly builds bone.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How is romosozumab given, and what follows the course?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: A fixed 12-month course of monthly subcutaneous injections, then followed by an antiresorptive (bisphosphonate or denosumab) to maintain the gains.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which patients is romosozumab used for?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Severe postmenopausal osteoporosis with a prior major fragility fracture (very high imminent fracture risk), specialist-initiated.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the key restriction on prescribing romosozumab?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: A cardiovascular event signal - do NOT use in anyone with a history of MI or stroke.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What else must be managed with romosozumab besides cardiovascular risk?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Correct hypocalcaemia and ensure calcium/vitamin D replete before and during treatment (monitor calcium). It can also rarely cause osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical fractures.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Contrast antiresorptive and anabolic osteoporosis drugs - which drugs fall into each group?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Antiresorptive drugs block osteoclasts to reduce bone breakdown: bisphosphonates and denosumab. Anabolic drugs build new bone: teriparatide/abaloparatide (PTH/PTHrP analogues) and romosozumab (anti-sclerostin, dual action). Anabolic agents are reserved for the highest-risk patients and are followed by an antiresorptive.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What class effects are shared by bisphosphonates, denosumab and (rarely) romosozumab?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Osteonecrosis of the jaw (arrange dental check first) and atypical femoral fractures (thigh/hip/groin pain -> image both femurs). All require hypocalcaemia to be corrected and calcium/vitamin D to be replete before starting.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A patient with osteoporosis and severe CKD cannot tolerate oral bisphosphonates. What is a suitable alternative and its key caveat?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Denosumab (anti-RANKL, 6-monthly SC) - it is not renally cleared so is usable in CKD. Caveat: high risk of severe hypocalcaemia in CKD (correct calcium first, monitor closely), and it must never be stopped without switching to a bisphosphonate to avoid rebound vertebral fractures.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How do oestrogen (HRT) and raloxifene protect bone?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Both act on bone oestrogen receptors -> reduce bone resorption (antiresorptive). They suppress RANKL and raise OPG, reducing osteoclast activity.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What type of drug is raloxifene?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: A SERM (selective oestrogen receptor modulator). It acts as an oestrogen-receptor agonist in bone (protecting against fracture) but an antagonist in breast tissue.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why is HRT not first-line for osteoporosis on its own?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: It carries risks of breast/endometrial cancer, VTE and stroke. It is mainly reserved for younger postmenopausal women (<60 or within 10 years of menopause) who ALSO need relief of vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A 52-year-old woman with troublesome hot flushes and low bone density wants a treatment covering both. What is reasonable?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: HRT is appropriate here - she is within 10 years of menopause, and HRT both relieves vasomotor symptoms and provides antiresorptive bone protection. For osteoporosis alone (no flushes) a bisphosphonate would be preferred first-line.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is raloxifene used for, and what two risks does it reduce?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Postmenopausal osteoporosis. It reduces the risk of VERTEBRAL fractures and reduces breast-cancer risk (antagonist in breast).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Does raloxifene help hot flushes?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: No - it does not help and may WORSEN vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes) and can cause leg cramps. It is unsuitable for a woman whose main problem is flushes.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the key shared serious risk of both HRT and raloxifene?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Venous thromboembolism (VTE). Both increase VTE risk, so a personal history of VTE is a contraindication.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What additional vascular risk does raloxifene carry, and what practical advice follows?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Increased risk of FATAL stroke. It should be stopped before and during prolonged immobilisation (e.g. surgery, long-haul travel, bed rest) because of the raised thrombotic/stroke risk.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A woman with an intact uterus is started on HRT. What must be added and why?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: A progestogen. Unopposed oestrogen stimulates the endometrium and causes endometrial cancer, so a progestogen is added to protect the endometrium. Oestrogen alone is only used after hysterectomy.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: List key contraindications to HRT / raloxifene.
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: History of VTE; oestrogen-dependent cancer (e.g. breast); undiagnosed vaginal bleeding (investigate first); active liver disease.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: A woman on HRT reports new vaginal bleeding. What is the priority?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Investigate the bleeding before continuing - undiagnosed vaginal bleeding must be worked up to exclude endometrial cancer. Do not assume it is a benign side effect.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What extra cancer risks does HRT add beyond VTE?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Increased risk of breast cancer and (if oestrogen is unopposed) endometrial cancer, plus increased stroke risk.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the role of calcium and vitamin D in osteoporosis management?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: They are a foundational adjunct to ALL osteoporosis therapies - calcium provides the substrate and vitamin D drives its absorption, needed for bone mineralisation and to suppress secondary hyperparathyroidism.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: How is vitamin D activated to its active form?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Vitamin D is a pro-hormone: it is activated first by the liver, then by the kidney, to active vitamin D. The active form increases intestinal calcium absorption.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Why must a patient be calcium/vitamin D replete before or alongside a bisphosphonate or denosumab?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: If the patient is calcium/vitamin D deplete, antiresorptives work poorly AND can precipitate hypocalcaemia. So correct/co-prescribe calcium and vitamin D.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Besides osteoporosis adjunct use, name other indications for calcium + vitamin D.
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Vitamin D deficiency and osteomalacia, and in the housebound/elderly and patients with chronic kidney disease who are at risk of deficiency and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the main GI side effect of calcium supplements?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Constipation (and general GI upset).

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What can happen if calcium/vitamin D is over-supplemented?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria. Excessive calcium (classically with alkali/antacids) can cause milk-alkali syndrome. Hypercalcaemia is a contraindication to further supplementation.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: Which drugs have their absorption reduced by calcium, and what is the practical fix?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Levothyroxine, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, iron and oral bisphosphonates. Separate the doses in time - e.g. take levothyroxine about 4 hours apart from calcium.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What should be monitored with long-term or high-dose calcium/vitamin D, especially in renal impairment?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Plasma calcium, to detect hypercalcaemia/hypercalciuria.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is burosumab and how does it work?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: A monoclonal anti-FGF23 antibody. In X-linked hypophosphataemia (XLH), excess FGF23 causes renal phosphate wasting and impairs vitamin D activation; blocking FGF23 restores renal phosphate reabsorption and vitamin D activation, improving bone mineralisation.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What conditions is burosumab used for?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets/osteomalacia (XLH) and tumour-induced osteomalacia. It is a specialist, targeted therapy given as a weight-based subcutaneous injection.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What must be done before starting burosumab, and why?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Stop conventional oral phosphate and active vitamin D first - continuing them alongside burosumab risks hyperphosphataemia.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What is the main side effect of over-treatment with burosumab, and what does it lead to?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Hyperphosphataemia, which if sustained can cause nephrocalcinosis. Injection-site reactions also occur.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: What monitoring is required on burosumab?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Regular FASTING serum phosphate (titrate dose to avoid hyperphosphataemia) and screening for nephrocalcinosis with renal ultrasound.

pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.front: In which patients should burosumab be avoided?
pharmacology__Rheumatology & Musculoskel.back: Those with severe renal impairment (and it must not be co-given with oral phosphate or active vitamin D).

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: A patient on chemotherapy attends A&E with a temperature of 38.5°C and neutrophils of 0.3 x10⁹/L. What must you do, and how quickly?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: This is neutropenic sepsis, an oncological emergency. Give IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam) within 1 hour. Do NOT wait for the neutrophil count, cultures or specialist review before starting.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Before starting cytotoxic chemotherapy in a young patient, what important issue should you raise regarding future family planning?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Many cytotoxics cause infertility. Fertility preservation (e.g. sperm/egg/embryo storage) should be offered and discussed BEFORE chemotherapy is started, as damage may be permanent.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: What are the shared toxicities you should warn a patient about before starting almost any cytotoxic chemotherapy?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Myelosuppression (infection, bleeding, anaemia), mucositis, alopecia, nausea and vomiting, infertility, and a small long-term risk of second malignancies. Anti-emetic prophylaxis is chosen according to how emetogenic the regimen is.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: A patient with a bulky lymphoma develops high potassium, high phosphate, high urate, low calcium and an acute kidney injury shortly after starting chemotherapy. What is this and how is it prevented?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Tumour lysis syndrome, from rapid tumour cell breakdown (especially bulky/haematological tumours). Prevent with IV hydration plus allopurinol or rasburicase.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Which class of vaccine is contraindicated in a patient receiving chemotherapy?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Live vaccines (e.g. MMR, yellow fever, live attenuated influenza, BCG) are contraindicated during chemotherapy because immunosuppression risks disseminated infection.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: How do alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide and chlorambucil kill cancer cells?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: They add alkyl groups to DNA and cross-link the DNA strands, preventing replication. This is cytotoxic and cell-cycle non-specific.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Besides cancer, what non-oncological role does cyclophosphamide have?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: It is used as a potent immunosuppressant in severe autoimmune disease, e.g. severe/organ-threatening lupus and vasculitis.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: A patient on high-dose cyclophosphamide develops visible haematuria. What is the mechanism and how is it prevented?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Haemorrhagic cystitis caused by the toxic metabolite acrolein irritating the bladder. Prevent with MESNA plus generous hydration. There is also a late risk of bladder cancer.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: What is MESNA given with cyclophosphamide (or ifosfamide) for?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: MESNA binds and detoxifies acrolein in the urine, protecting the bladder from haemorrhagic cystitis. It is given with hydration at higher doses.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: A patient on high-dose cyclophosphamide develops hyponatraemia with concentrated urine. What is the likely cause?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: SIADH, which high-dose cyclophosphamide can precipitate, causing water retention and dilutional hyponatraemia.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Why should a patient taking procarbazine avoid tyramine-rich foods (mature cheese, cured meats) and sympathomimetics?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Procarbazine is a weak MAO inhibitor, so tyramine or sympathomimetics can trigger a hypertensive crisis.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: What reaction can occur if a patient drinks alcohol while taking procarbazine?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: A disulfiram-like reaction (flushing, headache, nausea, tachycardia), so alcohol should be avoided.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Which alkylating agent is classically associated with pulmonary fibrosis, and what is this nicknamed?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Busulfan, causing 'busulfan lung' (progressive pulmonary fibrosis).

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Which alkylating agent is a component of the ABVD regimen for Hodgkin lymphoma?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Dacarbazine (the 'D' in ABVD: adriamycin/doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine).

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: How do platinum compounds such as cisplatin exert their cytotoxic effect?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: They form DNA cross-links (similar to alkylating agents), blocking DNA replication and killing the cell.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Which platinum-based curative regimen is used for testicular cancer, and what does it contain?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: BEP: bleomycin, etoposide and cisplatin. It is curative in many testicular germ cell tumours.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: What are the characteristic dose-limiting toxicities of cisplatin?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity (tinnitus and hearing loss), peripheral neuropathy, severe nausea and vomiting, and hypomagnesaemia from renal tubular magnesium wasting.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: How do you reduce the risk of cisplatin nephrotoxicity when giving it?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Give aggressive IV hydration (sometimes with mannitol) before, during and after the infusion, and monitor renal function and magnesium.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Cisplatin is highly emetogenic. What anti-emetic prophylaxis should be given?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Triple therapy: a 5-HT3 antagonist (e.g. ondansetron) plus dexamethasone plus an NK1 antagonist (e.g. aprepitant).

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: How does carboplatin's toxicity profile differ from cisplatin's, and how is it dosed?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Carboplatin is 'kinder' - its main toxicity is myelosuppression, with much less nephro-, oto- and neurotoxicity. It is dosed according to renal function (Calvert/AUC formula).

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: A patient on oxaliplatin reports painful tingling in the hands and throat triggered by touching cold objects or drinks. What is this?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Oxaliplatin's characteristic cold-induced peripheral neuropathy. Patients are advised to avoid cold exposure during and after infusion.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Which drugs increase the nephrotoxic and ototoxic risk of cisplatin when co-prescribed?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Aminoglycosides, vancomycin, loop diuretics and amphotericin - all add to nephro-/ototoxicity, so combine with caution and monitor closely.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: What monitoring is essential in a patient receiving cisplatin?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Renal function, serum magnesium and audiometry (hearing), plus FBC. Nephro-, oto- and neurotoxicity are all dose-related.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: How do antimetabolites like methotrexate and 5-FU stop cancer cells dividing?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: They mimic normal metabolites (folate/nucleosides) and block the enzymes of DNA/RNA synthesis - methotrexate is an antifolate; 5-FU/capecitabine block thymidylate synthase.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: After high-dose methotrexate, what 'rescue' agent is given and why?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Folinic acid ('leucovorin') rescue - it bypasses the folate blockade to protect normal cells from methotrexate toxicity.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Why is high-dose methotrexate avoided in patients with renal impairment or a large pleural effusion/ascites?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Methotrexate is renally cleared and accumulates in third-space fluid (effusions/ascites), from which it slowly re-releases - both cause delayed, severe toxicity (pancytopenia, mucositis).

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Besides marrow and mucosa, which two organ toxicities are characteristic of methotrexate?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Pneumonitis (dry cough, breathlessness) and hepatotoxicity.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Which common drugs dangerously increase methotrexate toxicity, and what is the consequence?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: NSAIDs/aspirin, trimethoprim/co-trimoxazole, penicillins and PPIs reduce methotrexate clearance, risking fatal pancytopenia. This is a key PSA prescribing error to avoid.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: What test is mandatory before starting 5-FU or capecitabine, and why (MHRA)?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: DPYD (DPD) genotyping. DPD enzyme deficiency causes severe or fatal fluoropyrimidine toxicity, so testing is required before starting.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: A patient on 5-FU develops chest pain with ischaemic ECG changes despite normal coronaries. What is the likely cause?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: 5-FU-induced coronary vasospasm, which can mimic acute coronary syndrome. The drug should be stopped.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: A patient on capecitabine develops painful red, peeling, tender palms and soles. What is this?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Hand-foot syndrome (palmar-plantar erythrodysaesthesia), a characteristic capecitabine toxicity managed with dose reduction and emollients.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: What supplements must be given with pemetrexed and why?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Folic acid and vitamin B12 supplementation, which reduce its myelosuppression and mucositis.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: What toxicities are characteristic of cytarabine?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Conjunctivitis and cerebellar toxicity (ataxia, dysarthria, nystagmus), in addition to marrow suppression.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: What happens to the INR when a fluoropyrimidine (5-FU/capecitabine) is given to a patient on warfarin?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: The INR rises, increasing bleeding risk - monitor INR closely.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: How do taxanes such as paclitaxel and docetaxel work?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: They stabilise microtubules and prevent their breakdown, so the mitotic spindle cannot disassemble - cells arrest in mitosis (M-phase) and die.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Why are patients premedicated with corticosteroids and antihistamines before paclitaxel or docetaxel?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: To prevent hypersensitivity/infusion reactions caused by the drug's solvent. Nab-paclitaxel is solvent-free, so it needs no routine premedication.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: What is the main dose-limiting non-marrow toxicity of the taxanes?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Peripheral neuropathy (sensory), alongside neutropenia. Also seen: alopecia, arthralgia/myalgia, and fluid retention (particularly docetaxel).

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: How do vinca alkaloids such as vincristine work, and how does this contrast with taxanes?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: They inhibit microtubule assembly (bind tubulin, preventing spindle formation), arresting mitosis - the opposite action to taxanes, which stabilise microtubules.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: What is the dose-limiting toxicity of vincristine, and how does it present?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Peripheral neuropathy - sensory first, then motor and autonomic (constipation/ileus). Notably vincristine relatively spares the bone marrow.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: How does vinblastine's toxicity differ from vincristine's?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Vinblastine causes more myelosuppression with relatively less neuropathy - the reverse of vincristine, which is neurotoxic but marrow-sparing.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: By which route must vincristine NEVER be given, and why?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Vincristine must be given IV only. Intrathecal administration is fatal - an NHS never-event - so it is dispensed and labelled specifically to prevent this error.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: A vinca alkaloid infusion leaks into the surrounding tissue at the cannula site. Why does this matter?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Vinca alkaloids are vesicants - extravasation causes severe local tissue damage. Manage with a warm compress and hyaluronidase.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: What is the mechanism of action of the anthracyclines (e.g. doxorubicin)?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: They intercalate into DNA and inhibit topoisomerase II, and also generate iron-mediated free radicals (reactive oxygen species) -> DNA damage. The free-radical mechanism also underlies their cardiotoxicity.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Name the anthracycline chemotherapy agents.
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Doxorubicin, epirubicin, daunorubicin and idarubicin. They form the backbone of many breast cancer, lymphoma, leukaemia and sarcoma regimens.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: What is the signature dose-limiting toxicity of the anthracyclines?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Dose-dependent cardiotoxicity - a cardiomyopathy leading to heart failure. It can be acute or appear years after treatment, and risk rises with the cumulative lifetime dose.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: A patient is starting doxorubicin. What cardiac monitoring is required before and during treatment?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Assess cardiac function (ejection fraction by echo or MUGA scan) before starting and monitor during treatment. Also track the cumulative lifetime dose, as cardiotoxicity is dose-related.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Roughly what cumulative lifetime dose of doxorubicin is associated with a marked rise in cardiotoxicity risk?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Around 450-550 mg/m2. Cardiotoxicity is dose-related, so the cumulative dose is tracked across a patient's lifetime and the drug avoided once this threshold is approached.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: What agent can be given to reduce anthracycline cardiotoxicity, and how does it work?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Dexrazoxane - an iron chelator. By chelating iron it reduces free-radical formation in the heart. Liposomal formulations of doxorubicin also lower cardiac risk.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Why are anthracyclines contraindicated in a patient with significant cardiac impairment or a low ejection fraction?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Because their signature toxicity is a dose-dependent cardiomyopathy/heart failure. Poor baseline cardiac function greatly increases the risk of decompensation, so the drug is contraindicated.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: A patient on doxorubicin is alarmed that their urine has turned red. What do you tell them?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Red discolouration of the urine is a harmless, expected effect of doxorubicin and settles after treatment. It is not haematuria and needs no action.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Why must anthracyclines be given with great care to avoid extravasation?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: They are severe vesicants - leakage from the vein causes tissue necrosis. Extravasation is managed with a cold compress and dexrazoxane.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Besides cardiotoxicity, list the other distinctive side effects of anthracyclines a student should recognise.
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Myelosuppression, mucositis, alopecia, harmless red urine, and severe vesicant extravasation injury (tissue necrosis).

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: How do topoisomerase inhibitors kill cancer cells, and which enzyme does each target?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: They inhibit topoisomerase enzymes that relieve DNA supercoiling, causing DNA strand breaks. Etoposide targets topoisomerase II; irinotecan and topotecan target topoisomerase I.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Match each topoisomerase inhibitor to a typical cancer: etoposide, irinotecan, topotecan.
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Etoposide - small-cell lung cancer, lymphomas and testicular cancer; irinotecan - colorectal cancer; topotecan - ovarian cancer.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Irinotecan is a prodrug. What is its active metabolite, and which patients get more toxicity?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Irinotecan is converted to the active metabolite SN-38. Patients with reduced UGT1A1 activity (e.g. Gilbert's syndrome variants) clear SN-38 poorly and suffer more toxicity.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: A patient develops profuse diarrhoea and sweating during an irinotecan infusion. What type is this and how is it treated?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: This is acute cholinergic diarrhoea (a cholinergic syndrome). It is treated with atropine.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: A patient develops severe diarrhoea several days after an irinotecan dose. How is this delayed diarrhoea managed?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Delayed irinotecan diarrhoea is treated with high-dose loperamide. It can be severe and life-threatening, so prompt aggressive treatment is important.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Why should atropine be kept ready when giving irinotecan?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Irinotecan can cause an acute cholinergic syndrome with diarrhoea (also sweating, cramps, salivation) during or soon after the infusion, which is reversed with atropine.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: What happens if etoposide is infused too quickly?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Rapid infusion can cause hypotension. It should therefore be given as a slow infusion with blood pressure monitoring.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Which topoisomerase inhibitor carries a recognised risk of secondary acute myeloid leukaemia?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Etoposide (a topoisomerase II inhibitor) is associated with a secondary/treatment-related AML - a 'topo-II' leukaemia.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: What is the mechanism of bleomycin?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: It causes free-radical DNA strand breaks, which is cytotoxic. Unusually for a cytotoxic, it produces minimal myelosuppression.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: In which cancers is bleomycin used?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Hodgkin lymphoma (as part of the ABVD regimen) and germ-cell/testicular tumours.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: What makes bleomycin unusual among cytotoxics with regard to the bone marrow?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: It causes minimal myelosuppression - very little marrow toxicity compared with most chemotherapy agents.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: What is the signature dose-limiting toxicity of bleomycin?
pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.back: Pulmonary fibrosis / pneumonitis. It is dose-related, so the cumulative dose is tracked and lung function (PFTs) monitored.

pharmacology__Oncology & Immunosuppressi.front: Why must future anaesthetists or ITU teams be warned about a patient's previous bleomycin exposure?
